item.content:encoded:
Fitzy already took you through the highlights (such as they were) from yesterday's press conference. We've gotten plenty used to the front office telling us about how pained they are by failing to meet their goals, so there wasn't much actual news in that sense. But we did get some actual substantive information regarding Roman Anthony. After a lost season that saw him bow out of the playoffs in the middle of the first game, Anthony will not need surgery on his mysteriously strained hand. "What we've been told [is] that we don't even know what surgery we would do," said Craig Breslow. And, yeah, that sentence doesn't inspire much confidence in me, either. (Sean McAdam, MassLive)
Roman Anthony having a healthy and productive 2027 season is key to the Red Sox having a productive 2027 season. But considering that the team's biggest issue is home run power, he won't be able to fix things on his own. The Red Sox know that they need to add power to the lineup, but knowing something and doing something are two different things. "Despite identifying power as a priority entering last offseason, the Red Sox' lineup took a step backward. In 2025, the Sox hit 186 homers (15th in MLB), had a .324 on-base percentage (eighth), and a .421 slugging percentage (ninth). This year, the Red Sox hit 163 homers (26th), had a .319 OBP (12th), and slugged .398 (20th)." (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)
But maybe they already have some more power in the organization in the form of Curtis Mead, whom the Red Sox appear to be penciling in at second base as they head into the offseason. "He was acquired for a reason. You see the numbers that kind of project at least toward a 30-home run season. And adding that, we were really excited about that," said Chad Tracy. (Chris Cotillo, MassLive)
The Sox best source of power in 2026, Willson Contreras, didn't sound too happy the last time he spoke to the media, following the Sox' embarrassing exit from the playoffs. But the Sox brass is confident they smoothed things over with the slugger after Tracy and Breslow met with him for over two hours on Sunday. "We actually had a great conversation, Trace and I, with Willson," Breslow said. "Many of those [details] I will keep private just to protect or just to kind of preserve the relationship that we have. But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things. And Willson would be the right person to ask directly, but he spoke very, very highly of his time here, how much he's looking forward to 2027, and the way that he and his family appreciated the Red Sox." (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
The source of Contreras' unhappiness seemed to primarily be the early hook Tracy employed in removing Sonny Gray from Game 2 against the Yankees, a decision that Tracy is owning. "I do trust Sonny Gray," Tracy said. "I do trust the guys in the bullpen as well. So again, I think the easiest way to say is it was my call. It's my decision. It went south. I think the biggest thing for me coming into this was maybe dispelling any notion of people thinking that decisions get made prior to the game or with a piece of paper or with any computer. If I can do anything just to dispel that, say, those decisions are always going to fall on me." (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
At least Contreras can comfort himself with the fact that he's a finalist for the Hank Aaron Award. The award, given to the player who had the most outstanding offensive season is, for some bizarre reason, voted on by the fans. So if you want to throw some love Willson's way, you can cast your ballot online. (MLB.com)

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox's Sonny Gray Reportedly Was Investigated by MLB Over Potential Use of Sticky Substance
Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray drew some attention on social media for appearing to have a sticky substance on his neck during last week's wild card loss to the New York Yankees.
However, Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com reported that MLB investigated the matter, and Gray "obviously passed in-game standard checks without penalty, which suggests he is in the clear." Cotillo added that "any discipline would likely have been levied by now anyway."
Regardless of whether Gray tried to use a sticky substance, it didn't help the Red Sox much as they suffered a 9-2 loss to get swept out of the playoffs. Gray lasted 4.2 innings and gave up two earned runs on six hits with five strikeouts.
After the game, Gray didn't address the substance on his neck, but he made it clear that he wasn't happy with being pulled from the game after throwing just 70 pitches.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that's a fact," Gray told reporters. "I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment. ... I felt good. I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I think I got clipped for a solo home run and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I'm frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions."
On Monday, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy took the blame for his quick hooks of Payton Tolle in Game 1 and Gray in Game 2.
"The decisions are mine," Tracy said, per Ian Browne of MLB.com. "Not one time since I've been here has anybody scripted a game or has anybody told me to use this number right here to decide in this inning. Those decisions, they're mine. So, as far as that specific one [in Game 2 with Gray], that didn't, obviously, go great. That falls on me. Do we have data analytics? Of course we do. Everybody does. Is somebody standing there pushing me, saying you need to do this, this, and this? Absolutely not."
While Gray likely won't face punishment for the questionable substance, he will have to spend the entire offseason wondering what could have been if Tracy allowed him to finish off his playoff start against the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Year in Review 2026: Looking Back at Willson Contreras' Season originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Red Sox reached the postseason in spite of long-term injuries to Garrett Crochet and Roman Anthony, and much of that is owed to the team's offseason additions.
Willson Contreras, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez all delivered for Boston, while Caleb Durbin's hot streak after a rough start coincided with the team's summer surge.
Contreras in particular was often the heartbeat of the lineup for the Red Sox, both before their July win streak and deep into the summer.
Here's a look back at Contreras' first season in Boston.
Red Sox Year in Review 2026: Willson Contreras
There is no doubt Contreras' first season with the Red Sox was a success, even if the year didn't end the way the organization envisioned.
The 34-year-old, acquired in a late December trade with the Cardinals, posted the highest-WAR season of his career, hit a career-high 27 home runs and led all qualified Red Sox hitters in OPS. Contreras not only mashed, but he walked more than he had in any other season.
Contreras is no stranger to nagging injuries, and he would miss time down the stretch with a hamstring issue before a minor hand injury from a hit-by-pitch popped up. Still, in a season of wild ups and downs for the team, he was remarkably consistent. Contreras posted an OPS of at least .850 in each of the season's first four months, and he carried an above-average OPS+ in all six months, albeit over a limited sample size in September.
For what the Red Sox gave up to get him, Contreras more than fulfilled expectations in 2026.
Willson Contreras' Most Memorable Moment
Contreras had plenty of highlights for the Red Sox in 2026, but this monster 452-foot home run against the Giants may lead the way:
Contreras' 3-run moonshot off Logan Webb sailed over the Green Monster and gave the Red Sox a 3-1 lead, setting the stage for a Friday night win. The Red Sox were appropriately wearing their City Connect Green Monster-themed uniforms, and Contreras celebrated with an emphatic bat flip.
Willson Contreras' Stats for 2026 Season
| Games | AVG | HR | RBI | OPS | H | fWAR |
| 130 | .275 | 27 | 81 | .901 | 123 | 4.0 |
Contreras missed 32 games but still produced a full season's worth of numbers, batting .275 with 27 home runs and a .901 OPS. The 34-year-old's OPS ranked second among all qualified hitters in the AL, as did his .386 on-base percentage.
With 27 home runs, Contreras set a new career-high even while missing most of September.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round in embarrassing fashion. A rotation that had been so good all season was exposed by an injured New York team, and a weak offense was exposed.
Sonny Gray was a big part of the Red Sox in-season turnaround. However, he was lifted after just 4.2 innings in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series after giving up two runs. The floodgates opened after that, and Boston lost.
However, there is an interesting caveat to this. Gray was investigated by MLB for allegedly using sticky stuff in his Game 2 start, according to MassLive’s Chris Cotillo.
What Did Boston Red Sox’ Sonny Gray Do?
Gray drew some attention on social media for appearing to have a sticky substance on his neck. MLB reportedly investigated this, but according to Cotillo, he should be fine.
“I’m told MLB looked into Sonny Gray potentially using sticky stuff in his Game 2 start in the Bronx last week — but he obviously passed in-game standard checks without penalty, which suggests he is in the clear,” Cotillo wrote. “Any discipline would likely have been levied by now anyway.”
Whether or not Gray used a sticky substance, that didn’t seem to affect Boston’s chances of winning. The Red Sox lost that game 9-2. While Gray didn’t address the substance on his neck during his postgame press conference, he was upset for other reasons.
Gray was pulled from his start at 70 pitches, and he was clearly not happy.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time,” Gray said. “I think that’s a fact. I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment. … I felt good. I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I think I got clipped for a solo home run and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I’m frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions.”
Gray won’t face punishment for the alleged sticky stuff, but that start may have further ramifications.
What Does This Mean for Gray?
The three-time All-Star enjoyed a career renaissance, winning a league-high and career-high 18 games. He also pitched to a 2.72 ERA with 149 strikeouts in 169 innings. He was arguably Boston’s best starter in a deep rotation.
It was a great trade for Boston, who traded Richard Fitts and some minor leaguers for the veteran pitcher.
However, Gray is turning 37 years old at the beginning of November, with a team option looming. He has a $30 million option with a $10 million buyout. The Red Sox are increasingly likely to decline that option and try to negotiate a new contract with Gray.
However, after the quick hook he got in Game 2 and the subsequent reaction, it’s fair to wonder if Gray wants to come back to Boston.
This might be the question of the offseason for Boston as a lockout looms.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] No matter how Craig Breslow tries to frame it, the Red Sox haven’t proven anything under his watch - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Christopher L Gasper
item.description: We’ll always have 27-3 … That should be the epitaph for the 2026 Red Sox, who held their season sign-off press conference at reliably available in October Fenway Park on Monday. item.content:encoded:
We’ll always have 27-3 …
That should be the epitaph for the 2026 Red Sox, who held their season sign-off press conference at reliably available in October Fenway Park on Monday.
Here’s the state of the Red Sox after another blink-and-you-missed-it postseason cameo that ended with Boston getting obliterated, 18-2, by the Yankees in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series: The team’s best starting pitcher, Sonny Gray, isn’t granted enough leeway. The chief baseball officer, Craig Breslow, receives unlimited latitude and gratitude, even though he hasn’t delivered yet on any of the stated goals of the Sox during his three-season tenure: a deep playoff run, earnestly contending for the AL East title, and winning 90-plus games.
Rarely have baseball bosses been afforded so much credit for underdelivering on performance pledges. Breslow boasts more option years picked up on his contract (two, 2029 and 2030) than playoff series wins (zero) as Sox CBO. Yet, he’s a home run hire in the eyes of ownership, the Golden Child. Bres has constructed playoff teams each of the last two seasons. But Breslow is the Roman Anthony of baseball executives. He possesses enviable potential and promise and has displayed flashes of brilliance on the job. But he hasn’t proven it yet.
Breslow’s Sox remain stuck in a liminal state between playoff field seat-filler and genuine World Series contention. They’ve finished third in the AL East all three years of the Breslow Era. Like the postseason, they’ve failed to advance.
Breslow sounded downright Dan Duquette-esque (“More days in first place …) while attempting to ambivalently own another abbreviated postseason. He utters all the appropriate words, but can’t resist garnishing them with justifications, rationalizations, and qualifiers.
The clearest sign of that is how Breslow characterized the 32-5 stretch, highlighted by the outrageous fortune of a 27-3 run, that saved our summer and the Red Sox season. After that hardball deliverance, the Sox went 23-26, including the postseason, and averaged a major league-low 3.55 runs per game.
He was asked if such an anomalous sample of overperformance complicated evaluating the team.
“I think I’d also maybe push back a bit on this was kind of 35-ish games of excellence and 127 games of mediocrity,” said Breslow. “When you think about or look at the overall totality of the record from July 1 on, it was three months of playing at I think like a 104-kind-of-win pace. Even [in] September, we certainly didn’t play as well as we did in August and July — we had a bunch of guys on the [injured list] — we were .500.
“Is that good enough? No, but I think really good teams, they go 32-5 over a stretch, and teams that are mired in mediocrity over the course of the other 125, they don’t. So, I think this was more than just a run. I think it showed some true underlying talent. But we obviously have a lot of work to get where we want to go heading into 2027.”
There are 10 teams since 1900, the ‘26 Resurrection Red Sox being one of three since the advent of divisional play in 1969, that have reeled off a 27-3 run. An organization that prides itself on dispassionate data-based evaluations should view it as the outlier of all outliers.
Instead, they keep leaning into the sugar rush of confirming their own team-building prowess. The Sox have pegged the future of their organization on the Midsummer Mirage when assorted Seiglers, Sogards, Chengs, and Joneses couldn’t lose if they tried, and Andruw Monasterio channeled Nomar Garciaparra to erase a 32-46 start. Then, the contender carriage turned back into a Run Prevention 2.0 pumpkin.
At this same year-end press conference in 2024, Breslow said, “It’s time to deliver the team that is capable of winning the AL East [and] making a deep playoff run.” Last year, he offered, “This window of contention is upon us.”
This time, Breslow offered Duquette-esque explanations.
⋅ He said the Sox “own the struggles that we had in the postseason,” but mentioned that both games of the Wild Card Series with the Yankees were “very, very close for the first five innings or so before they got away late.” Sure, and the Celtics would’ve beaten the 76ers if they stopped the series after 4½ games.
⋅ Breslow acknowledged that “our offense was inconsistent,” but that it was important to “call out” seven players set career-highs in home runs, a list that presumably includes Mickey Gasper (10), Monasterio (6), Sogard (5), and Seigler (3).
⋅ He pointed to sweeps of the Yankees and Rays during the 32-5 run as partial proof that the 87-75 Sox were on par with their AL East rivals.
⋅ He referenced missing ace Garrett Crochet from late April until a bumpy relief appearance in Game 2, and Anthony’s recurring ring finger/wrist malady while discussing win total projections. Neither of those players was available during the 32-5 midsummer dream he championed.
Perhaps the Sox are correct. Breslow is a visionary who will build the Next Great Red Sox Team. However, such confidence seems — like the de facto extension they handed him — premature.
At spring training in February, Breslow said, “2026 is a really important season for us, for our fans. They deserve kind of more.”
When is more coming instead of the Sox settling for more of the same and labeling it success?
Christopher L. Gasper is a Globe columnist. He can be reached at christopher.gasper@globe.com. Follow him @cgasper and on Instagram @cgaspersports.

item.title: [Orlando Sentinel] Craig Breslow and Chad Tracy push back that analytics drove Red Sox postseason decisions
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: By KYLE HIGHTOWER After getting eliminated from the playoffs by the rival New York Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year, several Boston Red Sox players questioned the role analytics played in some in-game decisions. item.content:encoded:
By KYLE HIGHTOWER
After getting eliminated from the playoffs by the rival New York Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year, several Boston Red Sox players questioned the role analytics played in some in-game decisions.
First baseman Willson Contreras was one of the loudest among those voices.
“It’s not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that’s telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” Contreras said last week after the Red Sox pulled both their starting pitchers in the fifth inning of close games against New York only to get outscored 18-2 overall.
On Monday, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy were adamant there is no franchise-wide directive regarding how analytics are used on or off the field.
“I would push back on the notion that somehow the role of the scout or the importance of the scout has been diminished in this organization. That’s not the case,” Breslow said. “We are constantly looking at how we can make the best decisions, whether those are players that we acquire or invest in, or the way that we create a roster. … So I think it’s important that I have the chance to say that the value of scouts, the role that they fill here, it’s not diminished, it is not going away.”
The Red Sox were riding a wave of optimism after Tracy took over when Alex Cora was fired and then guided the team on a 32-5 run this summer that led Boston back to the postseason. The turnaround included Sonny Gray’s ascension to No. 1 starter after Garrett Crochet was sidelined with left shoulder inflammation and spent the next five-plus months recovering.
But it was Gray who was removed after only 70 pitches and 4 2/3 innings with Boston trailing 1-0 in Game 2 against the Yankees.
New York proceeded to tee off against what had been baseball’s best bullpen during the regular season, and the Yankees pulled away for a 9-2 victory.
Tracy also came under scrutiny after Boston’s 9-0 defeat in the opener, when he yanked rookie starter Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings and 83 pitches in a 1-0 game.
Gray, who went 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA during the regular season to tie for most wins in the majors and lead the American League in winning percentage, said he “would have liked to have been trusted in that moment.”
Asked directly if he’d ever gotten any input from the front office regarding his decisions this season or whether there was any predetermined script the team used, Tracy quickly pushed back.
“(Those) decisions are mine. We have information, just like all the other 29 teams have information. Everybody has that,” Tracy said. “But not one time since I’ve been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me use this number right here to decide in this inning. Those decisions, they’re mine.”
But he also made it clear he isn’t turning a deaf ear to his players’ concerns. That included meeting for multiple hours with Contreras in the days after his comments following the Game 2 loss.
“I have a very good working relationship with him and I’ve had numerous conversations with him throughout the course of the year,” Tracy said. “But I was able to talk to him, it’s in a fine place while also understanding his feelings.”
No surgery scheduled for Anthony
Breslow said it’s still not yet clear whether Roman Anthony will need surgery or if an operation would help the injury that caused him to make a premature exit from the postseason.
Anthony left Game 1 against the Yankees and was removed from Boston’s roster before the Red Sox were eliminated in Game 2 after he sustained a new right hand injury during the series opener.
Anthony was sidelined from early May to late August with an injury to the same hand.
“Still working through what the kind of right course of treatment is,” Breslow said. “At this point, it doesn’t seem that there’s any type of surgical intervention, that rest is likely the best path to recovery.”
___

item.content:encoded:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Just a few days after the Red Sox’ roller-coaster 2026 season came to an end in the Bronx, manager Chad Tracy, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow, and president/CEO Sam Kennedy addressed the media at Fenway Park.
Despite Boston’s impressive 32-5 surge in the summer and mid-year turnaround, the theme of Monday’s press conference was one of disappointment.
“The way it ended Wednesday night in New York was painful and deeply disappointing to all of us,” Kennedy said.
Here are five takeaways from Monday’s presser:
Breslow met with Willson Contreras for two hours after ‘computers’ comment
Beyond the disappointment of the Red Sox’ season coming to a close with a listless showing against the Yankees last week, Wednesday’s postgame press conferences with Red Sox players in New York were rife with grievances and head scratches from a few veterans.
First baseman Willson Contreras raised a few eyebrows when he seemingly insinuated that the Red Sox organization has been too reliant on data and analytics — which he believes doesn’t always translate to success out on the field, especially in October.
“It’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” Contreras said. “The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I’ll state it like that.”
Breslow was asked directly about Contreras’ comments and whether or not he’s had discussions with the veteran over the state of Boston’s baseball operations.
“I saw Willson’s comments,” Breslow said. “My interpretation is a little bit different than there are clearly things that he wants fixed and changed.”
Before the players went their separate ways to begin the offseason, Breslow said that he had an extended conversation with both Contreras and Tracy on Sunday.
“We met for over two hours and we talked about a host of things,” Breslow said. “Many of those I will keep private just to kind of preserve the relationship that we have. But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things.
“Willson would be the right person to ask directly, but he spoke very, very highly of his time here, how much he’s looking forward to 2027 and the way that he and his family appreciated the Red Sox.”
Tracy says ‘decisions are mine’ with managing pitching staff, roster
Chad Tracy earned Boston’s full-time managerial title this fall after righting the ship with this roster.
But the Red Sox manager found himself in hot water during Boston’s two-game series against New York when it came to quick hooks with his starting pitching.
A strong rotation was a foundational piece in the Red Sox’ success this season. But Tracy opted to pull both Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4.2 innings of work in Games 1 and 2, respectively, against New York.
At the time, both righties had only given up one run and kept Boston in close contests in the Bronx, only for the Yankees to feast on the Red Sox bullpen.
In both games, Tracy immediately turned to lefty Erik Miller to close out the fifth inning — with the southpaw giving up a solo shot to Ben Rice in Game 1 and surrendering an RBI single to Cody Bellinger in Game 2.
Tracy’s approach to Boston’s pitching staff in the playoffs raised questions over whether or not there was a set plan or “script” in place for the Red Sox to turn to their bullpen immediately — rather than let their starters face New York’s line for a third time through the order.
Tracy pushed back against that sentiment, adding that all of Boston’s decisions on the field last week were his and his alone.
“Not one time since I’ve been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me, ‘Use this number right here to decide in this inning,’” Tracy said. “Those decisions are mine. As far as that specific one, my decision. That obviously didn’t go great, and that falls on me.
“Do we have data and analytics? Of course we do. Everybody does. Is somebody standing there pushing me saying, ‘You have to do this, this and this?’ Absolutely not.”
Boston’s bullpen was also a strength all year long, only for it to splinter in the postseason. While Tolle and Gray allowed two earned runs over their 9.1 innings of work, Boston’s relievers coughed up 15 earned runs over 6.2 innings.
“Believe me, I see both sides and I don’t need to get too deep into defending this or that because I certainly could have gone the other way with that and that could have gone well,” Tracy said. “We wouldn’t even be having this conversation. But I do trust Sonny Gray and I do trust the guys in the bullpen as well.
“There is a factor of having a really strong bullpen that was pretty heavily left-handed in our sense. Was there scripts? No, there wasn’t anything scripted out. Just games got to certain points where you felt like it was time to go. We didn’t also want to ignore that we had some pretty good arms in our bullpen if we could get there and use those.”
Clearing the air with Gray
Tracy’s decision to pull Gray after just 4.2 innings of work in Game 2 clearly rankled the 36-year-old veteran once Boston’s season came to an end.
“I would have liked to be trusted in that moment,” Gray declared after Boston’s loss on Wednesday.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time,” Gray added after getting the hook after 70 pitches and one run allowed. “I think that’s a fact. I would have liked [for Tracy] to live or die with me in that moment, but that’s the competitor I am.”
Despite Gray’s blunt comments — including the pending free agent not exactly committing to a potential return to Boston — Tracy said on Monday that he’s hashed things out with the Red Sox’ top starter this season.
“Yes, I have had a chance to talk to [Gray]. The relationship there is good. Do I think he was wanting to stay out there? Quite obviously,” Tracy said. “But five months of relationship-building. I think there are some things that get painted sometimes, that that [ending] stained it or ruined it. No.”
“I have a very good working relationship with him and have had numerous conversations with him throughout the course of the year. I was able to talk to him and it (the relationship) is in a fine place, while also understanding his feelings [about] it.”
Offseason needs
While Boston’s pitching was strong for most of the 2026 campaign, its offense left a lot to be desired.
Boston was outscored, 18-2, and outhit, 26-7, in its two-game series in New York. But the Red Sox dealt with inconsistent offense and a dearth of power throughout the 2026 campaign.
The Red Sox closed out the 2026 season ranking 23rd in baseball in runs scored (689) and 26th in home runs (163).
Much like last offseason, Breslow said that Boston needs to prioritize adding more pop to the lineup in the coming months.
“Our offense was inconsistent. We got on base at a decent clip, but we didn’t really slug, didn’t hit a ton of home runs, and I’m not sure that we took advantage of the unique venue that we play in,” Breslow said. “So naturally, we’re going to spend some time thinking about how we can improve our offense, particularly how we build a roster that can thrive at Fenway Park.”
“There are a lot of reasons to believe the existing offense should be better in 2027,” Breslow added. “But we’re also going to do everything we can to improve beyond that.”
Injury updates
The 2026 campaign was a lost season for Roman Anthony, who missed over 100 games in the regular season due to a nagging wrist/hand injury — only for it to resurface in the playoffs and keep him out of Boston’s eventual season-ending loss last Wednesday.
Speaking on Monday, Breslow said that he doesn’t expect Anthony to need surgery this winter to correct his ailing injury.
“He’s had a bunch of follow-up appointments, including imaging,’’ Breslow said of Anthony. ”We’re still collecting information, still working through what the right course of treatment is, and at this point, it doesn’t seem as there’s any type of surgical intervention [needed], and that rest is likely the best path to recovery.”
While months of rest didn’t exactly help Anthony fully recover in time for the playoffs, Breslow said that a full offseason for Anthony should help him turn the corner — rather than a few months of intensive rehab in the summertime, as was the case from May through August of this year.
“Yes, he was trying to get healthy,” Breslow said, “but he’s also trying to do everything he could to get back on the field. And when he felt comfortable and confident, he pushed to get back on the field. … He was trying to swing and doing tee work and dry swings as soon as he could, and a couple of times, he tried and had to take a step back and would try again.
“Versus now having this window to rest it completely and make sure we don’t progress to step two until it’s completely clear.
Breslow also shared that Garrett Crochet is “fully healthy” going into the offseason — adding that Boston had no regrets over not trying to rush him back on the mound in August or September.
“There maybe could have been an opportunity to get him back on the field in what would have been an accelerated timeline, but it would have required unnecessary risk to do so, and potentially have longer-term implications,” Breslow said. “So we wanted to make sure that we had checked every box as it related to his return to play, and get his shoulder strength back up to where it was, or even better than it was at any point in 2025 when he pitched a full, healthy season.”

item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy has taken responsibility for the decision to pull Sonny Gray early in the Boston Red Sox's season-ending loss to the New York Yankees. Tracy said the move was his call after Boston fell 9-2 in Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series.
Gray was removed with two outs in the fifth inning and Boston trailing 1-0. He had thrown 70 pitches and allowed two runs on six hits with five strikeouts before Erik Miller replaced him.
The decision drew attention because Gray had put together one of the best regular seasons of his career. He finished 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA, 149 strikeouts and a 1.15 WHIP across 29 starts.
Chad Tracy says pulling Sonny Gray in Game 2 was his call.
“The biggest thing, for me, coming into this, was dispelling any notion of people thinking that decisions get made prior to the game, or with a piece of paper, or with a computer.”
(Via: @NESN) pic.twitter.com/BPW9MTR4Av
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 5, 2026
According to Foul Territory on X, Tracy said the decision was his and that he wanted to dispel the idea that decisions were made before games through a predetermined plan or computer. His comments came after Gray openly expressed frustration with the early hook following Boston's elimination.
Gray said he wanted the chance to face Cody Bellinger for a third time through the lineup. He had held opposing hitters to a .180 average the third time through during the regular season, which was the best mark among qualified American League pitchers.
The decision became more difficult to defend when Miller allowed an RBI single to Bellinger after replacing Gray. The Yankees then broke the game open with a six-run sixth inning, turning a one-run game into a 9-2 victory and completing the two-game sweep.
Boston's season ended after a dramatic turnaround that saw the Red Sox recover from a 32-46 start and make the postseason. They finished 87-75, third in the AL East behind the Tampa Bay Rays and Yankees, before being outscored 18-2 in the Wild Card Series.
Tracy's explanation now provides more context for one of the biggest decisions of Boston's short postseason run. With the Red Sox eliminated, the focus shifts to the offseason and whether the club will continue with Tracy while determining Gray's future after a standout 2026 campaign.
This story was originally published by Athlon Sports on Oct 5, 2026, where it first appeared in the MLB section. Add Athlon Sports as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Willson Contreras Met With Red Sox Manager, Exec for 2 Hours After Comments Following Yankees Loss

item.description: Willson Contreras Met With Red Sox Manager, Exec for 2 Hours After Comments Following Yankees Loss Willson Contreras didn't mince words after the Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Round, seemingly taking aim at analytics in particular after Sonny Gray was pulled in the fifth inning of Game 2 despite throwing just 70 pitches and giving up just two earned runs. "It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to d
item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras Met With Red Sox Manager, Exec for 2 Hours After Comments Following Yankees Loss
Willson Contreras didn't mince words after the Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Round, seemingly taking aim at analytics in particular after Sonny Gray was pulled in the fifth inning of Game 2 despite throwing just 70 pitches and giving up just two earned runs.
"It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to do. Because this is baseball," Contreras told reporters. "And the data is here to help us. But at the end of the day, you're gonna have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
TOP NEWS
Aaron Boone Calls Out Yankees Catcher 🗣️
Wells on Getting Thrown Out 👀
Rays Hype Drew Rasmussen
On Monday, Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said he met with Contreras and manager Chad Tracy and had a constructive discussion.
"We met for over two hours and we talked about a host of things," he told reporters. "Many of those I will keep private just to kind of preserve the relationship that we have. But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things. Willson would be the right person to ask directly, but he spoke very, very highly of his time here, how much he's looking forward to 2027 and the way that he and his family appreciated the Red Sox."
Contreras was not alone in his frustrations regarding the Gray decision, especially considering the bullpen went on to give up another seven runs.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that's a fact," Gray told reporters. "I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
Tracy, meanwhile, said the decision to pull Gray was his and wasn't a predetermined move coming from the front office or analytics department.
"The decisions are mine," he told reporters. "We have information, just like all the other 29 teams have information. Everybody has that. I've said this before: Since I've been here, do I sit in the office and talk through who's available throughout the entire season, who's available today, what's the best way to deploy them, who's down every single day? You do that. But not one time since I've been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me, use this number right here to decide in this inning. Those decisions, they're mine. So as far as that specific one, my decision that obviously didn't go great. That falls on me. Do we have data, analytics? Of course we do. Everybody does. Is somebody standing there pushing me, saying, 'You need to do this, this, and this?' Absolutely not."
The Gray conversation—and pitching struggles overall during Wild Card Round—has somewhat overshadowed the fact that Boston's offense managed just two runs in the two losses against the Yankees.

During Monday’s hour-long year-end press conference, Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy said they’d met with both players to help clear the air. Breslow said he and Tracy bo
item.content:encoded:
In the immediate aftermath of the Red Sox’s season-ending loss to the Yankees in Game 2 of last week’s Wild Card Series, both Willson Contreras and Sonny Gray — two of the club’s most respected veteran leaders — expressed frustration with the way decisions were being made by the organization.
During Monday’s hour-long year-end press conference, Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy said they’d met with both players to help clear the air.
Breslow said he and Tracy both spoke to Contreras for two hours on Sunday, covering a wide range of topics. Breslow wouldn’t delve into specifics but described the conversations as productive while pushing back on the notion that Contreras wants things fixed and changed.
“We had a great conversation, Trace and I, with Willson yesterday, we met for over two hours and we talked about a host of things, many of those I will keep private to preserve the relationship that we have,” Breslow said. “But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things, and Willson would be the right person to ask directly but he spoke very very highly of his time here and how much he’s looking forward to 2027 and the way he and his family appreciated the Red Sox.”
Tracy said he spoke to Gray as well and, while the veteran understandably disagreed with his decision to pull him in the fifth inning of Wednesday’s loss, their relationship is in a good place.
“I didn’t suspect most starters, especially in that case, guys are going to be happy about being pulled. I thought he answered the questions that were asked of him in a very professional manner and yes, I have had a chance to talk to him. The relationship there is good,” Tracy said. “Do I think he was wanting to stay out there? Quite obviously. But five months of relationship building with players and I think there’s some things that get painted sometimes that that’s stained it or ruined it and I have a very good working relationship with him and I’ve had numerous conversations with him throughout the course of the year. But yeah I was able to talk to him, it’s in a fine place, while also understanding his feelings on it.”
Both Gray and Contreras expressed unhappiness about Tracy’s decision to pull the starter early, with Gray telling reporters postgame that he would have “liked to have been trusted in that moment” while Contreras simply zipped his lips when asked.
Contreras was willing to speak more directly on his frustration with the club’s heavy reliance on data and analytics, saying that ultimately teams need experience and veteran players to win games.
“There’s a lot of things to get better at in each area of the game,” Contreras said last week. “You have to do a lot of different stuff, and it’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that’s telling you what to do. Because this is baseball. And the data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you’re gonna have to need experience and veteran guys to win games. And yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but not saying.”

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox manager Chad Tracy owns playoff pitching decisions: ‘My call’
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: Six days after managing his first-ever postseason game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy sat in the Fenway Park interview room on Monday morning and answered perhaps the biggest question viewers had while watching the team be outscored 18-2 and swept by the hosting New York Yankees in last week’s Wild Card round: Who made the call? Specifically, who thought it best to pull Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4 2/3 innings in their respective Game 1 and Game 2 starts? Who thought struggling left-han
item.content:encoded:
Six days after managing his first-ever postseason game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy sat in the Fenway Park interview room on Monday morning and answered perhaps the biggest question viewers had while watching the team be outscored 18-2 and swept by the hosting New York Yankees in last week’s Wild Card round:
Who made the call?
Specifically, who thought it best to pull Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4 2/3 innings in their respective Game 1 and Game 2 starts? Who thought struggling left-hander Erik Miller should relieve the starter not one, but both nights?
Was it the rookie manager, whose interim tag had been removed barely one week before the playoffs? Or was it chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and by extension, the front office, drawing up a pre-game road map for Tracy to follow?
“None,” Tracy said Monday. “The decisions are mine.”
Miller, the trade deadline addition from the Marcelo Mayer deal, had allowed earned runs in four consecutive appearances before a scoreless performance in his last regular-season game on Sept. 24. During that stretch, the 28-year-old southpaw openly admitted he was “working through some stuff.”
“Well, his last outing here at Fenway was exceptional, so he obviously fought it for much of September,” Tracy said, adding that Miller also had a “very good” extended side session before the end of the regular season. “Believe me, I see both sides. I don’t need to get too deep into defending this or that, because I certainly could have gone the other way with that, and that could have gone well, and we wouldn’t be having the conversation.”
Tolle’s pitch count was 83 after 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball. He struck out four, walked one, and yielded five hits in his first career postseason start. There were moments in which the rookie left-hander was grinding, but it was a 1-0 game and the Boston bullpen had lost several key arms to injuries, including righties Tyron Guerrero and Justin Slaten.
Tracy went to Miller after Tolle retired Yankees No. 9 hitter Paul Goldschmidt on one pitch. Ben Rice turned Miller’s third pitch into a solo home run. Though Miller only faced the minimum three batters before Tracy went to righty Greg Weissert, Rice’s homer was the dam-burster moment that led to a 9-0 Yankees win in Game 1.
With earned runs allowed in five of his last six appearances between the regular season and playoffs, it was even more stunning to see Tracy turn to Miller in nearly the same situation in Game 2.
Gray was on even better footing than Tolle, with 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball on just 70 pitches when Tracy went to the mound to take the ball. Though Gray allowed singles to Trent Grisham and Rice to put runners on the corners in the fifth, he also dominated the third time through the order all the regular season, holding opposing lineups to a .180 batting average and .515 OPS, and just seven extra-base hits in 162 plate appearances.
“I felt good, I felt crisp, I felt sharp, I felt like I was just out there competing,” a clearly-frustrated Gray said postgame. “I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact.”
“I would have liked to live-or-die with me in that moment,” Gray added. “I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment.”
Yet again, it was Miller who emerged from the bullpen. And again, Rice immediately scored to double the Yankees lead, this time on an RBI single by Cody Bellinger. The Red Sox ultimately lost 9-2 to end an even shorter playoff run than the year before, when they at least won Game 1 against the Yankees before dropping the remaining two.
With the entire Boston bullpen well-rested for Game 1, and all of the top arms available for Game 2 after not pitching in the series opener, doubling down on Miller seemed baffling that it could only be a decision handed down from the powers-that-be.
But not according to Tracy.
“We have information, just like all the other 29 teams have information,” Tracy said. “I’ve said this before, since I’ve been here, do I sit in the office and talk through … who’s available today? What’s the best way to deploy them? Who’s down? Every single day, you do that.
“But not one time since I’ve been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me, ‘Use this number right here to decide in this inning.’ Those decisions, they’re mine. So as far as that specific one (to pull the starter), my decision, that obviously didn’t go great. That falls on me.”
Tracy added: “Do we have data analytics? Of course we do, everybody does. Is somebody standing there, pushing me, saying, ‘You need to do this, this and this? Absolutely not.”
Tracy in the hour-long press conference again refuted that he was forced into those pitching changes by anyone else and said “the biggest thing for me coming into this was, maybe dispelling any notion of people thinking that decisions get made prior to the game, or with a piece of paper or with a computer.”
“I do trust Sonny Gray, I do trust the guys in the bullpen as well,” Tracy said. “I think the easiest way to say it is like, it was my call. It was my decision. It went south. Here we are.”

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox president of baseball operations Craig Breslow said that he, Willson Contreras, and manager Chad Tracy met “for over two hours [on Sunday] to discuss a host of topics.”

We assume the primary topic was Contreras’ locker room comments after the Game 2 loss to the Yankees, where he insinuated, pretty strongly, that the Red Sox were far too reliant on data to make decisions for the team. Tracy has been roundly criticized for his decision to pull both Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4 2/3 innings in each of the games. As a first-year manager, Tracy could use the experience and the subsequent meeting with Contreras as a learning experience heading into 2027.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Brutal Chad Tracy quote on Erik Miller move is exactly what Willson Contreras warned about

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Nation left the Wild Card round with more questions than answers after being embarrassed by the Yankees. Following the Game 2 loss, fans were left heavily questioning manager Chad Tracy's decision-making, especially with regard to his management of the bullpen. The quotes that followed the game didn't help his case.
The moment that really got fans riled up was following Sonny Gray's departure in the fifth inning. With two outs and runners on first and third, Tracy handed the ball to Erik Miller in relief. In Game 1, Tracy did the same thing when taking Payton Tolle out in the fifth inning, and Miller immediately gave up a left-on-left home run. In Game 2, with lefty Cody Bellinger at the plate, the scuffling (regressing?) Miller allowed an RBI single, giving New York a 2-0 lead.
Fans were rightfully upset by the decision to trust Miller again. Not only had the lefty struggled down the stretch in the regular season, but he'd just shown the game before that just didn't have it. In the postgame press conference, Tracy tried to justify his move.
Chad Tracy only made himself look worse with his reasoning to use Erik Miller in Game 2 of the Wild Card
"I think, where we were at in today's game, we pretty clearly knew who we were going to throw," Tracy said in response to being asked about bringing on a lefty to face Bellinger, who hits lefties well. "Those are the best ones we have to offer, so it was pretty obvious we were going to be aggressive..."
What it sounds like Tracy is referencing is a game script. That if the Sox were at a certain point in the game, with a certain score, it was predetermined that Erik Miller was going to be the man called upon.
That was exactly what Willson Contreras was talking about in his postgame comments. The veteran first baseman lamented the Sox approach to the games, saying they relied too heavily on analytics and didn't have any feel for the flow of the game.
You can add Sonny Gray's comments in here, too. He mentioned hoping for more trust in the moment he was pulled from the game. He also talked about being one of the best pitchers this season when facing a lineup for the third time (which was true). Anyone who's followed baseball recently knows that analytics-heavy teams don't like pitchers facing a lineup for the third time.
What happened in the game, plus the quotes after, has left Red Sox fans scratching their heads as to what changed. In the middle of the season, it felt like the whole team was running on feel for the game. They pinch-hit in the perfect moments, even if it didn't feel right. They would allow pitchers to work through jams on trust.
Now, Red Sox Nation heads into the offseason questioning the ability of their newly extended manager. They are questioning how much autonomy he actually has from the front office. These questions are going to loom over the entire offseason and into next season.

item.content:encoded:
A wild storm of news surrounding the Boston Red Sox, Driveline, and Driveline founder Kyle Boddy has come out in the days following the Red Sox Wild Card Game 2 loss to the New York Yankees. Fans were shocked to hear postgame comments from leaders in the clubhouse pushing back against manager Chad Tracy and CBO Craig Breslow after the team's mentality all season, and reporters who dug further have now revealed this wasn't the first time the fissure affected the club.
The quotes started with Willson Contreras, who pushed back against the Red Sox heavy use of analytics to drive in-game decisions. Those comments lined up with Sonny Gray pointedly saying he wished he was given more trust to get out of the jam he found himself in in the fifth inning of the game.
After the team seemed so close-knit during the regular season, always hyping each other and Chad Tracy up, to see comments immediately pushing back against the Manager and CBO post-game was a shock. According to MassLive's Sean McAdam, it's not the first time the clubhouse has pushed back against the organization this season
Red Sox players have seemingly been unhappy with the organization for much longer than the fans knew
In a State of the Team article published on October 2, McAdam referenced the fact that pushback from the players in the clubhouse earlier in the season was what led to the team severing ties with Driveline founder Kyle Boddy. There was a big to-do when it was announced that Boddy was no longer a member of the organization, with fans who had lamented the Driveline approach and thought it was ruining the hitting celebrating his departure. McAdam's piece originally referred to the players' push towards "severing ties with Driveline," but was edited to target Boddy specifically.
Boddy pushed back on the article, though.
Posting a reply to Section 10's Tyler Milliken, who posted the passage from McAdam's article to X, Boddy wrote, "This report is inaccurate for several reasons." He referenced that he was never part of Red Sox player development; he was with the Baseball Sciences and Research and Development departments, and that he left Boston due to a conflict of interest with his work with a team in Japan.
Two things can be deduced from this that are likely true in some way. The Red Sox player didn't like Boddy's involvement with the team. Just because he wasn't with player development doesn't mean he wasn't around the players and trying to provide tips they didn't appreciate. Boddy is probably trying to save face. He could have chosen the Japanese team over the Red Sox because he knew the Red Sox may have been trying to get him out the door anyway.
Red Sox Nation will likely never know the true answer as to what happened unless sources from inside the front office decide to shed light on what happened, which would seem unlikely. What is known is that the players have been unhappy with the team's heavy analytical approach.
This seems like something that could start to affect the team. As Milliken pointed out on X, there are still plenty of former Driveline employees working with the team, including John Soteropulos, the Sox's hitting coach. If free agents don't like the approach they are seeing from the team, or have a problem with Driveline, Boston may now be a place free agents stay away from.

item.title: [Over the Monster] Craig Breslow started building the 2027 Red Sox in 2026
item.dc:creator: Mike Carlucci

Two games in a row ended the Red Sox season. This wasn’t the plan. As all the Sox players returned from the WBC to Fort Myers, many riding hot streaks, this looked like a team ready to rocket. item.content:encoded:
The Wild Card series against the Yankees was probably the worst way for the 2026 season to end. Everything that was a problem at any point - struggles to score runs, the bullpen, injuries - all happened at the same time and within a matter of minutes. Two games in a row ended the Red Sox season. This wasn’t the plan. As all the Sox players returned from the WBC to Fort Myers, many riding hot streaks, this looked like a team ready to rocket. Yes, there were questions entering the season. But there were answers that hadn’t been fully formed yet.
After the 2025 season, the Sox were desperate for infield help. Trevor Story, not a guarantee of health or success himself, since arriving in Boston, was coming off a tremendous year, his best for the Red Sox. The rest of the infield was a question mark. Third base was more-or-less vacant after Alex Bregman opted out. Second base was going to be a battle with the future potential of Marcelo Mayer as a leading contestant. First base? Triston Casas? Maybe? Catcher, using the more generous definition of infield, was a tandem based on Carlos Narváez hitting in 2025 and Connor Wong, who couldn’t hit at all. There were at least two guys, which was more than could be said about first base.
Craig Breslow looked at the free agent market. He looked at the trade market. He looked at his own farm system. And in two phases he built the roster that he would live or die with.
We know about phase one. Caleb Durbin was acquired from the Milwaukee Brewers. Willson Contreras was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals. Isaiah Kiner-Falefa was signed to platoon (kinda) with Mayer.
On the free agent market, the Red Sox went in the opposite direction. The promise/hope was two bats. And they passed on Pete Alonso, Alex Bregman, Bo Bichette etc. Aside from Contreras there were no big bats.
What Durbin would share with Willson, besides become Mini Bowser to his Bowser, was control. Contreras was guaranteed to be in town through 2027 with an option for 2028. Durbin will not hit free agency until the 2030s. The same with Mayer. Ranger Suarez, on the other side of the ball, also was signed long-term.
As it would turn out Willson Contreras would not even sniff competition from Triston Casas, who would face a series of injuries that would cost him the season. Not that anyone was worried about having too many first basemen. Caleb Durbin would start off slow with the bat, glacial even, but provide solid defense. He’d go on to set a new career high in home runs while, likely, competing for a Gold Glove.
Marcelo Mayer would underperform and then get hurt. Carlos Narváez would revert to his reputation as a bat-second player. While Connor Wong would provide some offense in a bounce-back season, the catcher tandem as a whole was underwater.
Phase two would be at the deadline. With Durbin rounding into form as The Durbinator, Breslow and his team set their sights on second base and catcher. Turning Connelly Early into Curtis Mead gave them another second baseman with control for years to come. And while the sample size is small, Mead hit 17 home runs in just 87 games. Adding a 30-homer threat to second base would be a tremendous pillar of the offense. Mayer would be traded separately, Mead would get hurt, but the plan was in place.
Similarly, the massive all-in prospect trade for Adley Rutschman was for 2026 and 2027. Connor Wong isn’t a free agent until after the 2028 season so catcher is set for another year and they have time to evaluate Rutschman or find a replacement before 2028. For Breslow’s plan through this summer, when he didn’t know he’d be extended, that’s all that mattered. Build then best team for what could be his last season if they struggled.
Entering 2027 the Red Sox have two catchers. They have an entire starting infield, plus top prospect Franklin Arias. They have Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Wilyer Abreu (plus control of Jarren Duran, and Masataka Yoshida, and Kristian Campbell) in the outfield.
The rotation has Payton Tolle, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, and Jake Bennett. Boston holds an option on Sonny Gray that he can opt out of, but potentially the entire rotation is headed back for 2027. Starters 6-10 might be a concern, but for a healthy Opening Day major league roster, Breslow took care of that already.
We never actually got to see this team assembled together in 2026. Even if Curtis Mead came into the last game of the season while Garrett Crochet was on the mound, Roman was out. This year, unless there is a big trade to accommodate a move, the Hot Stove season won’t be the same. The roster is basically set. Did Breslow see the lockout as an obstacle? Maybe! He might have been thinking that teams would scramble to make moves before and after and he’d be set. For a team that was seeing it’s window open in 2025, it seems too intentional to put together the whole thing one year in with really only the Story to Arias transition as a big roster move to facilitate.
The performance of the team in 2026 was up and down, but overall we saw a number of good years from this group - Tolle, Abreu, Contreras, Rafaela, and Durbin all provide reasons to be optimistic. Roman Anthony had a good run around the hand injury. Six months off sure would be nice to let that heal. There’s reason to think 2027 can be fun. Maybe distributed a little better too.
Your Opening Day 2027 Boston Red Sox:
C: Rutschman, Wong
1: Contreras
2B: Mead, Sogard
SS: Story, Arias
3B: Durbin
OF: Roman, Rafaela, Abreau, Duran (if he’s not moved/non-tenderd), Campbell
DH: Yoshida

item.title: [Over the Monster] Was Red Sox manager Chad Tracy right to remove Sonny Gray from Game 2 against the Yankees?
item.dc:creator: Jacob Roy
item.description: Baseball is a game of numbers. It’s played on the field, with balls and bats and gloves, but every action, decision, and outcome is measured by a number. Those numbers are presented to us during broadcasts, in gambling ads, and by people like me on Twitter and in pieces here on OTM. Most of the numbers we see are presented without context. item.content:encoded:
Baseball is a game of numbers. It’s played on the field, with balls and bats and gloves, but every action, decision, and outcome is measured by a number. Those numbers are presented to us during broadcasts, in gambling ads, and by people like me on Twitter and in pieces here on OTM. Most of the numbers we see are presented without context.
Just this week, there was plenty of chatter about how Payton Tolle has reverse splits and performs better against righties than he does against lefties. If you say that Tolle stats against righties are superior to those against lefties, you are correct. If you claim that opponents should start lefties against Tolle for that reason, citing that stat as evidence, you’d be a little bit off base.
In short, Tolle’s stats against lefties were worse than those against righties because he only throws to the best left-handed hitters. If he faced a lineup of nine lefties, he’d rack up strikeouts and groundball outs because of the pitches he has at his disposal. Tolle isn’t the point of this piece, though, so I digress.
Another example of this came after the final game of the season. The Red Sox bullpen got caved in by the Yankees, and the season ended in embarrassing fashion. During the postmortem, Sonny Gray, who was pulled after just 4.2 innings and 70 pitches, expressed his displeasure at not being allowed to continue. He said that he’s the best pitcher in the American League at facing a lineup for a third time.
His numbers facing hitters for a third time are in fact excellent: .515 OPS against, 21.6% strikeout rate, 6.8% walk rate, and a .180 batting average in 162 plate appearances across 28 games this season. Despite this, Gray wasn’t allowed to see Cody Bellinger for a third time; Erik Miller came in and gave up a run, and the game snowballed from there, ending the Red Sox season.
If you read my work, you know I like numbers. I do my best to provide context and try to blend the stats with on-field applications, but I admit that I tend to believe what the numbers say even if they go against conventional wisdom. Those choices that go against conventional wisdom have come to be known as “analytics”. If people don’t agree with something, they blame “analytics” without knowing what information was actually used in that decision.
In this case, the consensus was that Gray was removed because “analytics” say that seeing a lineup for the third time is a disadvantage. The numbers presented above disagree with that sentiment, but the Boston Red Sox, who pay people to research these types of things, aren’t making decisions based on slash lines in 150 plate appearance samples. Still, the decision was, at least in some part, motivated by statistics.
This piece is not in defense of Chad Tracy, Craig Breslow, or anyone else who might have had a hand in the decision-making process or game planning. In fact, I’ll go as far as to say that I staunchly disagree with the decision. I didn’t have a suite of statistics at my disposal at the time, but I thought Gray had a better chance of getting the out than Miller. I actually messaged the rest of the OTM staff and said: “So this is insane, right?” Before the game, I published a piece on how the Red Sox needed Sonny Gray to go deep into the game, for the sake of both Game 2 and a potential Game 3. Even after looking at the numbers that I’ll share momentarily, I disagree with the decision, although that’s easy to do in hindsight.
Instead of supporting or tearing down the decision, what I’m trying to do here is reverse-engineer the thought process and provide some context, because despite what sports talk radio or faceless Twitter accounts might tell you, it is much more nuanced than “third time through the order bad”. Let’s do it.
I’ll set the scene. It’s the fifth inning with the Yankees leading, 1-0. Trent Grisham has reached on a single to start the inning, and swapped places on the bases with Austin Wells, who grounded out to second base but beat the throw from Trevor Story to break up the double play. Ryan McMahon struck out on a good sweeper, and Ben Rice singled on a hard ground ball through the infield to move Wells up to third base. After 70 pitches and one earned run, Gray walked off the mound.
The first thing I’ll look at is Bellinger’s other at-bats against Gray. In his first trip to the plate, he roped a first-pitch sinker to Nick Sogard, who made a great pick to get the out. His second time up, he grounded out again, this time after fouling off three two-strike pitches and spitting on a good sweeper to his back foot. If you’re judging based on those two matchups alone, I could understand the decision to not give Bellinger a third crack at Gray. Bellinger looked like he was seeing the ball well.
Next, let’s look at how Gray approached the lineup to that point.
Against the eight lefties in the Yankees’ lineup, Gray used his four-seam and sinker a combined 59% of the time. The rest of his arsenal was made up of 12 sweepers, 10 curveballs, and three changeups. The fastballs were in the zone (~60% zone rate on both the four-seam and the sinker), while all three of his secondary pitches returned zone rates between 20% and 33%. While that might seem intuitive — fastballs in the zone, putaway pitches below it — that’s not always the case for Gray. He’s usually willing to flip his curveball in for called strikes, and occasionally does the same with his sweeper. On Wednesday, the plan was clearly to attack with fastballs for strikes, and breaking balls below the zone.
The Yankees’ lefties had the second-highest hard-hit rate against in-zone breaking balls from righties this season, as well as the seventh-highest barrel rate. They had the second-highest whiff rate, but Gray’s breaking balls didn’t miss bats in the zone this season. With those statistics in mind, it’s likely that Gray wasn’t going to change his game plan.
Now let’s look at the fastballs. The third time through the lineup, their performance seriously suffers. Entering the postseason, he threw his four-seam and sinker each about 18% of the time. He also used his cutter 15% of the time, but didn’t throw a single cutter to lefties on Wednesday and used it sparingly in his final start of the regular season, so it appeared to be removed from his game plan. The fastballs that he did use weren’t nearly as effective as they were early in games. The shape and velocity held, but the results did not. His four-seam ideal contact rate jumped from 40% to 56%, as the pitch found the middle of the plate often.
The sinker returned weak contact, but that was likely because the zone rate dropped from 60% the first two times through to 40% the third time through. Because of this, the called strike rate plummeted, and the strike rate fell to near 50%.
His breaking stuff wasn’t much better. The curveball had a huge swinging strike rate and chase rate, but when hitters did connect, it was hammered to the tune of a 67% ideal contact rate. The sweeper, his best whiff pitch, saw its chase rate drop 15% the third time through, thanks to bigger misses off the plate.
Bellinger is an excellent breaking ball hitter. Gray’s fastballs lose effectiveness later in games, and hitters don’t expand the zone as frequently against his sweepers. If those are your cards, you probably want to fold that hand in favor of another. The card that Tracy chose to play is a whole other can of worms, but there was a case for Gray to be removed.
If you read this and thought, “the analytics have gone too far, who cares that Gray’s sweeper is less effective the third time through the order it’s playoff baseball you pitch with your nuts not your arm blah blah blah”, I don’t blame you. As I wrote this, I questioned if I was too in the weeds myself, and still would have probably rolled the dice with Gray. Regardless of whether you agree or disagree with Gray’s early exit, I hope this provided some insight into what the team might have been thinking, because it really is deeper than blanket truths discovered by “analytics” that have been parroted 1,000 times by people who think Billy Beane ruined baseball.

item.title: [heavy.com] Boston Red Sox All-Star Outfielder Gets Blunt Message on Disappointing 2026 Season

item.content:encoded:
After beginning the season 32-46, the Boston Red Sox went on a 32-5 run over the summer to go from the bottom of the American League standings to safely in a wild-card spot.
However, after that streak, the Red Sox struggled in the second half of August and September. They ended up being swept in the AL wild-card series by the New York Yankees. For Boston to go on the run they went on with the injuries they had, they needed some players to step up, and that was the case.
One of those players was right-handed pitcher Sonny Gray. When Garrett Crochet went down in April with an injury, he became the de facto ace for manager Chad Tracy. However, as well as how Boston played as a team, there were some players who were disappointments. Joel Reuter of Bleacher Report listed each MLB team’s biggest surprise and disappointment. For Boston, their biggest disappointment is not a surprise.
Jarren Duran Tabbed as Boston Red Sox Biggest 2026 Disappointment
One player who took a step back was outfielder Jarren Duran. It was just two years ago that he was the All-Star Game MVP. This season in 151 regular season games, he slashed .207/.266/.361 with 20 home runs and 69 runs driven in. He stole 21 bases, but his WAR was eye-opening for a 20/20 player.
“There have been 527 individual 20/20 seasons in MLB history, and Duran’s 0.4 WAR this year is tied for 519th among them. The counting statistics still point to some offensive value, but his overall production and defensive value declined sharply. He has fallen well short of both his 9.0-WAR peak two years ago and his 4.9-WAR campaign in 2025,” wrote Reuter.
Against the Yankees in the wild-card round, Boston’s offense struggled. Duran went 0-for-3 combined in both games with a walk. Given the logjam of outfielders the Red Sox have and the potential of adding one through free agency, trading Duran is a real possibility this offseason.
Jarren Duran’s Future With the Boston Red Sox is in Doubt
Changes are coming this offseason for the Red Sox. Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow has some decisions to make. One of them is Duran. He has two years of team control remaining, and Zachary D. Rymer of Bleacher Report thinks that could be a selling point for a team to put a package together to take him off Boston’s hands.
“It just feels like it’s time for the Red Sox and Duran to break up, doesn’t it? He’s been a regular in trade rumors for two years, and the energy he brings to the team isn’t always positive,” Rymer wrote. “The Red Sox can market him as an All-Star outfielder with two years of club control before free agency.”
Many questions remain about what the offseason will look like with a potential work stoppage looming. However, plenty of rumors will surround players before December. Duran’s name will be out there, and it would be surprising if he were moved before a stoppage, should it happen. However, when it comes to Breslow, expect the unexpected.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Sonny Gray and 3 other Red Sox who won't be back after embarrassing Yankees series
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: As paintul as it is to lose to the New York Yankees in the playoffs (for the second year in a row, no less), it hurts more to know that the Boston Red Sox's loss was more self-inflicted than anything. Boston's offense fell apart in September and the complete lack of momentum cursed it when it mattered. Pitching has been the Sox's single-biggest strength all season but Chad Tracy trusted the wrong arms at the wrong times. The moves could've cost the Red Sox any chance they had at a reunion with i
item.content:encoded:
As paintul as it is to lose to the New York Yankees in the playoffs (for the second year in a row, no less), it hurts more to know that the Boston Red Sox's loss was more self-inflicted than anything.
Boston's offense fell apart in September and the complete lack of momentum cursed it when it mattered. Pitching has been the Sox's single-biggest strength all season but Chad Tracy trusted the wrong arms at the wrong times. The moves could've cost the Red Sox any chance they had at a reunion with impending free agent Sonny Gray, who was vocal about his disappointment following his 4.2 inning outing.
“I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact,” Gray said. “I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am, and yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys, and they felt the same way."
The veteran has recently dropped hints that he might retire after this season, but after the Sox's loss he changed his tune, saying he's "got a lot of baseball left in [him]." Despite Boston's need for a right-handed pitcher next season, it's hard to foresee a reunion with Gray now.
The Sox have another impending free agent who likely won't want to come back after some explosive postgame comments, as well as some other players who could be moved after a disappointing loss.
Sonny Gray and 3 other Red Sox who won't be back after embarrassing Yankees series
Isiah Kiner-Falefa
Isiah Kiner-Falefa is yet another veteran who came to the Red Sox organization and revealed issues with the club's internal workings. Before the Red Sox went off on their tear over the summer, Kiner-Falefa called out some outside distractions that kept them from performing. He called the Sox's Wild Card loss "unacceptable" after Game 2.
Falefa didn't appear in the Wild Card series against the Yankees and he doesn't have a place in the Red Sox's infield next year — Trevor Story is under contract for one more season, Franklin Arias should be in the big leagues on Opening Day, Curtis Mead should be healthy and Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler will be options off the bench. But Kiner-Falefa has also called out the behind-the-scenes drama in the Red Sox organization and most likely prefers to play for a better-run team next year.
Patrick Sandoval
Patrick Sandoval didn't make the Red Sox's Wild Card roster, and there's a good reason for it. The lefty posted a 5.12 ERA and a 1.68 WHIP over 70.1 innings this year. He struggled in August and September with a 5.79 ERA between the two months. Seven of his eight decisions were losses.
The Red Sox certainly don't need another lefty starter in their rotation given the group they'll carry into next season. Boston's post-UCL surgery rebound projects have largely been unsuccessful and Sandoval did not change that.
Jarren Duran
The Red Sox hoped to rely on Jarren Duran as a veteran presence and an offensive threat this season and he was neither. He finished the season with a .207/.266/.361 slash line and 165 strikeouts in 151 games, the worst marks of his career so far.
Boston was already past the point of getting a good trade return for Duran last season, but the return doesn't matter at this point. The Red Sox need right-handed power and consistency and it makes the most sense to add it in the outfield.

item.content:encoded:
Happy Friday, everyone. I know this week hasn’t gone the way we had hoped, and that October baseball is now over for the Cubs, but the postseason rolls on, and we’ll still be keeping an eye on its progress as the month goes on. Today, we look at how the Astros fans turned on their own club as the disappointment of being swept out of the postseason got the best of them. We see how the Yankees proved they could win even without Aaron Judge, and how their ability to avoid rigid lineups might have helped them best the Red Sox. We also share takes from several players who were none too pleased with how the postseason turned out for them.
So let’s just get right into it.
- Jay Jaffe looks at how the Yankees bested the Red Sox to advance to the ALDS.
- Michael Baumann explains why the Yankees were the only ones constructing their Wild Card roster correctly.
- Brendan Gawlowski shares how the Padres advanced to the NLDS, but we might not want to relive that one just yet.
- Eric Longenhagen assesses how the White Sox were able to push past the Astros and onto the ALDS.
- Karl Rasmussen had some key takeaways from the White Sox series sweep of the Astros.
- Torey Lovullo will be sticking around as the Diamondbacks manager. (ESPN)
- Andy McCullough looks at how the ABS system is already changing October baseball. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Katie Woo explains why this might be the final year of the Dodger dynasty. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Willson Contreras has some feelings about Big Data.
- Davy Andrews explains why the Orioles will have some tough times ahead due to injury.
- Henry Palettella looks at the best moments from Wild Card history.
- Ryan Phillips and Tom Verducci draft the ultimate postseason pitching roster.
- Tom Verducci looked at how the Yankees proved they could win, even without Aaron Judge.
- Astros fans weren’t afraid to share how they really felt after the team was swept from the Wild Card series. Story by Karl Rasmussen.
- Sony Gray shared his displeasure at being pulled from the Wild Card game after only 70 pitches. (AP)
- It’s very hard not to like this guy.
- Cole Jacobson looks at which parks have the best home-field advantage for the postseason.
- Keegan Matheson shares how the Blue Jays are feeling about Guerrero Jr and what their focus is for this offseason.
- Andy Nesbitt looks at how things actually got worse for the Red Sox once they got back to their clubhouse after their Wild Card loss.
- How to watch SI’s original Shohei Ohtani documentary. (SI)
- Tyler Kepner explains why a rigid bullpen blueprint ultimately sank the Red Sox. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Get ready to feel very old.
And tomorrow will be a better day than today, Buster. Make it so.

item.dc:creator: Christian Arnold
