While the Yankees walloped the Red Sox to complete the sweep, plenty of baseball fans noticed what appeared to be a strange substance on Gray’s neck when he was on the mound, raising plenty of questions. Gray appeared to touch it at various times while on the mound
item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball did in fact look into the substance that many people seemed to notice on Sonny Gray’s neck during the Red Sox’s Game 2 wild-card series loss to the Yankees, sports talk host Craig Carton said on WFAN on Thursday.
While the Yankees walloped the Red Sox to complete the sweep, plenty of baseball fans noticed what appeared to be a strange substance on Gray’s neck when he was on the mound, raising plenty of questions.
Gray appeared to touch it at various times while on the mound, and baseball fans were quick to point out the discoloration on the right side of his neck.
However, Carton said he was told by Major League Baseball that it was on top of the situation and that the umpires had checked his hat, glove and hands after every inning he pitched.
“He was checked after every inning. The spin rate was not up at all compared to his starts throughout the regular season,” Carton said. “They did a full check because, obviously, if you’re watching the game, like we all are, you saw the right side of his neck was discolored.”
An MLB spokesperson did not immediately reply to a request for comment from The Post on Thursday.
Gray pitched 4 ⅔ innings and allowed only a solo home run to Luis Garcia Jr. before he was pulled from the game at 70 pitches.
The veteran right-hander seemed to question the decision to pull him from the game.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact. I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that’s the competitor I am,” he told reporters. “You can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. I felt strong. I felt confident.
“I felt convicted. What can you do? You know.”

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Sonny Gray says there’s ‘a lot of baseball left in me,’ but is undecided about what’s next - The Boston Globe

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — In the first moments after the end of another season, Sonny Gray was right where he wanted to be: with his kids.
Brothers Gunnar, 11, and Declan, 8, were periodic presences around the Red Sox since the start of spring training. They hung around with their father and his teammates in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium late Wednesday, a cheerful, youthful salve for the wound of sudden elimination from the postseason.
It illustrated the position Gray finds himself in after 14 years in the majors. On the mound, he remains eminently capable, having just turned in another high-end season, with a 2.72 ERA across 29 starts. Away from the field, he feels the pull of family, well aware of what it would mean to be a full-time dad back home in Tennessee.
In the immediate aftermath of a season-ending loss to the Yankees, Gray was noncommittal about pitching in 2027. As he mulls retirement, though, he emphasized that he needs time to figure it out.
“I don’t know what the future holds for me,” he said. “I do know that I walked off of that mound with my chest back and my chin up, and I can definitely be proud that I left it all out there until the ball was taken out of my hand.”
Gray, who turns 37 in November, is due to become a free agent, and is a virtual lock to decline his mutual option for next season and get a $10 million buyout instead.
If he does play next season, would the Red Sox be a destination?
“I don’t know,” he said.
Gray was sour after manager Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning of an eventual 9-2 loss — a 1-0 game at the moment Gray exited.
“I would’ve liked to have been trusted in that moment,” he said.
Cognizant of the emotion surrounding that managerial call, as well as the end of the season, Gray emphasized patience.
“I do know that in moments like this, it’s never beneficial for any party involved to make rash decisions,” he said. “You’re a train going down the tracks, and it just gets stopped immediately. I know step No. 1 is to not make any rash decisions. I think I just try to take it one thing at a time for now. And No. 1 would be getting my bags packed, getting in the shower, getting some food, getting back to the hotel, seeing my family, and getting back to Boston, and then we’ll go from there.”
After coming off the field, Gray went around the room hugging teammates, a parade that “just felt right” and was “not a planned thing,” he said.
Acquired from the Cardinals via trade last November, Gray was supposed to be the Red Sox’ No. 2 starting pitcher, solidifying the rotation behind Garrett Crochet. Instead, he led it, emerging as a stabilizing force as Crochet missed more than five months because of a shoulder injury.
“I was telling him that a second ago: Whatever him and his family decide, it was a joy to watch this year,” Crochet said. “I still think he’s got a lot to give the game, but there’s something to be said about going on your own terms, I suppose. Whatever he ultimately decides, that’ll be something that — us as a team — that we support him on. But it was a pleasure having him here in Boston.”
Gray told the Globe recently that “I’ll be done in a heartbeat” when his family makes it clear he’s wanted back home.
Does he still have baseball left in him?
“I think that’s an easy answer,” he said, breaking into a smile. “I got a lot of baseball left in me.”
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [puckettspond.com] Twins fan favorite Doug Mientkiewicz takes shots at Willson Contreras, Red Sox after early exit

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox were completely embarrassed by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series this week. The Yankees swept the Red Sox in two games, winning 9-0 on Tuesday and 9-2 on Wednesday. Boston is now eliminated from the postseason, while New York will play the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series.
With two outs in the bottom of the second inning in Wednesday's game, Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. hit a ball up the middle that Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story smothered on a nice diving play. There appeared to be a play at first base, but Contreras wasn't covering the bag, allowing Chisholm to reach. Luckily for the Red Sox, Contreras' misplay didn't come back to haunt him.
It's one thing for a player to make a defensive mistake once in a game. It's a whole other story if the player makes two defensive gaffes. That's exactly what Contreras did.
Red Sox's Willson Contreras makes defensive mistakes in Wild Card Game 2 loss to Yankees
Boston left-hander Garrett Crochet entered the game in the bottom of the sixth inning with the Yankees leading 2-1. Crochet got the first batter he faced, Spencer Jones, to strike out swinging. However, Jones swung at a ball in the dirt that got away from catcher Adley Rutschman, who was notably slow to retrieve the ball and throw it to first base, allowing Jones to reach first despite striking out.
Contreras was covering first base, but he was positioned on the back of the bag. It wasn't completely Contreras' fault that Jones reached first, but if he had his foot on the front of the bag and stretched to catch the ball, Jones likely would have been out.
Jones stole second base and reached third on a throwing error from Rutschman. He scored on an RBI single from George Lombard Jr. The Yankees scored five more runs in the inning, increasing their lead to 8-1.
It's worth noting that Contreras did his job at the plate Wednesday, going 2-for-2 with a home run and two walks. Unfortunately, his defensive gaffes are what's gaining more attention after Boston's rough loss.
After the loss, Contreras essentially told the media that he believes the Red Sox rely too much on data. Notably, the Red Sox pulled right-hander Sonny Gray from Wednesday's game after he allowed two runs on just 70 pitches over 4 2/3 innings.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said. "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I'll state it like that."
Former Twins fan favorite Doug Mientkiewicz, a member of the Red Sox's 2004 World Series team, took a shot at Contreras and the Red Sox after the Boston first baseman's comments.
"How about cover first- or maybe one of your 15 coaches should say something," Mientkiewicz wrote on X. "Oh but they will shoot balls out of a tiny machine on a slab of turf though during pregame. Embarrassing."
Mientkiewicz played for the Twins from 1998-2004. The Twins traded the first baseman to the Red Sox at the 2004 trade deadline.
During his seven years with the Twins, Mientkiewicz hit .275/.367/.408 with 43 home runs and 266 RBI. After his stint with Boston in 2004, Mientkiewicz played for the New York Mets, Kansas City Royals, New York Yankees, Pittsburgh Pirates and Los Angeles Dodgers. He retired after the 2009 season.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Insider Weighs in on Red Sox, Sonny Gray Substance Speculation
item.dc:creator: Curt Bishop
item.description: The Boston Red Sox's season is over. With two blowout losses to the New York Yankees in the American League wild card series, they were swept out of the playoffs and now will look towards 2027. Plenty of moments stood out in the loss, specifically when Sonny Gray was pulled in favor of Garrett Crochet, which resulted in the Yankees blowing the game open. However, some fans on social media took it a step further, suggesting that when the right-hander tapped his neck before throwing a pitch during
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's season is over. With two blowout losses to the New York Yankees in the American League wild card series, they were swept out of the playoffs and now will look towards 2027. Plenty of moments stood out in the loss, specifically when Sonny Gray was pulled in favor of Garrett Crochet, which resulted in the Yankees blowing the game open.
However, some fans on social media took it a step further, suggesting that when the right-hander tapped his neck before throwing a pitch during the game, he had a substance there and was trying to doctor the baseball.
However, neither the umpires, nor the Yankees seemed to take any issue with it. On Thursday, Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic appeared on Foul Territory and shared that he doesn't think it's a big deal.
"That is something the umpires would have needed to catch and address, and they did not, so I don't know that retroactively, MLB is going to step in simply by looking at video when you can't touch Sonny Gray's neck anymore and see what's going on," Rosenthal said.
"I know what the videos look like, I know we live in a conspiratorial kind of society right now where we all think something's up all the time. But if the umps didn't flag it, the Yankees didn't flag it, I think we've got kind of a non-issue."
"If the umpires or Yankees didn't flag it, I think we've got kind of a non-issue."
– @Ken_Rosenthal on the speculation about a substance on Sonny Gray's neck. pic.twitter.com/GlMXQmTxXa
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 1, 2026
Ken Rosenthal Doesn't Believe Sonny Gray Substance Rumors
In this day and age, umpires are all over pitchers who use substances. They have been cracking down on that for several years now, so in truth, if they thought there was an issue, they likely would have flagged it and checked Gray. It's important too to remember that ever since the league cracked down on spider tack and other substances, umpires have been checking pitchers as they walk off the mound each inning.
The Yankees likely would have noticed as well, and at no point did they suggest that there was something off about what Gray was doing or ask the umpires to check him.
Even if there was a concern at all during last night's game, it's too late for the league to do anything to punish Gray. The Red Sox lost the game and are eliminated, and Gray has even hinted at retirement at the end of this season, so there isn't anything that can really be done about it.
Sonny Gray's Future With Boston Red Sox
Gray was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals in November to stabilize the Red Sox's rotation. In 29 starts, the 36-year-old veteran went 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA over 169 innings of work. The right-hander also struck out 149 batters and posted a 4.3 WAR.
If this is the end for Gray, he at least will finish his career on a high note, having posted one of the best seasons of his career. It will be interesting to see if he decides to keep pitching or chooses to retire once the postseason comes to an end.

The post Insider Weighs in on Red Sox, Sonny Gray Substance Speculation appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Scout affirms what Willson Contreras was hinting at after embarrassing Red Sox ending

item.description: The Boston Red Sox's season is officially over after they were embarrassed by the American League East rival New York Yankees, getting swept in two games in the Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium. After Boston got eliminated on Wednesday night, first baseman Willson Contreras hinted that there is too much reliance on data within the organization. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's season is officially over after they were embarrassed by the American League East rival New York Yankees, getting swept in two games in the Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium. After Boston got eliminated on Wednesday night, first baseman Willson Contreras hinted that there is too much reliance on data within the organization.
In back-to-back games, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy lifted his starting pitcher after just 4.2 innings. First it was Payton Tolle who only threw 83 pitches and was cruising in Game 1, and then it was Sonny Gray after just 70 pitches last night. Both moves ultimately backfired as Boston's bullpen, which led baseball with a 3.00 ERA during the regular season, imploded in each contest.
Red Sox relief pitchers were charged with 15 runs across two games. This mark was very unorthodox for this unit based on what occurred during the regular season, but Boston should've gone with its starters longer.
Why one scout agrees with Willson Contreras' critique of the Red Sox
One National League scout who spoke with FanSided seemed to concur with what Contreras had to say during his postgame availability about the Red Sox's decision making.
"The Red Sox were beleaguered by injuries, but their mid game pitching decisions made the series a laugher," the scout said. "Seems like they are leaning so hard on the large sample size that they are ignoring what their eyes were telling them. In a must win game, the choice to never use (Aroldis) Chapman until the series was over, has had people fired for less."
Regarding Chapman, the Red Sox didn't put the closer, their best reliever, into the game until it was already out of hand in Game 2, with Boston trailing 9-2 in the eighth inning. Despite having a 1.92 ERA this season, Chapman only appeared in one of two games in the series once things were out of reach. He struck out the side in his lone low-leverage appearance.
In the postseason, teams often go to their closer earlier than the ninth inning in order to pitch them in high-leverage spots to help preserve the game. If the Red Sox had taken this approach with Chapman, they might have been able to keep themselves in the game in one or both of these contests.
Instead, the Yankees blew the Red Sox out in both games. The Red Sox were outscored 18-2 across these two games, which resulted in a series sweep. Beyond its bizarre pitching management, Boston's bats didn't show up in the Wild Card series either. The team and organization will now have a long time to think about the way their season ended now that it's officially over.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox’s Willson Contreras Takes Shot at Chad Tracy for Controversial Sonny Gray Move
item.dc:creator: Owen Crisafulli

Once again, the Sox got virtually no production on offense, while their bullpen fell apart down the stretch thanks to a bevy of head-scratching moves from manager Chad Tracy. The most consequential decision from Tracy was his controversial decision to remove Sonny Gray from the game after 4.2 innings of work in fav
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's 2026 campaign officially came to a close on Wednesday night, as they suffered a 9-2 loss at the hands of the New York Yankees in Game 2 of their wild-card series. Once again, the Sox got virtually no production on offense, while their bullpen fell apart down the stretch thanks to a bevy of head-scratching moves from manager Chad Tracy.
The most consequential decision from Tracy was his controversial decision to remove Sonny Gray from the game after 4.2 innings of work in favor of Erik Miller, who had just given up a crucial home run in Game 1 of this series the day before. Gray made it very clear after the game that he was not a fan of Tracy's decision to pull him, and it seems like All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras agrees with his teammate.
Willson Contreras Makes Thoughts Clear on Chad Tracy's Sonny Gray Move
In Game 1 against the Yankees, Tracy removed Payton Tolle after 4.2 innings of work and turned to Miller to face Ben Rice. Tolle was at 83 pitches on the night, but he had generally pitched well. The move immediately backfired, as Miller gave up a solo home run to Rice that woke up the rest of New York's lineup.
Tracy's decision to remove Gray in Game 2 was even more jarring, though. While a pair of runners were on first and second base, Gray had largely cruised through his outing, and this time, he was only at 70 pitches on the night. Tracy once again went to Miller out of the bullpen, and he quickly got burned again, with Miller giving up an RBI single to Cody Bellinger.
Gray did not hold back after the game when discussing Tracy's decision to pull him, saying he would have liked to be trusted in that situation after putting together such a successful season with the team. When asked about Tracy pulling Gray out of the game prematurely, Contreras didn't say anything, and instead pantomimed himself zipping his mouth shut and throwing away the key.
Red Sox Finish 2026 Campaign With Dispiriting Series vs. Yankees
So much went right for the Red Sox in their mid-summer turnaround that resulted in them finding their way to the postseason. At the end of the day, though, this team's weaknesses were too much to overcome. The lineup, which has been a weakness all year, did nothing aside from a pair of solo home runs from Contreras and Nick Sogard in Game 2, the bullpen faltered, and the lights were clearly too bright for Tracy, as every single move he made proved to be the wrong one.
Boston finds itself in the same exact spot it was in last offseason, as it clearly needs to make sweeping upgrades to its lineup in order to take the step forward it appears capable of taking. You'd think the front office would have figured this out after being subjected to the same fate in last year's playoffs, but if it puts together another weak offseason of work, the Red Sox could quickly find themselves stuck in the purgatory of being a consistently mediocre team.

item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed

Earlier this year, the 36-year-old pitcher noted that he is open to retiring if his family wants him to hang it up. He had a great year and revealed after the game that he thinks he has a lot of baseball left in him. However, he needs to decide if playing is what's best for him and his family. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series, and Sonny Gray now faces a decision on his future.
Earlier this year, the 36-year-old pitcher noted that he is open to retiring if his family wants him to hang it up. He had a great year and revealed after the game that he thinks he has a lot of baseball left in him. However, he needs to decide if playing is what's best for him and his family.
"I was telling him that a second ago, whatever him and his family decide, it was a joy to watch this year," ace Garrett Crochet said after the loss to the Yankees, per MassLive's Chris Cotillo. "I still think he's got a lot to give the game, but there's something to be said about going out on your own terms, I suppose. Whatever he ultimately decides, that'll be something that as a team, we support him on. But it was a pleasure having him here in Boston."
Even if Gray continues to play, his postgame comments open the door for him to leave the Red Sox. He has a $30 million mutual option, which will likely be declined by the Red Sox. He could re-sign as a free agent, but when he was asked if Boston was a destination he would consider after the year he had, he said "I don't know."
Gray stepped up big time for the Red Sox this year. They needed the entire rotation to play better with Crochet hurt. Having him and Crochet together in the rotation, along with Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez, would be great for the Red Sox.
More MLB: White Sox Finally Win Playoff Series For First Time In Decades

item.content:encoded:
Will Red Sox' Sonny Gray retire? Garrett Crochet hints at very real possibility appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox entered the offseason with one question hanging over Sonny Gray. Garrett Crochet acknowledged that retirement is a real possibility after Boston's Wild Card sweep by the New York Yankees. Gray, who joined the Red Sox from the St. Louis Cardinals last offseason, delivered an ace-level season. He finished 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA and 4.3 WAR. Now, his next move remains uncertain.
Boston Globe reporter Tim Healey asked Gray whether Boston could remain a destination if he pitches in 2027.
"I don't know," Gray said.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
That answer leaves the Red Sox staring at a rotation decision. Gray turns 37 in November, but his production suggests he can still help a contender. His future may come down to something bigger than numbers. Family, timing, and the chance to walk away on his own terms could matter just as much.
Red Sox' Garrett Crochet offers emotional Sonny Gray message
Red Sox beat writer Chris Cotillo shared Crochet's reaction as Gray weighs retirement.
"I was telling him that a second ago, whatever him and his family decide, it was a joy to watch this year. I still think he's got a lot to give the game, but there's something to be said about going out on your own terms, I suppose. Whatever he ultimately decides, that'll be something that as a team, we support him on. But it was a pleasure having him here in Boston."
Crochet's message captured the mood after a painful ending. Boston's season ended quickly, with the Yankees sweeping the Wild Card series and sending the Red Sox home.
Still, Gray gave Boston stability all season. He became one of the club's most reliable starters and finished with some of the best numbers of his career. Under the postseason lights, his final appearance may have become his final MLB start.
If so, Sonny Gray would leave on his terms. If not, could one more season with the Red Sox be waiting?
Related: Red Sox most to blame for embarrassing AL Wild Card Series sweep by Yankees

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now.
Essentially all of last offseason was spent with the premise that the Red Sox had too many outfielders and that one was bound to get traded.
That never came to fruition, though, and so Duran remained in Boston for the 2026 season.
He struggled mightily, batting just .207 with limited power, and so questions will arise again.
The Red Sox still have the same amount of outfielders. Duran might not be worth as much, but he also might not be as crucial for Boston to keep around.
A year later, could a trade materialize?
That’s one question being asked as the Red Sox enter their offseason after being swept in two games in the AL Wild Card Series by the rival New York Yankees.
There are big questions for the sport of baseball to answer as a whole this winter. In Boston, though, Duran is going to be one of the biggest things to solve, one way or another.
Jarren Duran Trade Plans
ESPN’s David Schoenfield wrote about this question almost immediately following the Red Sox season ending, and he seems to arrive at the conclusion that a trade could definitely be coming.
“That leaves trading Duran on the agenda,” Schoenfield writes. “Roman Anthony’s nearly four-month stint on the IL meant the four-outfielders-for-three-positions problem never actually turned into a problem, but after hitting just .207/.266/.361, Duran is clearly fourth on the depth chart. His trade value took a nosedive, but he still somehow has two years left of team control, and the Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.”
There is certainly value for an acquiring team in the fact that Duran still has two more years under contract. Especially considering what a shortened season might do to player value, a team knowing it would also have Duran for 2028 could be appealing to anyone who still believes in his talent.
There may not be a lot of suitors, but Schoenfield writes that the “Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.” It’ll just be up to Boston at that point to follow through on the deal.
Why Red Sox Offseason Might Be Slow Otherwise
Aside from Duran, Schoenfield doesn’t think Boston will be very busy. They’ve already taken care of a bunch of things.
“While the Red Sox had a revolving door at shortstop and second base in 2026 — six different players started at short and seven at second — those positions will probably be resolved in 2027 with top prospect Franklin Arias and Curtis Mead, the trade deadline acquisition the Red Sox were going to play at second base until he got injured his first game with the team,” Schoenfield writes. “Trevor Story still has one more year left on his contract, but there’s no reason he should be playing ahead of Arias next season.”
Schoenfield also references the recent trades for Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Erik Miller as limiting the need for moves, since those guys all are under contract still.
His only other question: Does Sonny Gray retire, or return, or neither? The Red Sox still have things to figure out, just maybe not as much as some years.

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] Sonny Gray not happy with Chad Tracy's bullpen decision in Red Sox' season-ending loss
item.dc:creator: Michael Hurley

He certainly can't be aware of all of them, but there's one this year that he clearly knew by heart. "I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time," Gray said Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, after the Boston Red Sox were swept out of the Wild Card Series against the rival New York Yankees. item.content:encoded:
Having been in the big leagues since 2013, Sonny Gray has accumulated a lot of stats in his career. He certainly can't be aware of all of them, but there's one this year that he clearly knew by heart.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time," Gray said Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, after the Boston Red Sox were swept out of the Wild Card Series against the rival New York Yankees. "I think that's a fact."
Indeed, the 36-year-old was great when facing a lineup for a third time this year, holding hitters to a .180 average while posting a 1.99 ERA.
Yet, while the crafty veteran was aware of his effectiveness the third time through the batting order, his manager was either unaware or not interested in letting Gray pitch out of a miniature jam with Boston's season on the line.
After Gray allowed two singles with the Yankees leading 1-0 in the fifth, first-year manager Chad Tracy strode to the mound and inexplicably called upon lefty reliever Erik Miller for the second straight night at the same exact point in the game.
That move backfired immediately in Game 1, when Miller replaced Payton Tolle and surrendered a home run on his third pitch. And it failed again in Game 2, with Miller giving up two hits to the only batters he faced. The first was Cody Bellinger, who ripped an RBI single off Miller's slider to double the Yankees' lead to 2-0.
Gray, who will finish in the top three of AL Cy Young voting this year, felt he should have been given the chance to at least finish the fifth inning.
"I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. I think you could probably ask the guys, and they felt the same way," Gray said. "I felt strong, I felt confident, I felt convicted. But what can you do?"
Gray added: "I would have liked to been trusted in that moment."
Certainly, Gray's work both this season and throughout his career earned him a start in the playoffs over Ranger Suarez, who's one of the best postseason pitchers in baseball history. And at just 70 pitches, and after getting proper rest down the stretch, Gray was far from being on the ropes when Tracy made his call.
More Red Sox Coverage
Even though the decision to go to Miller allowed the Yankees to instantly double their leads in both games of the sweep, Tracy defended his decisions.
"[Tolle and Gray] are great, yeah. Our bullpen's been great all year, too," Tracy said. "It's a case sometimes of depending on what the score is and how much wiggle room we have, if we were able to put up some runs and maybe have some more breathing room, we might be able to [keep the starters in the game]. But trying to be aggressive and create tough matchups, and it just didn't work out."
Tracy's assertion that the bullpen has been great all year is true overall, but it doesn't apply to Miller specifically.
After joining the Red Sox as the return in the Marcelo Mayer trade, Miller made a strong first impression, posting a 0.63 ERA and 1.047 WHIP in his first 14 appearances. He struck out 25 batters and walked just six in that span, earning a trusted spot for high-leverage, late-game situations for Boston.
But his effectiveness nosedived late in the year, when he posted a 12.46 ERA and 2.538 WHIP over his final five appearances, walking six batters while striking out just four.
Those struggles clearly continued in Game 1, when Miller gave up a home run and an infield single in his one-third of an inning, but Tracy — with his full complement of high-leverage bullpen arms available — went right back to Miller in Game 2. For a second straight night, Miller could not deliver.
Tracy and the Red Sox felt comfortable giving the ball to Tolle in Game 1 on the road in Yankee Stadium. Yet with two outs and nobody on in the fifth, and with Tolle at just 83 pitches, Tracy took that ball away and gave it to a reliever in whom the manager should have lost trust.
Tracy and the Red Sox then felt comfortable giving the ball to Gray in Game 2, this time with the season hanging in the balance. Yet with two outs and two runners aboard in the fifth, Tracy again took the ball out of the hand of the trusted starter to place it in the shaky left hand of Miller.
Both times, the move did not work. And though the correlation may not be strictly scientific, both bullpen moves led to Game 1 and Game 2 spiraling out of control from that point forward.
Gray, who's set to become a free agent this offseason unless he retires, said that Tracy did not give him an explanation for the move. Gray was also asked if Boston would be a "destination" if he does choose to pitch again next year.
"I don't know," he answered.

item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray sends frustrated message to Red Sox manager Chad Tracy over early pull in elimination game originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Red Sox suffered the most ignominious of results during their AL Wild Card series, seeing their postseason hopes dash in just two matches against the Yankees.
The contests weren't all that competitive. New York blanked Boston in the opener before advancing courtesy of a 9-2 win on Wednesday.
The Red Sox's bats failed to muster much of a murmur when confronted with the Pintstripers' pitching. And yet, it was Chad Tracy's decision to relieve ace Sonny Gray of the ball after with one out left in the fifth inning that proved especially disorienting to those cloaked in Boston regalia.
Gray spoke out about his premature exit after the game ended. Suffice to say, he was less than pleased.
Sonny Gray reacts to Chad Tracy's early pull in elimination game
Gray was left dismayed by Tracy's decision to hand him his walking papers before the end of the fifth inning. Speaking with media following the contest, Gray reaffirmed that he was feeling confident about his ability to deliver from the mound when Tracy took the ball from him.
"I felt crisp, I felt sharp, I felt like I was just out there, competing," Gray said. "I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I was just executing what I wanted to do."
The 36-year-old acknowledged that he surrendered more contact than he would've liked across his 4.2-inning appearance, citing Luis Garcia Jr.'s home run, as well as a gaggle of singles. Nevertheless, he tends to get better the deeper he goes into contests — a fact he made sure to highlight during his post-game presser.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time," Gray said. "I think that's a fact. Yeah, I mean, I would have liked to deliver with me in that moment. But that's the competitor that I am.
"I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way."
Gray held hitters to a .515 OPS when facing them the third time in the order in 2026. His 38 split OPS+ was comfortably better than the league's average. Hitters posted a .515 OPS when facing Gray the third time in an order, the third-worst mark in baseball (and worst in the American League) among pitchers to face at least 100 batters in that situation.
In other words, if there was ever a candidate to stay in the game for longer than conventional wisdom might suggest, it was Gray.
"I would have liked to been trusted in that moment," Gray said.
He's not the only one to think so. Willson Contreras blasted the organization for prioritizing data over intangibles in its postseason run. According to Mass Live's Chris Cotillo, Gray's premature exit was at the heart of the catcher's frustrations.
""It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said. "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I'll state it like that."
None of this is what those of a Red Sox disposition would want to hear at the end of the season. At 36, it's unclear what Gray's future plans are. He has a year left on his contract with Boston, but has an out should Boston attempt to exercise its club option. Garrett Crochet suggested that retirement is a possibility for the aging hurler, who posted some of the best numbers of his career in 2026.
Regardless, Tracy's decision to pull him is certain to leave a sour taste in Gray's mouth, something that could prove difficult to grapple with when it's time to figure out if he'd like to return to Fenway in 2027.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Another unsuccessful Red Sox season ends with early exit, leaves players venting about Sonny Gray's early hook

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — For the second year in a row, the Red Sox season ended where it began: at Yankee Stadium.
On Wednesday night, before September officially turned to October, marking the true beginning of the postseason, the Red Sox were sent packing, again, by the Yankees. Unlike last year in this round, there was no need for a third game. No need for Aaron Judge. No need for Giancarlo Stanton. The Red Sox lost 9-2 on Wednesday night, a day after getting blown out 9-0 in the opener.
Instead, only embarrassment lived. Only quietness existed inside a clubhouse that will have to chew on two humiliating losses in the American League Wild Card Series.
There will be plenty from this season worth pointing to.
The Red Sox were once 14 games under .500. Then came the midsummer streak when they rattled off 15 straight wins and went 27-3 from the start of July through the beginning of August. Willson Contreras's season was vital to this club's success. Caleb Durbin's toughness and grit helped set the tone. The offense showed some malleability, deviating from its pull-side approach and becoming less one-dimensional.
All of that happened. All of it mattered.
But don't let any of it obscure the reality. Don't let the front office twist this. Don't let it off the hook too easily. The front office pivoted to Durbin only once it missed out on Alex Bregman.
And when October arrived -- pardon, the end of September -- the Red Sox finished their season with one fewer postseason win than they had a year ago.
It has now been five years since postseason baseball was last played at Fenway Park, the longest October drought for the ballpark since 1976-85.
Don't be fooled by the summer surge. Don't be fooled by the progress.
This season wasn't a success.
"Uncompetitive." Isaiah Kiner-Falefa said afterward. "We got boat-raced. To lose in the Wild Card is unacceptable."
"I mean, right now it's, regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series," manager Chad Tracy said. "And that ended for us tonight."
'I would have liked to have been trusted'
Frustration mounted in the clubhouse afterward, too. For a second straight night, Tracy pulled his starter early for Erik Miller, and it immediately backfired.
This time, it was Sonny Gray, who had allowed just one run, a solo homer to Luis García Jr. in the top of the fourth. In the fifth, Gray worked around a Trent Grisham leadoff single, recording two outs on a force out and a groundout. Yet, after a Ben Rice single put runners at first and third, Tracy inexplicably ended Gray's evening at just 70 pitches with Cody Bellinger looming.
Instantly, much like Tuesday night, the Yankees capitalized. Bellinger laced a single to right, extending the lead to 2-0.
Forced to piece together the rest of the game with a bullpen that included appearances from Garrett Crochet and Garrett Whitlock, the Red Sox watched the Yankees pour on eight runs against their relievers.
A disgruntled Gray didn't hold back his sentiments following the outing.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League the third time through the order," Gray said. He then paused for a moment. "I think that's a fact. I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
Gray was spot-on. He, indeed, was the best starter in the American League the third time through the order, carrying a 1.99 ERA in 45 ⅓ innings pitched, a large enough sample size.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball and the data is here to help us," Contreras said. "But at the end of the day, we're going to need experienced and veteran guys to win games."
That points to a larger issue that has followed lead executive Craig Breslow.
The April firing of manager Alex Cora and his staff might have been the right decision. Tracy (who was named the full-time skipper last week), ideally, is the manager that Breslow envisioned at the helm. But don't let their torrid summer misconstrue the split in the clubhouse. Some players remain convinced the new coaching staff had little to do with their success.
That might have been Gray's last time in a Red Sox uniform -- or in any uniform, as the 36-year-old has contemplated retirement. Asked if he would want to return next season to the Red Sox if he decided to play:
"I don't know," Gray responded.
Roster questions looming
Roman Anthony needs to prove he can stay healthy. He was pulled from Game 1 after re-aggravating the same right hand that kept him out for 101 games. Anthony went for an MRI in Boston early Wednesday morning before returning that afternoon. It's still unclear if he needs surgery.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," he said. "But I think for me, it was to a point where it was tolerable, and I was taking certain swings that were sketchy but was still able to come back and recover enough to just be in there every single day. But ultimately, I just took a few swings here recently where that wasn't the case."
Remember the Big Three? Anthony, Kristian Campbell and Marcelo Mayer were supposed to represent the next wave of the Red Sox.
What do the Red Sox do with Campbell, who was stuck in Triple-A all season and put up subpar numbers? Mayer was supposed to be the heir apparent to Trevor Story. He was traded to San Francisco.
Surely, Story has aged out of being an everyday shortstop.
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela and right fielder Wilyer Abreu are proven everyday players. But if Anthony isn't healthy, the Red Sox will need to patch up left field. Jarren Duran might have played his last season in a Red Sox uniform, with many suspecting he will be traded in the offseason.
And, despite the offense coming alive this summer, that could be viewed as fool's gold. During their 37-game surge, the Sox hit .258 with a .445 slugging percentage and their run creation was 15% better than league average. Over their final 47 games, those numbers fell to a .236 average, .382 slugging percentage and they created runs 6% below the league-average mark.
Their late-season woes looked much more like the offense from the first 78 games, when the club hit .244 with a .385 slugging percentage, than the one that transformed its season.
"Obviously disappointed," Story said on getting bounced from the postseason. "A lot of thoughts, but proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the hate and everything going around, the way this team came together, we really turned the season around to get back into this position. It was something that was special."
The summer run was special, yes.
But don't let this club off the hook.
The season wasn't a success.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox players miffed by Chad Tracy’s decision to pull stater early
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: NEW YORK — Sonny Gray has been one of the top pitchers in the American League all season, and for much of Wednesday night he did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game. But with two outs in the bottom of the fifth, with his team clinging to a 1-0 lead and runners at the corners after Yankees slugger Ben Rice tagged him for a single, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy decided to take the ball from his starter and go to Erik Miller to face Cody Bellinger, opting for a lefty-on-lefty matchup e
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Sonny Gray has been one of the top pitchers in the American League all season, and for much of Wednesday night he did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
But with two outs in the bottom of the fifth, with his team clinging to a 1-0 lead and runners at the corners after Yankees slugger Ben Rice tagged him for a single, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy decided to take the ball from his starter and go to Erik Miller to face Cody Bellinger, opting for a lefty-on-lefty matchup even though Gray was only at 70 pitches and Miller has been shaky to close the season.
The move didn’t work out. Bellinger hit an RBI single and the Yankees ultimately went on to score eight runs against the Red Sox bullpen, winning Game 2 by a lopsided score of 9-2 to complete the Wild Cad Series sweep.
Following the game Gray was candid about his displeasure with getting the hook.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact. Yeah I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment but that’s the competitor I am,” Gray said. “I think you can probably ask the guys and they feel the same way. I felt strong, I felt confident, I felt convicted, but what can you do?”
“I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment,” Gray continued, adding later that he hasn’t spoken with Tracy yet and wasn’t sure if there would be any point.
Gray wasn’t the only Red Sox veteran miffed about the decision. Asked for his thoughts shortly afterwards, first baseman Willson Contreras responded only by zipping his lips.
Tracy explained that he decided to go to Miller because they had fallen behind and he felt he had to be aggressive, especially given how much the offense was struggling to score runs. The Yankees had already gotten a couple of hits against Gray in the inning, and with how reliable the bullpen has been throughout the season he decided to play the matchup in hopes of putting out the fire.
“We’re trailing. We’re struggling to score runs. And when you get in spots where struggling to score runs and you’re already trailing, you feel like you’ve got to be aggressive and go,” Tracy said.
“Our bullpen’s been great all year,” Tracy continued later. “It’s a case sometimes of depending on what the score is and how much wiggle room you have, if we were able to put up some runs and maybe have some more breathing room, we might be able to do that. But trying to be aggressive and create tough match-ups, and it just didn’t work out.”
Tracy also went to the bullpen early in Game 1 as well, pulling Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings in Boston’s eventual 9-0 loss. Tolle’s pitch count was a relatively modest 83 pitches at that point, and though the rookie took a much more charitable view than his older teammates, he admitted any starter would rather keep going in that spot.
“As a competitor as you want to go as long as you can. I think for me I see it as there’s people that are going to – I trust our bullpen and the way they’ve gone about this year, I think they’ve been incredible, they’ve picked me up more times than I can count,” Tolle said. “It’s the postseason, you’ve got to limit as much as you can so whenever those situations happen, for me, ok, this is what’s going to be best for the team.”

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Willson Contreras Shades Red Sox's Use of Analytics in Video After Sonny Gray's Early Exit
item.dc:creator: Julia Stumbaugh
item.description: Willson Contreras Shades Red Sox's Use of Analytics in Video After Sonny Gray's Early Exit Willson Contreras indicated he felt overuse of analytics led Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy to pull Sonny Gray from Wednesday's Wild Card round elimination loss after just 70 pitches against the New York Yankees. Contreras initially responded to reporters asking about his reaction to Gray's fifth-inning exit from the 9-2 loss by miming zipping his lips before elaborating. "It's not enough when you have
item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras Shades Red Sox's Use of Analytics in Video After Sonny Gray's Early Exit
Willson Contreras indicated he felt overuse of analytics led Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy to pull Sonny Gray from Wednesday's Wild Card round elimination loss after just 70 pitches against the New York Yankees.
Contreras initially responded to reporters asking about his reaction to Gray's fifth-inning exit from the 9-2 loss by miming zipping his lips before elaborating.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said (h/t SNY). "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you're going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
When asked if he felt the Red Sox relied too much on data, Contreras nodded as he said, "If you watch the game."
Tracy, who had also pulled Game 1 starter Payton Tolle early, called Gray off the mound with two runners on base, one out remaining and the Red Sox trailing by one run in the bottom of the fifth.
Gray was replaced by Erik Miller, who on his third pitch of the game allowed a two-RBI single from Cody Bellinger.
Tracy then turned to Garrett Crochet for the sixth inning. Crochet allowed a run and loaded the bases until he was removed for Garrett Whitlock, who allowed five more runs before he was able to close out the frame.
Tracy said after the elimination loss he used the same reasoning to pull Gray as he had to remove Tolle from a Game 1 shutout loss to the Yankees.
"We're trailing. We're struggling to score runs, and when you get into spots where you're struggling to score runs and you're already trailing, you feel like you've got to be aggressive," Tracy told reporters Wednesday night.
The Yankees will now advance to face the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS, while the Red Sox will concede their second Wild Card loss in as many years. Ranger Suárez, who was slated to start a potential deciding Game 3, will not pitch this postseason.
The Red Sox fired former manager Alex Cora and turned to Tracy following a 10-17 start to the season. Tracy lost his interim tag and inked a three-year extension after leading the club to clinch a postseason berth.
Tracy will now be tasked with helping his club find a way to respond next fall to scoring two runs across their two postseason games.

item.title: [New York Post] Willson Contreras takes veiled shot at Red Sox front office after brutal sweep: ‘Computers telling you what to do’
item.dc:creator: Matt Ehalt
item.description: Willson Contreras provided one of the few good Red Sox swings in this embarrassing showing against the Yankees and then took another postgame whack at his team. The first-year Red Sox slugger seemingly took aim at the organization’s analytics philosophy after their 9-2 Game 2 loss to the Yankees in a wild-card sweep. “There’s a lot of things to get better at in each area of the game. If you watch the game, we have to get better at the game running, we have to get better at taking care of the ste
item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras provided one of the few good Red Sox swings in this embarrassing showing against the Yankees and then took another postgame whack at his team.
The first-year Red Sox slugger seemingly took aim at the organization’s analytics philosophy after their 9-2 Game 2 loss to the Yankees in a wild-card sweep.
“There’s a lot of things to get better at in each area of the game. If you watch the game, we have to get better at the game running, we have to get better at taking care of the stealers, we have to do a lot of different stuff,” said Contreras, who homered off Max Fried in the sixth inning. “It’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball.
“The data is here to help us but at the end of the day, you’re going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but I’ll state it like that.”
If there was any confusion about who Contreras, 34, was throwing under the bus, the line “you have computers telling you what to do” clears that all up.
The Red Sox, like any team that thrives in baseball, rely on analytics to help them.
There will always be a debate about how much of the human element should be blended into games versus specifically relying on data to make decisions.
Contreras received a follow-up question about whether the Red Sox rely too much on data, and provided a cryptic decision.
“If you watch the game,” he said, “if you watch the game.”
His shot at the “computers” is notable since it came after two seemingly analytics-driven decisions for the Red Sox backfired, one in each game.
First-year manager Chad Tracy pulled Payton Tolle in a 1-0 game to have lefty reliever Erik Miller face Ben Rice in the fifth inning in Game 1 and Rice promptly homered.
He tried a similar move Wednesday in yanking Sonny Gray in the fifth for Miller to face Cody Bellinger in a 1-0 game and the Yankees outfielder laced an RBI single.
When asked his thoughts on pulling Gray, Contreras did not verbally answer but said all he needed to say by instead pretending to sow his mouth shut.
Contreras also provided an interesting answer about what happened to the team’s once-scorching lineup, with Boston tearing the cover off the ball during its 32-5 run that saved its season and then slumping to end the regular season before this two-run showing over 18 postseason innings.
“That’s a good question,” he replied. I’m not going to answer it because I don’t want to give my honest answer. We got eliminated, that’s the bottom line.
Contreras is under contract with Boston for the 2027 season and the team holds a $17.5 team option for 2028, and he produced a career-best .901 OPS this past season.
Boston surely will aim this offseason to build a deeper lineup around him and Roman Antony and if the team value his two cents, it seems he’ll be telling them to forget the data and use their eyes.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Roman Anthony’s Hand Injury Reveals Darker Truth For Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Spencer Rickles
item.description: The worst news for Boston fans isn't that Roman Anthony is hurt. It is that the injury is worse than anyone thought. New scans revealed fresh muscle strains in his wrist alongside old damage. This changes everything for the Red Sox playoff hopes. Scans Show Worse Damage Anthony left Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with soreness after a checked swing. He struck out twice before getting pulled in a 9-0 loss. Manager Chad Tracy said the player was sent back to Boston for more imaging. The results we
item.content:encoded:
The worst news for Boston fans isn't that Roman Anthony is hurt. It is that the injury is worse than anyone thought. New scans revealed fresh muscle strains in his wrist alongside old damage. This changes everything for the Red Sox playoff hopes.
Scans Show Worse Damage
Anthony left Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with soreness after a checked swing. He struck out twice before getting pulled in a 9-0 loss. Manager Chad Tracy said the player was sent back to Boston for more imaging. The results were grim. "We sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist in addition to exasperating the old injuries. It's not great," Tracy told reporters, per ESPN.
This isn't a minor tweak. The 22-year-old missed 101 games earlier this year with a torn ligament in his right ring finger. He only played 55 regular season games before this latest setback. His stats dropped from a .292 average last year to .245 this season. The Red Sox signed him to a massive $130 million extension hoping for a star. Now that deal looks like a gamble on a broken body.
A Brutal Playoff Rule
There is a cruel twist in the rulebook that fans need to know. If a player gets removed from a playoff roster during a series, he cannot play in the next series either. This means Anthony won't just miss Game 2 against the Yankees. He will be ineligible for the entire ALDS if Boston advances. The team replaced Anthony on the roster with Curtis Mead, according to MLB Trade Rumors.
Tracy tried to frame it as a common issue for players coming off long layoffs. "He's obviously coming off that. You'll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it's fine, it goes away," Tracy said. But the reality is different today. "Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable," he added, per ESPN. The hope is gone. The pain is real.
The Cost of a Broken Star
The Red Sox are one loss from elimination. They need every bat they can get. Jahmai Jones is set to hit leadoff as the designated hitter. The lineup includes Adley Rutschman, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu. Sonny Gray will start on the mound against a former team. But the lineup is missing its most promising young hitter.
Anthony was supposed to be the centerpiece of the next decade. His wrist issues have already cost the team almost four months of the regular season. Now they lose him in the playoffs too. The $130 million contract is secure, but the on-field value is gone for now. Boston has to hope Mead or Seigler can step up immediately. The clock is ticking, and the scans say time is not on their side.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras Sound Off on Red Sox's ALWCS Loss vs. Yankees
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: For the second straight game, a Boston Red Sox pitcher tossed 4 2/3 good innings against the New York Yankees, only for the bullpen to fall apart afterward. Payton Tolle gave Boston a chance to win Game 1, but the bullpen couldn't keep it close. The same thing happened on Wednesday in Game 2 after Sonny Gray was pulled. In both cases, the Red Sox's starters gave Boston a chance to win the game but were yanked early. The final score from both contests doesn't tell the entire story. Boston lost Ga
item.content:encoded:
For the second straight game, a Boston Red Sox pitcher tossed 4 2/3 good innings against the New York Yankees, only for the bullpen to fall apart afterward. Payton Tolle gave Boston a chance to win Game 1, but the bullpen couldn't keep it close. The same thing happened on Wednesday in Game 2 after Sonny Gray was pulled.
In both cases, the Red Sox's starters gave Boston a chance to win the game but were yanked early. The final score from both contests doesn't tell the entire story. Boston lost Game 1, 9-0. The Red Sox lost Game 2, 9-2. Boston was blown out in both games, but not until the starters came out. After Game 2's loss, Gray spoke to the media and made it clear that he wanted to stay in.
"I would’ve liked to have been trusted in that moment," Gray said. " ... I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact. I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. You can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way."
Hindsight is always 20-20, but Gray was good on the hill and was Boston's ace all season. The bullpen was very good as well and was among the best in baseball. But after it struggled in Game 1, arguably the Red Sox should've stuck with Gray in that moment. Boston turned its season around and got the point of making the playoffs in general thanks to the starting rotation and Gray was the one who led the charge all year.
What Could Boston Have Done?
Clearly, there was a feeling within the team as well about the decision. Willson Contreras, Boston's outspoken leader throughout the 2026 season, was asked whether Gray got the hook too early. He made a "lips sealed" motion.
In the process, he also insinuated that Boston has relied too heavily on data, rather than the game itself.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or computers that are telling you what to do. This is baseball. The data is here to help us...but you need experience and to bet on the guys to win games," Contreras said.
Again, at the end of the day, hindsight is 20-20. If the Red Sox stuck with Gray, maybe things would've gone better. He was doing well before getting pulled and has done that all season. The emotions are always going to be high, especially after being knocked out of the playoffs by your rival. But the comments about the use of data were pointed and strong.
When the story of the 2026 season is told, there are going to be a lot of positive things to talk about. But also missed opportunities. The Yankees didn't have Aaron Judge. On paper, the Red Sox should've been able to come in and advance. The Yankees played well. New York rolled with Max Fried and Cam Schlittler and they dominated. But Boston's bullpen didn't show up, and neither did the offense. It could've been better, to say the least, and now Boston has work to do.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com
Follow patmcavoy

item.title: [boston.com] Willson Contreras vents about Red Sox’ struggles, data and analytics after season-ending loss
item.dc:creator: Conor Ryan

We didn’t hit. And when you don’t have those two, it’s tough to win. They pl
item.content:encoded:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Willson Contreras has never been one to hold back when speaking to the media, especially during his first year with the Red Sox.
As such, the veteran first baseman was candid when asked to summarize Boston’s brief two-game playoff series against the Yankees in the Wild Card round.
“We didn’t play good at all,” Contreras said. “We didn’t pitch. We didn’t hit. And when you don’t have those two, it’s tough to win. They played better than us. And that’s why they advanced.”
Boston was ultimately outscored, 18-2, and outhit, 26-7, in a lopsided playoff series against New York — with the Red Sox bats going cold for the second straight postseason.
Before Contreras clubbed a solo shot in the top of the sixth inning, the Red Sox had gone 26.2 innings without scoring a run in the playoffs — dating back to last year’s postseason series against New York.
Despite a 32-5 surge in July and August that revived Boston’s season, the Red Sox’ bats went quiet down the stretch — even before this two-game series. In September, Boston posted just a .219 batting average, including just a .163 batting average with runners in scoring position.
Speaking after Boston’s 9-2 season-ending loss on Wednesday, Contreras was evasive when asked what led to the Red Sox’ disheartening downturn after such a dominant stretch in July and August.
“That’s a good question,” Contreras said. “I’m not going to answer it because I don’t want to give my honest answer. But we got eliminated. That’s the bottom line. We didn’t produce. We didn’t execute any part of the game, and that’s why we [lost].
“I know that we had a really good stretch. I’m really proud of what we did in the past, like I said. We were able to turn the season around, for sure, 100 percent. But that’s not enough. It’s not enough. And at the end of the day, you win games in the regular season to clinch the playoff, but then falling short in the playoffs, it’s tough.”
While Boston’s dormant offense loomed large over this series, Contreras also seemed to take umbrage with Chad Tracy’s decision to pull Sonny Gray after just one earned run allowed and 70 total pitches on Wednesday.
After Gray was lifted after 4.2 innings of work, reliever Erik Miller immediately gave up an RBI single — giving New York a 2-0 lead at the time.
When asked about Gray’s quick hook, Contreras didn’t comment — instead signaling a “lips sealed” motion with his hands and mouth twice.
Whether it was inspired by the decision to remove Gray or other instances in which the Red Sox have leaned heavily on analytics or other tools in their baseball operations, Contreras stressed that teams can’t rely on those metrics to translate directly into results — especially in October.
“It’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” Contreras said. “The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I’ll state it like that.”
When asked if he feels there’s too much of a reliance on data and analytics in baseball today, Contreras replied: “If you watch the game. If you watch the game.”
Contreras — who set career highs in home runs (27) and RBI (81) in his first year with Boston — said that he’d be open to having conversations with chief baseball officer Craig Breslow about the team’s approach to data and analytics.
“At the end of the day, we can talk, we can share ideas, but like I said, I’m not making decisions,” Contreras said, per MassLive’s Christopher Smith. “And we’re not going to make decisions. We are employees. We get paid to play baseball and we get paid to be out there on the field to perform. I mean, that’s the bottom line. Of course, we can have some conversations.”
The Red Sox have plenty of work to do this offseason, whether that means bolstering their lineup and adding some pop to their batting order, clearing a logjam of underachieving players across the roster, or ideally getting several key cogs like Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet healthy.
Contreras, who suffered his fair share of bumps and bruises in 2026, said plenty needs to change if Boston wants to advance past the Wild Card round in 2027.
“At the end of the day, it’s not about data. It’s about executing the game plan,” he noted.

Both due to Boston’s 2026 season coming to a close after a 9-2 loss to New York — and the early hook from Red Sox manager Chad Tracy that pulled the veteran starter after just 70 pitches. “I would have liked to be trusted in that moment,” Gray declared after Boston’s loss on Wednesday. When Tracy emerged from t
item.content:encoded:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Red Sox Game 2 starter Sonny Gray did little to mask his disappointment on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium.
Both due to Boston’s 2026 season coming to a close after a 9-2 loss to New York — and the early hook from Red Sox manager Chad Tracy that pulled the veteran starter after just 70 pitches.
“I would have liked to be trusted in that moment,” Gray declared after Boston’s loss on Wednesday.
When Tracy emerged from the dugout to pull Gray from his start, the 36-year-old righty had limited New York to one run — a solo shot from Luis Garcia Jr. — over 4.2 innings, striking out five and giving up five hits.
“I felt good, I felt crisp, I felt sharp,” Gray noted. “I was executing what I wanted to do. I’m frustrated for sure. I’m not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions, but frustration was definitely one.”
But with New York running through its batting order for a third time, Tracy opted to pull his starter with runners on first and third and two outs.
For the second game in a row, Tracy turned to reliever Erik Miller as the next arm up.
In Game 1, Miller took over for Payton Tolle (4.2 innings, five hits, one earned run) and immediately gave up a solo shot to Ben Rice.
On Wednesday, Miller relinquished an RBI single to Cody Bellinger — with that run charged to Gray.
Postgame, Gray was candid about his limited workload and the decision to pull him before he faced the heart of New York’s order for the third time.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time,” Gray said. “I think that’s a fact. I would have liked [for Tracy] to live or die with me in that moment, but that’s the competitor I am.
“I think you can probably ask the guys and I think they felt the same way. So, I felt strong, I felt confident, I felt convicted. But what can you do, you know?”
For what it’s worth, Willson Contreras refused to comment — doing a “lips sealed” motion — when asked by reporters about his thoughts on Gray’s early hook.
As Brian Barrett of The Ringer noted, opposing hitters batted just .180 against Gray in their third plate appearance against him during his 2026 starts — ranking 6th out of 117 qualified starters.
But Tracy instead opted to roll with another reliever in Miller, noting postgame that he wanted to chase a matchup against Bellinger with runs at a premium.
Still, choosing a reliever who relies heavily on a slider like Miller was also a curious choice — considering that Bellinger batted .435 with three home runs in 23 at-bats against sliders delivered by lefties this season.
“We’re trailing, we’re struggling to score runs,” Tracy said. “And when you get in spots where you’re struggling to score runs and you’re already trailing, you feel like you’ve got to be aggressive and go. … Trying to be aggressive and create tough matchups. It just didn’t work out.”
It was a frustrating end for Gray, who remains uncertain about whether or not he’ll continue playing as he enters free agency this offseason. He was one of Boston’s top players this season — going 18-5 in the regular season with a 2.72 ERA.
“I don’t know what the future holds for me,” Gray noted. “I do know that I walked off that mound with my chest back and my chin up and I can definitely be proud that I left it all out there until the ball was taken out of my hands. I still left that mound with my chest up and my chin up and I can be proud of that.”
When asked if the Red Sox would still be a team he’d consider pitching for if he wants to continue playing, Gray replied: “I don’t know.”

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Sonny Gray unable to keep Red Sox season alive in season-ending loss to Yankees in Game 2 of AL Wild Card Series - The Boston Globe
