The brash statement might have been out of character for the relatively soft-spoken pitcher, but the hard feelings? Those were hard earned, borne from Gray’s disastrous two-season stint in New York, a 2017-18 swing through the worst performance of an otherwise all-star caree
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Sonny Gray, upon being traded to the Red Sox, had just the right words to win over the Boston fan base.
“It feels good for me to go to a place where it’s easy to hate the Yankees,” Gray memorably said in December.
The brash statement might have been out of character for the relatively soft-spoken pitcher, but the hard feelings? Those were hard earned, borne from Gray’s disastrous two-season stint in New York, a 2017-18 swing through the worst performance of an otherwise all-star career.
Gray was like an alien dropped on a foreign planet, so uncomfortable under New York’s big-city lights, so reviled by the home fans who booed him non-stop by the end of his tenure, that it seemed he might never rediscover the dominance he had shown in small-market Oakland.
He did, resurrecting his career through stops in Cincinnati, Minnesota, and St. Louis, earning his place once again among the league’s best starters and landing him squarely on the Red Sox’ offseason radar. The front office liked him enough to request he waive a no-trade clause to join their ongoing rebuild. Gray’s memorable line after saying “yes” was a way of reminding himself of all he had done to make that union possible.
And Wednesday, here were those damn Yankees again, this time looming across the diamond at Yankee Stadium, the only thing between Gray, his Red Sox, and a long, cold winter. Words weren’t going to do it this time. Gray was going to have to pitch his way past the Yankees to keep the Red Sox’ season alive, the key to staving off elimination after the Sox were laughed out of Game 1, 9-0.
“The season’s on the line for us and he can handle that,” manager Chad Tracy said.
Gray wound up allowing two runs on six hits over 4⅔ innings, pulled after 70 pitches when Ben Rice began Gray’s third run through the Yankees order with a single. Gray surrendered a solo homer to Luis García Jr. in the fourth inning to open the scoring, but as on Tuesday, things truly came apart against the bullpen, resulting in a season-ending 9-2 setback.
The man who tookthe mound in Game 2 was so far removed from the shell of his former self who departed New York in 2019, recording one of the best seasons of his life this year for the Sox. Gray’s 18-5 record with a 2.72 ERA and 149 strikeouts in 29 starts anchored a rotation that was without injured ace Garrett Crochet for most of the regular season. Gray’s 36-year-old wisdom and experience, not to mention his maniacal work ethic, helped mold a young staff. To top it off with a playoff game in New York is like a gift from the redemption gods.
Gray was indefensibly awful during his tortured tenure in New York. He appeared in 41 games, making 34 starts before being demoted to the bullpen toward the end of his second season. His overall ERA was 4.51, an even uglier 5.26 in the 23 starts he made in 2018. The Yankees traded him to the Reds in January 2019. He has spent the time since then not simply regaining his form, but analyzing his failures.
“That’s a good question and it’s a fair question,” he said Tuesday. “It’s one of those things that you have a snowball … and there’s a snowball that kind of starts rolling down a hill. If you don’t ever stop it, then the snowball just gets bigger and bigger and bigger, and it picks up traction and it just gets more snow. And it just continues to go down this thing. And the bigger the snowball gets, the harder it is to stop it or take a step back.
“And for me, it just took me to get away and get myself into a different environment and then reflect on those things, reflect on what was good, what was bad, what didn’t work. And that took some time.
“But I do know that playing here made me a stronger person, made me a better man, a better husband. Ultimately, it made me a better pitcher, a better baseball player. And that’s kind of what I take from my time here.”
Ultimately, Gray expressed gratitude for his time in New York.
“I think there’s a lot of people and a lot of players that can have one bump in the road and not get back on the tracks,” he said, “and for me, there’s been bumps along the way and that may have been a little bit of a bigger bump than others. But then to be able to recenter, to refocus, to continue to have confidence in yourself and not get off the wagon, get back on the wagon and continue to move forward in your career and in your life as well … ultimately it made me a better person.”
Gray relied on all of those skills as he navigated this utterly unpredictable, wholly unexpected Red Sox season. From the early-season firing of manager Alex Cora to the midseason catching change to Adley Rutschman, from the April and May cellar-dwelling standings to the remarkable 15-game winning streak and playoff turnaround, Gray told me earlier this season, “It’s been quite the journey. I’ve never been part of anything like this.”
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Cody Bellinger takes Chad Tracy's gift, ends Red Sox season in Yankees legacy moment
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: Though Cody Bellinger didn't spend much of his childhood in the new Yankee Stadium, that should've been all the more motivation for him to join the Yankees and make this place sound like the old one as often as he possibly could. On Wednesday night, with a chance to end the Red Sox season in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, and with his champion dad Clay in the building (first pitch duties), he responded directly to Sox manager Chad Tracy opening the door with a pair of punishing blows. Payton To
item.content:encoded:
Though Cody Bellinger didn't spend much of his childhood in the new Yankee Stadium, that should've been all the more motivation for him to join the Yankees and make this place sound like the old one as often as he possibly could. On Wednesday night, with a chance to end the Red Sox season in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, and with his champion dad Clay in the building (first pitch duties), he responded directly to Sox manager Chad Tracy opening the door with a pair of punishing blows.
Payton Tolle getting the 83-pitch early hook in Game 1 was somewhat defensible. He was losing grip. He's past a career high in innings. They have the horses. Removing Sonny Gray from this do-or-die game before the end of the fifth inning, midway through a masterpiece, was one of the silliest bits of overmanaging you'll see. Bringing in Erik Miller, who was victimized with two outs in the fifth in Game 1 to get victimized again was even sillier.
Bellinger smoked a two-out RBI single off Miller to add a second run to the Yankees' lead. The next time he strode to the plate, he made a much larger impact.
Cody Bellinger cements Yankees' ownership of the Boston Red Sox
Gone. Very gone. In a snap, the Yankees turned two productive outs and a three-run mash into an 8-1 ballgame. Losing Garrett Whitlock, who surrendered the bomb, might've been the Yankees' most prudent Rule 5 Draft move in franchise history. It's called the long game.
For those keeping track at home, the 2026 Red Sox rode a 32-5 midsummer stretch to the postseason, reached within a half-game of the Yankees and got high on their own supply. From that point forward, they were much closer to .500, losing impact role players and stars alike by the bowlful. Sox fans were undeterred. They continued to crow. They loved to laugh at Aaron Judge's injury troubles. They purported to be inside Cam Schlittler's head. If they truly were in there, they might've been able to pick up some knowledge on what it takes for a pitcher to go deep into games in the postseason and dominate.
And so, for the second season in a row, the Yankees have flushed the Sox out of the postseason - Boston actually doesn't even reach October this year, which begins tomorrow. Last year, it was Schlittler, the Massachusetts native, growing up on the big stage. He helped this year, too.
But this time around, it ended with Tracy hooking Gray for no apparent reason and Bellinger, a son of pinstripes, delivering the crushing blow. Maybe, just maybe, order has returned to the universe and karma has begun to punish the brashness of Bostonians in new and unique ways. Whitlock gagging, Garrett Crochet disintegrating after an Adley Rutschman slow play (the trade target the Sox outbid the Yankees for, by the way), and Caleb Durbin making the final out ... in a game Gray should've owned ... was a pretty clever way to get it done.
Thanks, Belli.

item.title: [wral.com] Fried, Bellinger and García lead Yankees over Red Sox 9-2 for 2-game Wild Card Series sweep
item.dc:creator: RONALD BLUM
item.description: NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston. Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep. Other WRAL Top Stories “We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said. New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series start
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston.
Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep.
Other WRAL Top Stories
“We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
“The fans were electric from the first pitch and the boys were hungry. We got a young, hungry team here," Yankees captain Aaron Judge said as teammates sprayed him with bubbly during the clubhouse celebration. “This makes me feel young every single time.”
Judge missed this series because of a calf injury and isn't sure whether he will play against the Rays, who beat New York 7-6 in the season series.
“Saturday’s a long ways away," he said.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston's 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke open the game with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out leading off — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBIs that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst that put New York ahead 8-1.
“Step one,” said Bellinger, who caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay, a 2000 Yankees World Series champion. “Now we got to go into Tampa and play against a tough team."
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, lost last year's wild-card matchup after defeating the Yankees in the opener.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there was quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series and that ended for us tonight, so it’s frustrating,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “There’s a lot of things you can say, but in the moment right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it’s going to take some time to get over that.”
Boston, which also got a seventh-inning homer from Nick Sogard off Will Warren, was missing leadoff hitter Roman Anthony because of a hand injury. The Red Sox were held to a .117 average in the series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and outscored 18-2.
New York hit .382 in the series. Boston's bullpen had a 20.25 ERA.
“We played great baseball in a lot of ways here, obviously anchored by our two great starters," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Yankees batters hit .450 (9 for 20) with runners in scoring position after finishing 19th among the 30 teams with a .246 RISP during the regular season.
“I feel like it’s a whole new level from regular season to these last two days,” Austin Wells said.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García's fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just relieved.
Gray was disappointed he wasn't allowed to face Bellinger.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. "I would’ve liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. And, yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. So I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted.”
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger's homer.
"I can’t believe they were willing to face a guy like Belli with men on base there," Rice said.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year's Wild Card Series opener, hadn't pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation when he bounced a sweeper off Adley Rutschman's chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled that Jones was out. The Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner's office.
“I couldn’t believe he was there,” Boone said. "I saw the ball squirt away a little bit. I didn’t think that much of it, and looked up and I was, like, 'Oh, he’s safe.'''
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Wells' sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout and Rice, who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“Definitely wasn’t sharp from the get-go but just wanted to challenge them, not try to give any free passes, especially in the first inning," Fried said.
After a night of celebration and a day off, the Yankees will head to Florida on Friday.
“There’s just so much more to do,” Bellinger said after the big night with his father on hand. “So obviously enjoy the moment, understand how cool it is, but keep on going.”
Up Next
New York RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy Shares Honest Take on Team's Season After Wild Card Loss to Yankees originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox looked like a team of destiny. That was the case during their red-hot summer. It wasn't meant to be, as they cooled down when it mattered most, losing two games to the Yankees in the Wild Card series.
For two straight games, manager Chad Tracy took out the starting pitcher early. The Yankees took advantage, outscoring Boston 18-2. It's the second straight season the Yankees beat the Red Sox in the Wild Card series.
The Red Sox started the season as one of the worst teams in the league. In July, the team heated up with a 15-game win streak. The team also had a nine-game win streak. Boston had a Cy Young favorite in Sonny Gray and got Roman Anthony back following months on the IL.
It didn't matter during the playoffs, and Tracy understood that.
"Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there was quite a few, the goal was to win the World Series. That ended for us tonight," Tracy said after the game.
"It's frustrating. There's a lot of things you could say, but in the moment, right now, the guys only care that we lost. It's going to take some time to get over that."
Anthony left Game 1 with an injury and was taken off the roster. Garrett Crochet, out since April with an injury, returned and let up four earned runs. Meanwhile, Cam Schlittler and Max Fried shut down the Red Sox's hottest hitters.
The Red Sox must now wait a long while for Spring Training to start, while the Yankees move on to face the Rays in the American League Division Series.

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] What we learned: Chad Tracy, bullpen and historically bad offense sink Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Michael Hurley
item.description: Heading into the Wild Card Series, one could make a case that the Red Sox had a chance to beat the Yankees. It would take two or three great starts from Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and/or Ranger Suarez, it would take some timely hitting to put two or three runs on the board per game, and it would take some lockdown relief innings from the back end of the bullpen. item.content:encoded:
Heading into the Wild Card Series, one could make a case that the Red Sox had a chance to beat the Yankees. It would take two or three great starts from Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and/or Ranger Suarez, it would take some timely hitting to put two or three runs on the board per game, and it would take some lockdown relief innings from the back end of the bullpen.
Yet the Red Sox only got decent starts from Tolle and Gray, they set a new franchise record for offensive utility, and their bullpen was a catastrophe.
And the cherry on top was that their manager, who inked a contract extension last week, showed he certainly does not know how to manage in the postseason.
Other than that, did you enjoy the series?
Here's everything we learned from the ever-so-brief two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series, as the 2026 team technically failed to get as far as the 2025 Red Sox.
Red Sox set ugly new franchise record
Red Sox history spans 126 seasons, so it was a bit surprising to see the broadcast note early in Game 2 that Boston was in the midst of rewriting franchise history with the longest scoring drought to start a postseason ever.
Obviously, the Red Sox' offense has been stagnant (or worse) for weeks, but 26 previous trips to the playoffs, you'd figure that they had started off with a scoreless game and a half before.
Alas, nope. This drought was historic. It ended at 14.2 innings, broken by Willson Contreras' solo shot with two outs in the sixth inning.
And while some of it may be explained by the absences of Roman Anthony and Mickey Gasper, there's no excuse for a playoff team to be this helpless at the plate.
Chad Tracy is not a big-game manager right now
There may have been a case for Chad Tracy to pull Payton Tolle for Erik Miller in Game 1. Not really, but there could have been a case made for Miller's sinker being more effective against Ben Rice than Tolle's fastball.
Yet there's simply no way to understand why one night later, Tracy made the exact same move.
With Sonny Gray at just 70 pitches and the Yankees leading 1-0 with two outs in the fifth inning, Tracy went back to Miller, this time with two runners on base and Cody Bellinger at the plate. The left-left matchup was presumably the reason for the call, but Bellinger crushes sliders from lefties. And when Miller threw a slider to Bellinger ... he delivered.
Bellinger singled home a run, and Miller then gave up another hit to Luis Garcia Jr. The Red Sox only got out of the inning because Rice was caught at home after an aggressive send on that second single.
Gray's pitch count of 70 was tied for his second-lowest of the season, and though he had allowed two singles in the fifth, his body of work over the season and over the past 13 years gave him a much better chance of escaping the mini jam than Miller, who had a 2.045 WHIP and 7.36 ERA in the month of September and who gave up a home run and a single while getting just one out the night before.
If Tracy was insistent that Gray had to come out of the game, he had, quite literally, every high-leverage arm available to him. Instead, he went with Erik Miller.
And with that same complement of arms available in the bottom of the sixth inning, Tracy went with Garrett Crochet, who hasn't pitched in a game since April 25. It didn't go well.
Tracy also showed a lack of feel for the moment when he let leadoff hitter Jahmai Jones, who batted .129 with a .432 OPS over the final 13 games of the regular season and who struck out looking twice, to take his third at-bat in the sixth inning, with the Red Sox trailing 2-0.
Given Boston's offensive ineptitude, the bullpen decisions are perhaps all moot. But had this been a close series, or if the Red Sox find themselves in one in the future, Tracy will carry some major doubt regarding his ability to manage those games.
Simply put, Chad Tracy did not do a single thing right in these two high-stakes games.
More Red Sox Coverage
Luis Garcia Jr.'s home run was great hitting, not bad pitching
It took until the fourth inning for the Yankees to get to Sonny Gray, but the solo homer he allowed to Luis Garcia Jr. didn't come on a bad pitch at all.
Leading off the fourth, Garcia was behind in the count 1-2 when Gray tried to bury a sweeper down and in to the lefty. Gray hit his spot with a pitch that was set to hit the bottom of the strike zone. But Garcia simply stayed on the pitch and went down and got it.
Luis Gar-SEE-YA 🦁 pic.twitter.com/GqxScAqskG
— New York Yankees (@Yankees) October 1, 2026
With the Red Sox starved for runs, Garcia's solo shot was a jarring reminder that all it takes is one good swing to put a run on the board.
Boston eventually got that swing from Contreras in the sixth, but that jolt of hope for the visiting team didn't last long.
What could have been with Garrett Crochet ...
If you just looked at the box score, you'd be shocked to see Garrett Crochet's line. He faced four batters, allowing all of them to score. He didn't record an out, despite getting Spencer Jones to chase strike three to start the sixth inning.
Of course, some of that outcome was fair, as Crochet allowed back-to-back singles. But Caleb Durbin couldn't get the out at first on what was intended to be a sacrifice bunt, Crochet left with the bases loaded, and Garrett Whitlock -- who had a dreadful night -- couldn't limit the damage at all.
Such an outcome was perhaps expected, considering Crochet has not pitched in a game since April 25 due to shoulder problems. But you also can't help but wonder what would have happened if Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras hadn't combined to bungle Crochet's inning-opening strikeout of Jones.
Rutschman took an extra beat to pounce on the ball that had bounced off his chest, and then he took an extra step before firing to first base. There, Contreras was planted on the back side of the base instead of the front. As a result, Jones was able to beat the throw.
Credit to Aaron Boone for challenging that call, which was initially an out on the field, but really, it wasn't even close.
Rutschman then compounded the matter by sailing a throw into center field when Jones stole second, allowing the runner to take third before scoring on a single. Had Rutschman made either of those two throws, it's fair to wonder how differently Crochet's inning could have gone.
Summing up the season
There will be plenty of time in the coming months to eulogize this season, but really, despite the 32-5 stretch in the summer, it wasn't one to celebrate.
Last year's team won a game in the Wild Card Series, a disappointing ending. This year's team couldn't even do that.
Injuries to Crochet and Anthony were certainly impactful, but this roster -- and particularly the offense -- was not built to contend for a World Series. The Red Sox scored two or fewer runs in 13 of their final 23 games, averaging 2.5 runs per game over that stretch.
With the season on the line, the Red Sox had Jahmai Jones, Nate Eaton and Nick Sogard in their starting lineup.
After trading three of their top-five prospects to acquire Adley Rutschman, the catcher batted .222 with a .688 OPS in the regular season before going 1-for-8 in the playoffs.
Willson Contreras, a 34-year-old former catcher with a lot of MLB miles on him, was worn down by the end of the season. Caleb Durbin, whose lows outnumbered his highs this year, went 0-for-7 in the playoffs. Ceddanne Rafaela posted the same numbers, too.
The return for Marcelo Mayer was Erik Miller, who made a strong first impression but played a pivotal role in sinking the team's chances in both postseason losses after an extremely unreliable final month of the season.
The starting pitching staff was excellent, and the bullpen was elite. But the overall roster construction will lead to plenty of questions about Craig Breslow's ability to build a real winner. Likewise, the two playoff games cast some serious doubt on whether Chad Tracy is a manager capable of winning games in October.
The 15-game winning streak and 32-5 stretch might have led to some internal victory laps and the decisions to stick with Breslow and Tracy for the foreseeable future. But the 2026 Red Sox, on the whole, were what they were: mediocre. And having been stuck in mediocrity (or worse) for half a decade, there won't be much more patience in and around Boston for it to continue.
Technically, the historic season turnaround may have been a positive, as making the playoffs beats bottoming out more often than not. But considering that the Red Sox likely could have loaded up on promising players by selling off veteran pieces like Contreras, Gray, Aroldis Chapman and anyone else at the deadline, that run in July may have hurt the Red Sox in the long term -- especially with the prospect haul that went out to acquire Rutschman.
In any event, the Red Sox finished as the third-best team in the AL East, and they failed to win a single playoff game, getting outscored 18-2 in their lone playoff series. That's the final word on the season as the long offseason -- potentially longer than most -- awaits.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Sonny Gray's premature exit curses Chad Tracy, Red Sox into brutal Wild Card ending
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans didn't want to see Chad Tracy emerge from the dugout in the bottom of the fifth inning. He should've learned from his Game 1 mistake.
But in Wild Card Game 2, Tracy pulled Sonny Gray after 4.2 frames to swap him for Erik Miller, just as he did with Payton Tolle the day before. Gray was having a better night than Tolle, though — he collected five strikeouts and allowed two runs on six hits. He was living on the edges and racked up swing-and-miss through 70 pitches.
Miller entered the game and immediately let up a single to Cody Bellinger. The Yankees took a 2-0 lead. The run was charged to Gray, but it didn't have to be that way. Miller posted a brutal September and struggled similarly in his first Wild Card outing. The choice to turn to him again, especially with the season on the line, is inexplicable.
Tracy's bullpen management didn't get any better. Garrett Crochet entered the game in the sixth inning and immediately got unlucky. Spencer Jones struck out swinging at a pitch in the dirt and Adley Rutschman couldn't get a good block on it, which allowed Jones to take first base. Crochet pitched decently well, avoiding the middle of the plate, but he couldn't collect an out before New York plated another run and loaded the bases.
Chad Tracy pulling Sonny Gray early led to the Red Sox's downfall in Wild Card Game 2, as it did in Game 1 with Payton Tolle
Going to Crochet while the game was still within reach was another strange choice by Tracy. Crochet hadn't pitched in the big leagues since April 25 due to two different shoulder injuries — the Red Sox had no idea how he would fare in a game, but went to him anyway despite having Jake Bennett available.
Tracy's bullpen management choices certainly didn't make the Red Sox any better this series, but their offense deserves some blame for the way the Wild Card series went. Willson Contreras and Nick Sogard contributed solo home runs to prevent another shutout, but no one else gave them any help. Four hits, seven strikeouts and 0-for-2 with runners in scoring position won't cut it against any playoff team, let alone the Yankees' utterly dominant pitching staff.
Even so, Boston got more offense in the win-or-go-home game than it did in Game 1, and bad bullpen management did the Red Sox in again. Had Tracy kept Gray in the game, the score could've stayed closer and the game might've actually been winnable. Instead, an incredible, memorable season came to an end without ever reaching October, and the Red Sox did it to themselves.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox ace Sonny Gray frustrated by lack of trust from manager during Yankees rout
item.dc:creator: MIKE FITZPATRICK
item.description: NEW YORK (AP) — With the Boston bats ice cold at Yankee Stadium again, a couple of quick hooks by Red Sox rookie manager Chad Tracy led to another early postseason exit. And top starter Sonny Gray wasn't happy about being lifted after only 70 pitches. "I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — With the Boston bats ice cold at Yankee Stadium again, a couple of quick hooks by Red Sox rookie manager Chad Tracy led to another early postseason exit.
And top starter Sonny Gray wasn't happy about being lifted after only 70 pitches.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact," Gray said. "I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
For the second consecutive season, the Red Sox were sent home for the winter by their biggest rivals as the New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory Wednesday night and a two-game sweep of their Wild Card Series.
Boston was outscored 18-2 overall and left to lament a miserable finish to this roller-coaster ride of a season that included Tracy taking over when Alex Cora was fired in April.
Tracy's decision-making came under scrutiny after both playoff games against the Yankees. In Boston's 9-0 defeat a night earlier, Tracy pulled rookie starter Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings and 83 pitches in a 1-0 game.
Last year, the Red Sox won their Wild Card Series opener before losing to New York in a deciding Game 3 as they got overpowered by Cam Schlittler, who pitched another playoff gem against his hometown team Tuesday night.
"To have it end here two times in a row is tough," shortstop Trevor Story said.
Facing a Yankees lineup missing injured slugger Aaron Judge, the Red Sox gave up 26 hits in two games despite a pair of effective performances from their starting pitchers.
At the plate, Boston mustered only seven hits and finally snapped a 26-inning postseason scoring drought that dated to last year when Willson Contreras homered just over the right-center fence in the sixth Wednesday.
"It's obviously been an eventful year," Tracy said. "In the moment right now you can't think much more other than anything but the fact that we just lost a playoff series."
Needing a victory to extend their season, the Red Sox sent Gray to the mound and the 18-game winner certainly gave them a chance. Boston trailed 1-0 in the fifth when the right-hander allowed a two-out single to Ben Rice that put runners at the corners.
Tracy then yanked Gray, eager to hand the ball to baseball's best bullpen during the regular season.
"I felt good. You know, I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I felt like I was just out there competing. And yeah, I mean, I got clipped for a solo homer and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I was just executing what I wanted to do," Gray said. "I'm frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions."
Asked about the move, Contreras put his finger over his lips to zip them shut.
"It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to do, because this is baseball," he said. "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day you are going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
In both games of the series, Tracy gave the ball to left-handed reliever Erik Miller after taking out his starting pitcher.
On Tuesday, Rice greeted Miller with a 423-foot solo homer to straightaway center field.
On Wednesday, Tracy summoned Miller to face a different left-handed hitter, Cody Bellinger — who batted .274 against lefties this season and .259 versus right-handers. In fact, his .310 batting average against left-handers over the past two years was the best of any left-handed hitter in the majors.
Bellinger made Tracy and the Red Sox pay, lining an RBI single to right field.
"We're struggling to score runs," Tracy said. "And when you get in spots where you're struggling to score runs and you're already trailing, you feel like you've got to be aggressive and go."
Back from a shoulder injury, ace starter Garrett Crochet entered in the sixth for his first outing since April 25 and first relief appearance since 2023 with the Chicago White Sox. The left-hander opened with a strikeout, but Spencer Jones reached safely on a wild pitch, and Crochet never got an out.
Bellinger's three-run homer off right-hander Garrett Whitlock capped a six-run inning that made it 8-1, and the Red Sox were done. A bullpen that led the majors with a 3.00 ERA during the regular season finished this series with a 20.25 ERA after giving up 15 runs, 15 hits and seven walks in 6 2/3 innings, with a .484 opponents' batting average.
Boston's latest downfall in the Bronx was a crushing end to a wild 2026 season for the Red Sox, who stumbled to a 32-46 start. Tracy was the skipper at Triple-A Worcester before getting promoted to interim manager in Boston, and the team finally began to take off with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway Park in late June.
After clinching a wild-card spot last week, the Red Sox removed the interim tag and named Tracy the 49th manager in team history, signing him to a three-year contract that runs through the 2029 season, with a club option for 2030. The team also exercised the 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
"I wasn't there for the highs and lows," Crochet said. "For this team to do what it did do, to make it to this point, was nothing short of miraculous."
Led by Gray and Contreras, among others, the Red Sox went on a 15-game winning streak in July that equaled a franchise record and used a 32-5 surge to climb back into contention. They became the fourth team in major league history to reach the postseason after falling 14 games under .500, and the first to qualify after losing as many as 44 of its first 75.
Gray, who can become a free agent after the World Series, went around the clubhouse to hug each of his teammates following Wednesday's defeat.
"I'm proud of what we accomplished," the pitcher said. "We were left for dead there for a while."
___

item.title: [wcvb.com] Roman Anthony out of Red Sox lineup in Game 2 of Wild Card Series against Yankees after hurting hand

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox's Roman Anthony diagnosed with right hand strain, ineligible to return until ALCS
The Red Sox announced that Roman Anthony would not be in the Boston Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of their AL Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees on Wednesday night, a day after leaving the opener because of hand pain.
In a statement on Wednesday, the team announced that Anthony was diagnosed with a right-hand strain and was substituted off the roster.
Anthony can no longer participate in the remainder of the Wild Card Series or the American League Division Series if Boston advances.
He would be eligible to return for the American League Championship Series.
"I feel sick to my stomach. I haven't slept much. It doesn't feel real, to be honest," Anthony said Wednesday. "I been through so many emotions and feelings to get the same news again and even worse, it's hard to have an answer to anything right now."
The team announced that infielder Curtis Mead will replace Anthony on the Wild Card Series roster.
Anthony said he wasn't sure what the treatment plan would be currently to remedy his hand injury.
"Once we decided I wasn't going to play today, that's all that really mattered," Anthony said. "All that mattered was putting the team in the best situation to win."
Batting leadoff as a designated hitter in his playoff debut Tuesday, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against Cam Schlittler before getting lifted for a pinch hitter with his team trailing by two runs in the sixth inning of a 9-0 loss.
Boston manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings. The 22-year-old Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29 with an injury to the same hand.
"Unfortunately, I checked swing on my second at-bat and I knew right then and there it was time to get it looked and put somebody else in the game that would have a better chance to win," Anthony said.
“He’s obviously coming off that. You’ll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it’s fine, it goes away,” Tracy said. “Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable.”
Jahmai Jones was set to hit leadoff as the DH with the Red Sox one loss from elimination, followed in the batting order by catcher Adley Rutschman, first baseman Willson Contreras, right fielder Wilyer Abreu, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, third baseman Caleb Durbin, second baseman Nick Sogard, shortstop Trevor Story and left fielder Nate Eaton.
Sonny Gray was set to start on the mound for Boston against one of his former teams.
One of baseball’s premier prospects when he debuted last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBIs and a .735 OPS in 55 games this season.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] AL Wild Card Series Game 2: Max Fried vs. Sonny Gray
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Nielsen
item.description: In the words of a Yankee legend, it was dèja vu all over again in the Bronx last night as Cam Schlittler continued crafting a legend of his own. Just like last season, Schlittler delivered a gem of a performance against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, staking New York to a 1-0 series lead and giving them an opportunity to close the affair out early tonight. But unlike last year's three-game set, in which the Yankee offense never fully erupted, the lineup finally achieved escape velocity. Be
item.content:encoded:
In the words of a Yankee legend, it was dèja vu all over again in the Bronx last night as Cam Schlittler continued crafting a legend of his own. Just like last season, Schlittler delivered a gem of a performance against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, staking New York to a 1-0 series lead and giving them an opportunity to close the affair out early tonight. But unlike last year's three-game set, in which the Yankee offense never fully erupted, the lineup finally achieved escape velocity. Ben Rice and his four hits, two homers, and six RBI, led the charge — but the bottom of the lineup contributed their fair share as well.
In other words, the Yankees played the perfect ballgame last night. Max Fried will be tasked with carrying the momentum into Game 2. Fried's second season in pinstripes has been marred by a couple of IL stints limiting him to just 20 starts and 112.2 innings, but when he's been healthy, he's been just as good as in 2025. He'll be pitching on seven days' rest in Game 2 — his last appearance was an up-and-down start against the Rays, in which Tampa clinched the AL East.
As far as the recent track record against Boston, Fried has been quite effective. He only faced them twice this season: one was a short start from when he was returning from his latest injury, the other an eight-inning masterpiece in April from before the Red Sox got it together under new manager Chad Tracy. In Game 1 of last year's WCS, he provided 6.1 scoreless innings, scattering four hits three walks while striking out six. The Yankees couldn't hold onto the narrow 1-0 lead he had defended, and sabotaged their own comeback effort after loading the bases with nobody out in the ninth inning. None of that was Max's fault, of course. Provided the lineup supports him, an effort like last year's will be more than enough.
Old friend Sonny Gray never caught on with the Yankees in 2017 and 2018, but he'll have no choice but to step up under the Yankee Stadium lights with Boston's season on the line. Over his first season with the Red Sox, the steady veteran turned in yet another outstanding season, leading the AL with 18 wins (don't think that doesn't mean anything to him) and pitching to a 2.72 ERA. That's the thing about the Red Sox' pitching: they have lots of exciting youngsters like Payton Tolle, who pitched last night, but they also routinely get the most out of their veteran pitchers too. Gray faced New York twice in June and pitched well both times. The latter outing was his best start of the season by game score — one hit, one walk, nine strikeouts over 7.1 scoreless innings.
Unsurprisingly, Aaron Boone's lineup for Game 2 is nearly unrecognizable when compared with the Game 1 starting nine. It's a history-making card: according to James Smyth of the YES Network, it's the first time a team has put eight lefty batters — switch hitters not included — in the same lineup in the postseason. The portside octet includes Trent Grisham, who entered late last night for his first action off the IL. Rice will ascend to the leadoff spot, with Cody Bellinger and Luis Garcia Jr. to follow. Spencer Jones hits cleanup and plays right field ahead of George Lombard Jr., the lone righty to get the start. Jazz Chisholm Jr. draws in at the keystone, Grisham bats in the seven-spot after him, Austin Wells will bat eighth, and Ryan McMahon starts at third and will hit ninth. Naturally, expect plenty of right-handed bats to come off the bench against a lefty-heavy Boston staff once Gray's start concludes.

First pitch: 8:00 p.m. ET

item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony out of Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of Wild Card Series
The Red Sox season will rest on the arm of starting pitcher Sonny Gray as the team takes on the New York Yankees on Wednesday in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series.
The Sox won't have the services of Roman Anthony, who appeared to reaggravate his hand injury during the team's 9-0 loss in Game 1.
"We actually sent him back to Boston last evening to get there so he could be early in the morning and re-image the hand, which shows additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. "So he's sore and obviously not in the lineup."
Anthony will be replaced on the roster by infielder Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist during his debut with the Red Sox on July 27. Anthony would eligible to return to the lineup for the American League Championship Series.
The Sox will have long odds to beat to continue their playoff run. Teams taking a 1-0 lead in a three-game wild-card series have gone on to win that series 21 out of 24 times, 17 times with a sweep.
Home teams have won all nine series in which they have won the first game.
On Tuesday, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler and the rest of the pitching staff held the Sox to just three hits.
Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle might have been the team's best player, but manager Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning of a 1-run game. Reliever Erik Miller immediately gave up a homer to Dartmouth College graduate Ben Rice, and it was all downhill from there.
On Wednesday night, Gray will pitch opposite Yankees starter Max Fried.

New York took a 1-0 lead in the best-of-three series with a 9-0 victory. Manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a
item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony is out for the foreseeable future and is no longer on the Wild Card roster after he left with a right hand injury Tuesday night.
Batting leadoff as the Red Sox designated hitter in his playoff debut, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against before getting lifted for a pinch hitter with his team trailing 2-0 in the sixth inning. New York took a 1-0 lead in the best-of-three series with a 9-0 victory.
Manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings. The 22-year-old Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29 with an injury to the same hand. Tracy said it doesn't appear the latest injury is necessarily related, as it involves muscles in the wrist.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," Anthony told reporters on Wednesday. "Last night just felt a little more intense, little bit more harsh than past swings have and lingered a little bit longer than the ones I was used to had. So it just was super alarming and got to the point where it was tough to grip a bat."
The manager said that after the game, Anthony returned to Boston for imaging on his hand, which found "additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before."
Anthony is not in Wednesday night's lineup, when the Red Sox must win to extend their season. Jahmai Jones is leading off at DH in Anthony's absence.
Wednesday night, the team announced that infielder Curtis Mead replaced Anthony on the Wild Card roster. That means that if the Red Sox advance to the ALDS, Anthony would be out for that round as well.
One of baseball's premier prospects when he arrived in the majors last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBIs and a .735 OPS in 55 regular-season games this season.
"He's a really good player. Certainly not something we wanted to happen and having him in there is important. But can't reiterate enough, we've dealt with things like this all year. But the show goes on, you've got to play tonight and be able to win a ballgame," Tracy said.
The manager added that it is not yet known if Anthony will need surgery.
Sonny Gray is on the mound for the Red Sox in Game 2, which is scheduled to start at 8:15 p.m.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Red Sox must hope Sonny Gray justifies their choice with Ranger Suarez's playoff pedigree looming
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: It's do-or-die for the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card series. Game 1 was a disaster — while Payton Tolle was able to hold the New York Yankees to one run in his 4 ⅔ innings, it really didn't matter because the offense couldn't get anything going the entire game. They now head into Game 2 with one thing in mind: put runs on the board. The offense will need to find something against Max Fried, and they are going to need the pitching staff to keep them in the game as best it can. Sonny G
item.content:encoded:
It's do-or-die for the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card series. Game 1 was a disaster — while Payton Tolle was able to hold the New York Yankees to one run in his 4 ⅔ innings, it really didn't matter because the offense couldn't get anything going the entire game.
They now head into Game 2 with one thing in mind: put runs on the board. The offense will need to find something against Max Fried, and they are going to need the pitching staff to keep them in the game as best it can. Sonny Gray will take the bump for the Sox in the pivotal matchup, but he may be the wrong choice.
Over the offseason, the Red Sox made two big pitching acquisitions: Gray and Ranger Suarez. Gray was a veteran who was essentially in the last year of his deal, meant to be a mid-rotation arm. Suarez was meant to be the No. 2 behind Garrett Crochet, and his playoff excellence was supposed to help after what the Red Sox starters struggled (besides Crochet) in the Wild Card last year.
Recency bias is influencing the Red Sox's starter decision for Game 2 of the Wild Card
Suarez is one of the best playoff pitchers in baseball ever. His 1.48 ERA in the postseason is the sixth-lowest for any pitcher with 40 or more playoff innings pitched. He has held hitters to a .201 batting average while striking out over nine per nine innings. His numbers in the regular season are great, but the selling point was what he could do in October.
Now, of course, the regular season played a part in the decision to start Gray in Game 2. The righty was dominant all year and could finish in the top five in Cy Young voting. Gray had a 2.72 ERA this season over 169 innings. It's hard not to guarantee a pitcher who performed so well in the regular season a start in the postseason when he was so influential in getting the team there. But Suarez is on the team for this exact moment.
In a win-or-go-home scenario, it's hard not to hand the ball to the pitcher who slows his heartbeat in the playoffs. If the Sox can win this game, it will be great to have Suarez pitching Game 3, but the Red Sox need to keep themselves in the game. Gray could be the one to do it, but the track record says Suarez is the better choice.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees vs. Sonny Gray: Batter-Pitcher Stats for Game 2

To end the best-of-three series early, the Yanks will have to hit well against Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are hoping to eliminate the Boston Red Sox on Wednesday night in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series.
To end the best-of-three series early, the Yanks will have to hit well against Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray.
The good news for the Yanks is that some of their lineup has a positive history against Gray.
The bad news for the Yankees is that Gray had an 18-5 record this season with a 2.72 ERA. Even at 36 years old, he's still one of the most effective pitchers in baseball.
Boston has to feel good about giving Gray the ball with their season on the line. It's do-or-die for them.
The Yankees will have confidence, too, coming off a 9-0 win in Game 1.
This rivalry rarely disappoints, and it shouldn't on Wednesday night, either.
Yankees vs. Sonny Gray
The Yankees' current roster as a whole has faced Gray for 161 at bats.
In that sample size, they've got 37 hits — for a .230 average — with a .642 OPS.
So all told, it's not a great look for the Yankees.
This is the hitter-by-hitter breakdown:
- Jose Caballero: 3-for-9
- Luis Garcia Jr.: 4-for-10, 1 double, 1 HR, 1 K
- Spencer Jones: 3-for-6, 1 double, 3 Ks
A couple things stand out.
First is that Goldschmidt line — he's one of the best hitters in this era of baseball and somehow has just one hit in 26 at bats against Gray.
The lines of Grisham, Garcia, Rice and Rosario are all encouraging, though. It'll be interesting to see how manager Aaron Boone might deploy them on Wednesday.
Sonny Gray Stats With Yankees
It's worth noting that Gray also spent time pitching for the Yankees.
He was traded to the Yanks from the A's midway through the 2017 season.
In the back half of the 2017 season while with the Yankees, Gray had a 3.72 ERA in 11 outings.
He then pitched 30 times for the Yanks in 2018 and had a 4.90 ERA.
There was concern that the small-statured Gray might not hold up over the long haul, and the Yankees didn't keep him around any longer.
But then he went to the Reds, and the Twins, and the Cardinals, and now the Red Sox — and Gray is still going strong.
Even if the Yankees had kept Gray longer, he likely wouldn't still be wearing the pinstripes by this stage. So he's trying to hand New York a loss on Wednesday night that would send this one to Game 3.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees vs. Sonny Gray: Batter-Pitcher Stats for Game 2 appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are in danger of watching their season come to a close in Yankee Stadium for the second consecutive year. The offense showed zero signs of life as the Yankees cruised to a 9-0 victory headlined by 10 strikeouts from growing Red Sox killer Cam Schlittler. Payton Tolle did enough on the mound as the Game 1 starter. His team was clearly just unable to do their part around them.
Now, the Red Sox fall into the need of a historic response given that just 3 of 24 teams to lose the opener in the Wild Card round have come back to win the series. For starters, Boston sends 18-game winner Sonny Gray to the mound. He flirted with a no-hitter the last time he faced New York in June and tallied a 1.98 ERA against the Yankees in 2026.
The Yankees counter with Max Fried, who has battled some inconsistencies in his ramp-up period from an injury return. The southpaw does have a sparkling 1.93 career ERA against the Red Sox in addition to a brilliant start in Game 1 last year with 6 1/3 scoreless innings, which his bullpen ruined in Boston's 3-1 victory. To best combat the talented lefty, Jahmai Jones slots in leading off as the designated hitter. Caleb Durbin moves up to the sixth spot and Nate Eaton – another right-handed bat – gets the nod in left field.
After being shut out in consecutive postseason games, the Red Sox must find a way to score runs and now do so without Roman Anthony, who will come off the ALWC roster with new and aggravated injuries in his right hand. It's an uphill challenge undoubtedly, though it's one Boston must be ready for in order to extend the season.

Needing to waive a no-trade clause for the deal to go through, Gray said one factor in the decision was that it felt good to “go to a place now where it’s easy to hate the Yankees.” “I never wanted to go there in the first place,” said Gray, who spent the end of 2017 and all of 2018 with the Yankees after a trade from the A’s. After struggling to a 4.90 ERA in 2018, the Yankees shipped Gray to the Reds, where
item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray didn’t mince words when he joined the Red Sox via trade this past offseason. Needing to waive a no-trade clause for the deal to go through, Gray said one factor in the decision was that it felt good to “go to a place now where it’s easy to hate the Yankees.”
“I never wanted to go there in the first place,” said Gray, who spent the end of 2017 and all of 2018 with the Yankees after a trade from the A’s. After struggling to a 4.90 ERA in 2018, the Yankees shipped Gray to the Reds, where he became an All-Star in 2019.
Now, the 36-year-old righty will get another up-close taste of The Rivalry.
Gray will get the start Wednesday as the Red Sox face elimination at Yankee Stadium in Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series. The Yankees won Game 1, 9-0, behind a dominant Cam Schlittler start.
“As far as reception, this or that, it will be what it will be,” Gray said before Tuesday’s game. “I'm not going to sit here and try to control something that I can't control because I ultimately have no control over that.
“It will be what it will be, and I'll just do my part to be ready to go out there and compete and to pitch and to go win a game.”
Gray described his time in New York as a “snowball” with “a lot of outside this, outside that, unfamiliarity with me and my situation and my family.” He added that it took time and a different environment to reflect on what happened.
“But I do know that playing here [New York] made me a stronger person, made me a better man, a better husband,” Gray said. “Ultimately, it made me a better pitcher, a better baseball player. And that's kind of what I take from my time here.”
Gray got back to his best self in his first year in Boston after two seasons with the Cardinals. Leading MLB with 18 wins in 29 starts, the 14-year veteran turned in a 2.72 ERA. He owned a 2.79 ERA in 2023 for the Twins, when he finished as the AL Cy Young runner-up.
Gray faced the Yankees twice in the 2026 regular season. The Red Sox won both games, one at Yankee Stadium and one at Fenway Park. Gray turned in 6 1/3 innings of three-run ball his first time and 7 1/3 scoreless frames the second, striking out nine and flirting with a no-hitter.
The Red Sox will need that version of Gray on Wednesday with their backs against the wall. After all, teams taking a 1-0 lead in a three-game Wild Card series have gone on to win the series 21 of 24 times (88%), including 17 two-game sweeps. Home teams have won all nine series in which they have gone ahead 1-0, including eight sweeps.
“I feel good,” Gray said. “I think the atmosphere will be a high-level, high-energy, intense playoff atmosphere, which, as a player that's played for a while, who's been around, that's what you want, right? For me, that's what keeps you wanting to continue to come back and play.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] The Red Sox season hinges on Sonny Gray
item.dc:creator: Jacob Roy
item.description: The Red Sox are up against the wall. Cam Schlittler, once again, shoved against the Red Sox in game one, throwing 117 pitches in a 6.1-inning shutout before handing it over to the bullpen. Paul Blackburn and John Schreiber shut the door, keeping the Red Sox off the scoreboard to win game one, 9-0. Coming into this season, the winner of game one has won 15 of 16 Wild Card series since playoff expansion. The only exception is the Yankees over the Red Sox last season. If the Red Sox want to keep th
item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are up against the wall. Cam Schlittler, once again, shoved against the Red Sox in game one, throwing 117 pitches in a 6.1-inning shutout before handing it over to the bullpen. Paul Blackburn and John Schreiber shut the door, keeping the Red Sox off the scoreboard to win game one, 9-0. Coming into this season, the winner of game one has won 15 of 16 Wild Card series since playoff expansion. The only exception is the Yankees over the Red Sox last season.
If the Red Sox want to keep their season alive, it comes down to Sonny Gray. Let's think about it in innings. The Red Sox used five relievers on Tuesday night: Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Alec Gamboa, Wyatt Olds, and Brayan Bello.
Erik Miller was excellent immediately after being acquired, but his September, as well as his career-long control issues, should reduce him to only low-leverage spots. Greg Weissert can potentially provide an inning, but he's not an arm to trust on back-to-back days in a sticky spot. Alec Gamboa and Wyatt Olds were both late additions to the roster, and neither looked particularly up to the job in game one, while Brayan Bello has never pitched two days in a row in the major leagues.
That leaves Ranger Suarez, Garrett Crochet, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman, and Jake Bennett as the unused pitchers, alongside today's starter Sonny Gray.
Ranger Suarez is set to start game three. Garrett Crochet is a complete unknown. He hasn't pitched since April, and he was ineffective when he was on the mound. If he's healthy, I'd expect him to be able to get outs, but who knows where he's truly at health-wise. Garrett Whitlock has been one of the best relievers in baseball, but his longest outing of the season is 1.1 innings. He's only thrown more than 30 pitches once this season, and it came in an outing in which he walked two hitters. Extending him for more than one inning could be a tricky proposition. And then there's Aroldis Chapman. Chapman, like Whitlock, has been fantastic, but hasn't got more than three outs in a game this season. If you put those three arms together and assign two innings to Crochet, that's four innings. Of course, given the stakes, they could extend Whitlock or Chapman, but their effectiveness after three outs is a relative mystery. If you want to give Jake Bennett an inning or two, you could, but he doesn't seem like an arm they'd go to unless they were trailing, and there's no need to eat innings in a do-or-die game.
The offense was, at least in terms of scoring, the worst in baseball in September. Roman Anthony was lost in the middle of game one, and the rest of the lineup couldn't touch Schlittler. If I were a betting man, I wouldn't put money on them putting a lot of runs on the board against Max Fried. If they want a chance to win the game, they'll need to keep the Yankees off the board, and with the lack of quality innings in the bullpen, that means getting length out of Sonny Gray.
Gray has been the Red Sox best starter by ERA this season. He's gone at least six innings in 22 of his 29 starts. In two starts against the Yankees, he's allowed three earned runs over 13.2 innings pitched with 12 strikeouts and 3 walks. Despite a 14-year career, Gray has only thrown in six postseason games. In those six games, he has a 3.26 ERA, but has only pitched more than five innings once (an 8-inning shoutout for the Athletics against the Tigers in 2013). For the Red Sox to win today, they need Sonny Gray to turn in one of the best postseason performances of his career.
Fortunately, Chad Tracy can unload the clip in game two, because in playoff baseball terms, game three might as well be in six months. The Red Sox need to play every card they have to keep the season alive, but Sonny Gray keeping the Yankees off the scoreboard for as long as possible is the key.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Red Sox’ Sonny Gray compares time with Yankees to a growing downhill snowball
item.dc:creator: James O'Connell
item.description: The Boston Red Sox starter in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card series on Wednesday needs no introduction to the boo birds. He’s got plenty of familiarity with the Bronx cheer, unfortunately for him, coming from his time with the Yankees. Sonny Gray will toe the slab for Chad Tracy’s squad in a pivotal playoff game back in the place that was home to arguably the lowest point of his MLB career. “I came from Oakland, and Oakland to [New York]. I think that maybe during my time there was a lot of outside
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox starter in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card series on Wednesday needs no introduction to the boo birds. He’s got plenty of familiarity with the Bronx cheer, unfortunately for him, coming from his time with the Yankees.
Sonny Gray will toe the slab for Chad Tracy’s squad in a pivotal playoff game back in the place that was home to arguably the lowest point of his MLB career.
“I came from Oakland, and Oakland to [New York]. I think that maybe during my time there was a lot of outside this, outside that, unfamiliarity with me and my situation and my family,” Gray said before Tuesday’s Game 1. “It’s kind of like one of those things that you have a snowball or whatever, right?
“And there’s a snowball that kind of starts rolling down a hill. If you don’t ever stop it, then the snowball just gets bigger and bigger and bigger, and it picks up traction, and it just gets more snow. And it just continues to go down this thing. And then the bigger the snowball gets, the harder it is to stop it or take a step back.
“And for me, it just took me to get away and get myself into a different environment and then reflect on those things, right, like reflect on what was good, what was bad, what didn’t work. And that took some time.”
Gray pitched 41 games during his season-and-a-half with the Bombers — 4.51 ERA — and Yankee faithful will surely remember his time with the team on Wednesday.
The veteran starter is expecting the obvious in terms of the reception he’ll receive as he goes out to try and win a postseason game for the Red Sox.
“I think it will be a playoff energy on the road, playoff atmosphere on the road,” said Gray. “As far as reception, this or that, it will be what it will be. I’m not going to sit here and try to control something that I can’t control because I ultimately have no control over that.
“It will be what it will be, and I’ll just do my part to be ready to go out there and compete and to pitch and to go win a game.”
Gray was acquired from the Athletics at the 2017 trade deadline prior to the Bombers’ unexpected and memorable run to Game 7 of the ALCS. The 36-year-old was acquired to be a frontline starter behind Luis Severino at the very beginning of the ‘Baby Bombers’ era.
The right-hander’s first run with the Yanks was respectable as he pitched to a 3.72 ERA in 11 games during the 2017 season and even added a strong ALCS start, throwing five innings and allowing one earned run against the Houston Astros. However, the wheels fell off in 2018, when he owned a 4.90 ERA in 30 games and heard an awful amount of boos from the home crowd before being shipped off to the Cincinnati Reds in the offseason.
Despite the rough experience, Gray greatly values his time in New York and attributes it not only to the pitcher, but to the man he is today.
“I do know that playing here made me a stronger person, made me a better man, a better husband. Ultimately, it made me a better pitcher, a better baseball player. And that’s kind of what I take from my time here. …
“I learned a lot. I learned what to do, what not to do. I mean, it was a bump in the road for me, but ultimately it made me a better person.”
Gray found success immediately after departing the Bronx. He was an All-Star for the Reds in 2019 and then again with the Minnesota Twins in 2023. The veteran enters the postseason riding a very successful season in which he pitched to a 2.72 ERA in 29 games with the Red Sox.
The Tennessean is not focused on any sort of revenge and doesn’t need any added motivation to stick it to the Yankees. Instead, he’s solely focused on trying to win for the Bo Sox.
“That’s kind of how I look at it. I don’t look at it as any other thing than that.”
