item.content:encoded:
After the Boston Red Sox went on their summer run to climb safely into an American League wild-card spot, that proved to be huge. Nobody can predict injuries, but it was a rough month of September in terms of injuries.
Not only did manager Chad Tracy lose Gold Glove outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela to an injury early in the month, but he also lost All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras to an injury with 10 days left in the regular season. Contreras was hit on the hand by a pitch against the Texas Rangers. He played in just one game after that.
He’ll be back in the Red Sox lineup for Game 1 of the AL wild-card series on Tuesday night against the New York Yankees. Boston is also getting Rafaela back in the Bronx, but the lineup will look different against Cam Schlittler.
Ceddanne Rafaela Batting Fifth in Game 1 vs. New York Yankees
Boston announced their lineup hours before Game 1 and Rafaela will be hitting fifth. Here is the lineup for the Red Sox,
Wilyer Abreu RF
Caddanne Rafaela CF
Nick Sogard 2B
Jarren Duran LF
Trevor Story SS
Caleb Durbin 3B
Rafaela was placed on the injured list with a right quadriceps strain, which caused him to miss 17 games. He returned against the Cleveland Guardians on Sept. 23 before exiting the game with right hamstring tightness while legging out a single. The next day, testing came back clean, and he was diagnosed with a hamstring cramp. He went 2-for-6 against the Guardians and Chicago Cubs in three games before the playoffs with a pair of singles.
Red Sox Big Wild Card Lead Led To Key Rest for Ceddanne Rafaela
If Rafaela can return and produce for Tracy, the big lead in the playoff race in the American League was huge. It allowed Boston to give not only Rafaela time to rest, but also Contreras as well.
Boston will be without utility infielder Mickey Gasper, who suffered an injury last Friday in Game 1 of a doubleheader against the Cubs at Fenway Park. He was placed on the 10-day injured list, which takes an underrated bat out of Tracy’s lineup and off his bench.
The Red Sox will send young left-hander Payton Tolle to the mound against the New York Yankees, who will send this lineup out for manager Aaron Boone,
Ben Rice DH
Heliot Ramos RF
George Lombard Jr. SS
Amed Rosario 3B
Anthony Vole 2B
New York won’t have Aaron Judge for the series, as he was not part of Boone’s roster. This figures to be a low-scoring series given the projected pitching matchups for the three games, if it goes that far. Boston getting Rafaela and Contreras back while the Yankees not having Judge feels like an advantage for the Red Sox. Winning Game 1 is big in a best-of-three series, especially for the Yankees, with Boston having Sonny Gray scheduled to go in Game 2 on Wednesday night.

item.title: [si.com] MLB Postseason Power Rankings: Strength and Weaknesses for Every Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Karl Rasmussen
item.description: The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series. The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team
item.content:encoded:
The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.
Follow Karlras920

item.title: [Over the Monster] Chad Tracy could swing the series between the Red Sox and Yankees
item.dc:creator: Keagan Stiefel
item.description: Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series. The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of
item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

Abridores para la serie Yankees vs. Red So
item.content:encoded:
Yankees y Red Sox revelan a sus pitchers abridores para la Serie de Comodines
Yankees y Red Sox se enfrentan por segundo año consecutivo al comenzar la postemporada de la MLB.
Velando armas para una nueva batalla en la que ambos se juegan la temporada, Yankees y Red Sox anunciaron a sus pitchers abridores con los que se enfrentarán a partir de este martes en una nueva Serie de Comodines para abrir los Playoffs 2026 en las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB).
Abridores para la serie Yankees vs. Red Sox
- Juego 1: Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03) vs. Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95)
- Juego 2: Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72) vs. Max Fried (5-5, 2.80)
- Juego 3: Ranger Suárez (8-5, 3.22) vs. Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61)
Juego 1: Cam Schlittler vs. Payton Tolle
Los Yankees apostaron todo al alinear a Cam Schlittler, el principal contendiente para competir por el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, para el Juego 1. Schlittler, quien creció a los alrededores de Boston siendo un aficionado de los Red Sox, fue el verdugo del equipo de su infancia el año anterior cuando tiró 8.0 entradas de 12 ponches para ganar el decisivo Juego 3.
Esta temporada, Schlittler tuvo efectividad de 0.74 pues apenas recibió dos carreras limpias a lo largo de 24.1 entradas ante los Red Sox este año, aunque admitió 4 carreras inmerecidas el 25 de junio.
Su antagonista será Payton Tolle, el novato zurdo que tomará por asalto la lomita del Yankee Stadium. Con 23 años y 332 días de edad, Tolle será el tercer pitcher más joven en abrir una serie de postemporada para los Red Sox. En dos actuaciones ante los Yankees, Payton tuvo marca de 1-0 con efectividad de 0.69 y 18 ponches, a cambio de solo tres pasaportes.
Juego 2: Max Fried vs Sonny Gray
Sonny Gray tomará la pelota para el Juego 2 por los Red Sox. El as en la rotación en la ausencia de Garrett Crochet tuvo un año increíble y busca trasladar ese éxito a la postemporada ante unos Yankees a los que dominó en dos aperturas: la primera en 6.1 entradas de 3 carreras, mientras que en la segunda tiró una joya de 7.1 entradas en un solo hit y 9 ponches.
Los Yankees optaron por Max Fried en el Juego 2, otro lanzador que fue dominante ante los Red Sox la postemporada anterior tirando 6.1 entradas en blanco pese a admitir 4 hits y regalar 3 bases por bolas; ponchó a 6 rivales. Desde entonces, Fried acumula 18.0 entradas de una sola carrera y 19 ponches ante los acérrimos rivales de los Bombarderos del Bronx.
Juego 3: Gerrit Cole vs. Ranger Suárez
En caso de un decisivo Juego 3, los Yankees saltarán al terreno con Gerrit Cole, el lanzador que históricamente ha sufrido ante los Red Sox. Cole no le ha ganado un juego a Boston desde el 17 de julio de 2022 y su efectividad de por vida ante los patirrojos es de 5.30, la segunda más alta que tiene ante cualquier rival, solo debajo de los Mets (7.28).
Ranger Suárez cerró fuerte para ganarse la confianza y ser el abridor de los Red Sox para el Juego 3 de esta Serie de Comodines. Durante el último mes de temporada en su año de debut con los Red Sox, el venezolano Suárez cerró con marca de 3-1 y efectividad de 1.09 en septiembre; sin embargo, ante los Yankees fue sumamente contrastante al admitir 10 carreras en 10.0 entradas de dos juegos que perdió y 6.1 entradas de una carrera en un juego sin decisión.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] If the Red Sox can get past the Yankees, the Chad Tracy story goes from a good one to a great one - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: NEW YORK — Because there are odds on everything these days, Will Venable is the favorite to be the American League Manager of the Year, with Kevin Cash the second choice. Venable led the White Sox to the postseason after losing 102 games last season. He deserves all the plaudits. But what about Chad Tracy? item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Because there are odds on everything these days, Will Venable is the favorite to be the American League Manager of the Year, with Kevin Cash the second choice.
Venable led the White Sox to the postseason after losing 102 games last season. He deserves all the plaudits.
But what about Chad Tracy?
Tracy was called away from managing a game with Triple-A Worcester on April 25 and told that Alex Cora was getting fired and he would manage the Red Sox the next day in Baltimore. It was the baseball equivalent of getting thrown out of a plane without a parachute.
After making the announcement, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said he couldn’t guarantee Tracy would finish the season as manager.
Five months later, the Sox are in the playoffs after a remarkable turnaround, and Tracy is the only rookie manager whose team is still playing.
It’s a good story, complete with Tracy agreeing to a three-year contract last week. But in two or three more days, it could be a great story.
The Sox have not won a postseason series since 2021. If they fall to the Yankees again this season, nothing will have changed. But if they beat their rivals and advance to the Division Series, it’s a major step forward for this largely unaccomplished group of players.
“It’s drastically different,” Tracy said Monday when asked to compare becoming manager to managing in his first postseason game. “It’s the playoffs. There’s more riding on it.”
Tracy said he gave himself some grace that first day in Baltimore. There was so much to learn, so much to do. He knew he wouldn’t be fully prepared. Plus, several of the players were still furious that Cora had been fired after only 27 games.
“It was go out and be with the guys and give them a hug and enjoy being with them and let the game go be what it is,” Tracy said.
Tracy leaned on his father for advice throughout the season. Jim Tracy managed 1736 major league games from 2001-12 for three teams and had plenty of good answers. But he was 2-6 in postseason games, losing first-round series with the 2004 Dodgers and 2009 Rockies.
As a manager’s son, Tracy suffered those losses, too.
“This is the playoffs. We’re at the point in the season for the teams that are remaining where it’s a three-game series. You’ve got to win the series or you go home,” he said. “There’s more riding on it.”
For 162 games, managers are forced to think about the next day, the next series, and the next set of roster moves. Bruised egos get massaged, and you move on. Even great teams lose dozens of games. That’s baseball.
Not in the playoffs. Everything goes into winning that day, and feelings are disregarded. Just win.
“When you get to this part of the year, it’s all hands on deck. I think everybody’s pretty aware in the playoffs it’s high intent and winning moments and being aggressive and all those things,” Tracy said.
“All of our guys that have been around understand that. They’re going to play their butts off, and we’re going to manage and try to do whatever we can to win the game.”
That would be the case if the Sox were playing the Astros. But it’s magnified by the power of 100 when it’s the Yankees.
The Sox made history against the Yankees with their comeback in the 2004 American League Championship Series. They brushed past the Bombers in the division round en route to the 2018 championship. Fenway Park was practically shaking during the 2021 Wild Card game.
“I don’t like to give that way more attention than it needs. But I won’t shy away from it,” Tracy said. “Two historic franchises, big rivalry, well aware of that.”
Tracy has already made one bold move, selecting Payton Tolle as his Game 1 starter instead of the more seasoned Sonny Gray. More big decisions are coming.
There’s no grace now.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are taking on the New York Yankees in an American League wild-card series beginning Tuesday, Sept. 29. Two teams with the most historic rivalry in baseball history square off with a chance to send the other home.
New York eliminated Boston in 2025, but with a new set of faces this year the Red Sox hope the result will be different.
One of those new faces is left-hander Payton Tolle. While Tolle debuted back in 2025 and appeared in the playoff series, he only made one appearance out of the bullpen. That will not be the case this time around.
Chad Tracy names wild-card series starters
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy spoke with reporters ahead of Game 1 and officially announced the rotation for Boston, per Bryan Hoch of MLB.com.
Tracy said Tolle gets the ball for Game 1, with veterans Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to follow in that order. That represents a completely different look than what the Yankees saw last year, as both Gray and Suarez were added this offseason.
It makes plenty of sense that Tolle gets the ball. The 23-year-old has posted a 3.03 ERA across 26 starts and has piled up 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings. Tolle has been superb in the second half and earned this moment.
Gray will get the ball for Game 2 and has been exactly as advertised in his first year with Boston. The 36-year-old veteran has posted a 2.72 ERA across 29 starts and has continued to age gracefully.
Suarez getting the ball third was the obvious choice as well. He has plenty of postseason experience from his time with the Philadelphia Phillies, and across 28 starts this year he has posted a 3.22 ERA with 140 strikeouts in 148 1/3 innings of work.
Boston’s lineup will have its work cut out against New York’s excellent rotation, but the Red Sox have the arms this year to match up against the Yankees in a way they simply did not a year ago.
Game 1 of the series is set for 8 p.m. ET Tuesday on NBC and Peacock.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox will start left-hander Payton Tolle in Game 1 of their American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees in New York on Tuesday night, manager Chad Tracy announced on Monday afternoon. Righty Sonny Gray, a former Yankee, will take the ball for Boston in Game 2.
Tolle, a rookie, has become a fireballing fan favorite in Boston, just as likely to strike someone out on a 98 mph heater as he is to wrap someone into a bear hug. The Red Sox have no reservations about putting the 23-year-old into the hostile territory Yankee Stadium figures to be.
The Yankees strongly considered left-hander Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA) to start Game 1, but ultimately chose AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler for the opener. Fried will follow in Game 2, with Gerrit Cole ready for Game 3, if necessary.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said Payton Tolle will start Game 1 of the Wild Card series against the Yankees.

Sonny Gray will start Game 2, with Ranger Suarez potentially lined up for Game 3. It seems that Tracy may be looking to break up his lefties. Tolle is certainly a worthwhile Game 1 starter. He finished the regular season with a 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 28.4 percent strikeout rate across 148 2/3 innings. He has never made a start in the postseason before, while Gray has previous experience. Gray also posted a 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, and 21.8 percent strikeout rate in 169 innings this year. Either way, the Red Sox have a nice duo set up to start the first two games of the series.

item.title: [sbnation.com] MLB Playoffs: Ranking all 12 teams by their World Series 2026 chances
item.dc:creator: Mark Schofield

item.content:encoded:
The MLB postseason is here.
There are 12 teams headed to the playoffs including the Houston Astros and the Philadelphia Phillies, who needed wins in Game 162 to punch their respective tickets to the dance. But now, records reset to 0-0, and all 12 teams have an equal chance to win the World Series.
At least in theory.
But some teams are in a better position than others as the playoffs beckon. Here are the 12 teams in the MLB Playoffs, ranked by their chances of winning the World Series.
12. Houston Astros (81-81)
The Houston Astros became the first team in MLB history to win the division without a winning record.
This is a team that can mash, as the Astros led the majors with 226 home runs, 42 off the bat of MVP candidate Yordan Alvarez. Four other members of the lineup topped 20 home runs as well: Christian Walker, Jeremy Peña, Isaac Paredes, and Cam Smith.
But the problem is pitching, as the Astros were 24th in MLB in ERA and 21st in WHIP. Closer Josh Hader was solid in the second half, racking up 16 saves and posting a WHIP of 0.682, and Bryan Abreu has been dependable in front of him, but the bullpen has been inconsistent beyond those two.
So if the rotation cannot pitch deep into games, that will be a problem.
11. Chicago White Sox (84-78)
After losing more than 100 games in each of the past three seasons, the Chicago White Sox were one of baseball’s best stories this year, leading the AL Central for much of the season before sliding into the playoffs with a Wild Card spot.
Chicago is powered by a lineup that features three players with more than 30 home runs — Munetaka Murakami, Colson Montgomery, and Miguel Vargas — and as a team the White Sox posted an OBP 0f .320, second only to the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League.
However, the problem in the playoffs might be starting pitching. As a staff the White Sox starting pitchers posted an ERA of 4.60 this season (26th in the majors) and a WHIP of 1.34 (25th in the majors). That sets up a tough matchup, starting with the Wild Card Series against Houston.
But, they do have the Pope on their side.
10. Philadelphia Phillies (88-74)
The Philadelphia Phillies cut their magic number for a playoff spot to one with a win over the Milwaukee Brewers last Tuesday.
They lost their next four games by a combined score of 23-3, needing a win on the final day of the season to book a postseason berth.
Philadelphia did that on Sunday, clinching the final Wild Card spot in the NL with a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays, and this star-laden team now gets a series with the Atlanta Braves to prove everyone wrong. Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Trae Turner bring the star power, and Jhoan Duran remains one of the best closers in baseball. Philadelphia also has Zack Wheeler and Cristopher Sánchez leading the rotation; however, manager Don Mattingly was forced to use Sánchez in the season finale, complicating his availability this week. Then there is Aaron Nola, who is coming off a spot start on short rest on Saturday and needs to play a big role despite some struggles this season.
Can a weary rotation, and a bullpen that has endured its own share of struggles in front of Duran, get the job done? That is the big question.
9. Cleveland Guardians (85-77)
While the Chicago White Sox were one of the biggest surprises of the MLB season, in the end the Cleveland Guardians clinched the AL Central, and a first-round playoff bye.
Their reward? After the bye Cleveland will have home-field advantage against the winner of the Houston-Chicago series, and they will avoid any of the AL East teams until a potential ALCS matchup.
The Guardians are led by their pitching, as Cleveland boasts both a strong rotation and a stellar bullpen. Gavin Williams and Parker Messick pace a starting staff that produced the ninth-best ERA among starters and the bullpen, led by closer Cade Smith and the trio of setup arms Hunter Gaddis, Eric Sabrowski, and Tim Herrin was even better, with the sixth-best ERA among bullpens in the majors.
If Cleveland gets enough production from the offense, that pitching staff could power them to the ALCS, where anything can happen.
8. Boston Red Sox (87-75)
After a brutal start cost manager Alex Cora his job, the Boston Red Sox used a 32-5 stretch to push into playoff contention.
But Boston cooled off after that torrid summer, and there are some questions facing this team as the playoffs loom. One is the health of the lineup. Ceddanne Rafaela is back after missing 16 games with a quad injury, but will Willson Contreras be fully healthy after getting hit by a pitch on his right hand in the final week of the season? A second question? Can the lineup bounce back after a difficult September. As a team, Boston posted an OPS of .651 in the month of September.
Pitching is not a question. The trio of Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez is one of the best left standing, and Aroldis Chapman has been dynamic at the back of the bullpen yet again. Boston could even get Garrett Crochet back from injury in a relief role, and Tanner Houck — who started Game 162 more than 500 days after his last MLB appearance, after working back from Tommy John surgery — could be in the mix out of the bullpen as well.
Which version of the Red Sox shows up, however, is the ultimate question.
7. Chicago Cubs (89-73)
The Chicago Cubs have one of the best offenses in baseball, led by MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong, the first center fielder in MLB history to produce a 40/40 season. This is a lineup that led the majors with a team OPS of .767, and a team slugging percentage of .428. Beyond Crow-Armstrong, Alex Bregman, Ian Happ, Michael Busch, and Seiya Suzuki all put 20 home runs on the board this season.
The Cubs also have one of the best defenses in baseball, again with Crow-Armstrong leading the way. The outfielder posted a Fielding Run Value (FRV) of +26 this season, tops in the majors, and the Cubs led all teams with a FRV of +72 this year, ahead of the St. Louis Cardinals who posted a +45.
The problem? Pitching. The Cubs starters posted a team ERA of 4.27 this year — worst among NL playoff teams — and only two teams gave up more home runs than the Cubs this year. And a staff that has been hampered by injuries faces another question on that front as the playoffs loom, as Kevin Gausman was injured on a tag play last week and suffered an injury to his non-throwing shoulder. Craig Counsell would love to have him for the series against the San Diego Padres.
The Cubs have the offense and the defense to win games, but do they have the pitching to win a series or two?
6. San Diego Padres (91-71)
If momentum could be measured, the San Diego Padres might be off the charts.
The Padres went 17-11 in August, and then 18-6 in September, to lock down a Wild Card spot. This was quite the turnaround for a team that was flirting with being sellers at the trade deadline. Leading the way was outfielder Fernando Tatis Jr., who did not homer over the first 55 games of the season but finished with 25 home runs and 38 steals, thanks to a torrid closing stretch. Jackson Merrill overcame a slow start of his own to finish with 26 home runs and 27 steals, giving the Padres their first 25/25 duo.
As a lineup, the Padres were second in both OPS and slugging percentage after the All-Star break, behind only the Cubs.
San Diego also has one of the best bullpens in baseball, with closer Mason Miller in form behind setup men Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez.
They’ll host the Cubs in the Wild Card Series, and while Chicago won the season series 5-1, that was before San Diego’s late-season turnaround.
5. New York Yankees (93-68)
When the New York Yankees lost Aaron Judge for an extended period of the regular season, the lineup stepped up in his absence. While Judge played just 66 games and hit 18 home runs, the Yankees managed to belt 223 home runs, finishing second in the majors.
But with his status in question for the Wild Card Series against Boston, the rest of that lineup will need to step up yet again. And the matchup against the Red Sox will be a tough one, as Boston will likely throw Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez against them — a strong start — and the Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in the game.
And that matchup will be even tougher without Judge’s bat in the lineup.
4. Atlanta Braves (94-67)
While the Atlanta Braves would have loved a first-round bye, with the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Milwaukee Brewers out of striking distance Atlanta was able to set their rotation for the Wild Card Series over the final week of the season. Chris Sale made his final start of the regular season last Wednesday on extra rest, and will be on extra rest when he gets the ball for Game 1. The same goes for Tyler Mahle, who will have extra rest ahead of an anticipated Game 2 start.
Plus the Braves get the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, who gave their fans something to worry about over the final few days of the season as they did not clinch a spot until Game 162.
3. Tampa Bay Rays (98-64)
Few people gave the Tampa Bay Rays a chance when the season began.
Leading with me, who put the Rays in the “True Longshots” category when the year began, along with the Diamondbacks, the Athletics, and the Twins.
But here are the Rays, the winners of the AL East and the team to beat in the American League. MCP candidate Junior Caminero has put up massive numbers for Tampa Bay — he slashed .276/.360/.524 this year along with 42 home runs — and is at the heart of a lineup that punishes pitchers from top-to-bottom. As a team the Rays hit .258 this season, the best number in the AL and tied with the Brewers for the top number in the majors, and the Rays also posted a team OPS of .728, behind only the Houston Astros in the American League.
Add in a staff that posted an MLB-best team WHIP of 1.14, tied with the Dodgers, and you have the recipe for a deep playoff run.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers (100-62)
The Los Angeles Dodgers got off to their annual hot start, endured a mid-season slump that raised more questions than answers about their chances at a three-peat, but enter the playoffs having found some of those answers.
Kyle Tucker’s season-long slump seems to be ending just in time for a post-season run, as he slashed .266/362/.557 in the month of September, his best stretch of the season by far. Shohei Ohtani and Will Smith are both back in the lineup, Edwin Diaz seems to have found his stuff — he was flawless in September, allowing just one hit in four appearances and striking out eight — and Mookie Betts is back to being Mookie Betts, as he slashed .345/.447/.690 in September, also putting up his best numbers of the season.
When you’ve won a pair of titles, you know when to turn it on.
The Dodgers seem to have done just that over the last month.
1. Milwaukee Brewers (103-59)
The Milwaukee Brewers top these rankings, as they topped 100 wins for the first time in franchise history.
But for this team, the real test comes in October. The Brewers have now won the NL Central for four consecutive years, and in five of the last six campaigns. What do they have to show for that? Two playoff wins, including a sweep at the hands of the Dodgers in the NLCS a year ago.
Jacob Misiorowski gives them a bonafide ace, as the big right-hander led the majors in ERA (1.86), ERA+ (225), WHIP (0.803), and K/9 (13.1) this season, and Logan Henderson has developed into a solid No. 2 for Milwaukee. If Kyle Harrison somehow recovers his first-half form (he was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the All-Star Break, but went 3-3 with a 7.31 ERA in the second half of the season) this team could finally break through to the promised land.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Get Timely Brayan Bello Boost Ahead of Wild Card Series

From Worcester to Red Sox Weapon Bello's 2026 started as badly as any seaso
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox needed pitching in Game 2 of Friday's doubleheader against the Chicago Cubs. Brayan Bello gave them four shutout innings.
When he walked off the mound for the last time in the regular season, the Fenway crowd rose. Bello got a standing ovation.
Five months ago, he was pitching in Worcester after being optioned out of the big-league rotation. Friday's ovation told the story of how far he has come since.
From Worcester to Red Sox Weapon
Bello's 2026 started as badly as any season can. He posted a 10.35 ERA across eight starts before the Red Sox sent him to Triple-A in late April. Something needed to change.
What changed was the role. Bello came back as a bulk reliever and the transformation was immediate. The fastball carried more life. The command sharpened. The confidence returned.
Since rejoining the big-league staff, Bello has posted a 2.28 ERA and a 1.01 WHIP over his last 51.1 innings across 13 appearances. The Red Sox eventually gave him starts again, and he responded with his best stretch of the season.
Over his last four outings spanning 18⅔ innings, Bello has allowed just one earned run. That translates to a 0.48 ERA heading into October.
What Friday Showed
Bello's performance capped a September that has erased any remaining questions about his role in the postseason. His 11-strikeout outing against the Athletics on September 19 was the exclamation point on a second half that turned his entire season around.
The standing ovation from the Fenway crowd carried weight because of everything that preceded it. This was not a player who cruised through the year. This was someone who got sent down, rebuilt his approach, and fought his way back into being one of the most trusted arms on the staff.
"I learned not to let bad moments dictate how the next one is going to be," Bello said.
Where Bello Fits in October
The Red Sox will likely use Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as their three starters in the Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees. That leaves Bello available out of the bullpen, where he has been at his best.
His ability to provide multiple innings of high-quality relief makes him a critical piece in a best-of-three format. If a starter runs into trouble early or the Red Sox need to bridge a gap between a short outing and the back end of the bullpen, Bello is the arm built for that moment.
The Red Sox invested in Bello believing in his ceiling. The second half of 2026 is the closest he has come to reaching it.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Brayan Bello got sent to the minors in April. He came back a different pitcher. The numbers since his return tell that story clearly, but the standing ovation at Fenway told it better.
The postseason starts Tuesday. Bello enters it on the best run of his career, with a 0.48 ERA over his last four outings and the confidence of a team that knows exactly what he can provide.
Five months ago, he was in Worcester. Friday night, the Fenway crowd was on its feet for him. That is the kind of arc that carries into October.

item.content:encoded:
Wilyer Abreu has been one of Boston’s most impactful all-around players, but lately the talented right fielder has been stuck in a serious rut.
Over the past few weeks Abreu has seen his offensive production fall off a cliff. Coming into the day he was batting .177 with a .546 OPS and four extra-base hits over his last 17 games since Sept. 3, and during Friday’s doubleheader he started 0 for 7 his first seven trips to the plate.
That kind of slump will put a strain on anyone’s confidence, but after striking out in the bottom of the sixth, Abreu said he was approached by veteran teammate Sonny Gray, who gave him a badly needed pep talk.
“It helped me a lot,” Abreu said. “He’s a vet, he’s got a lot of years here and how to handle those situations, so he give me good advice to feel good with my body, with my athleticism, and trust myself, try to get my confidence back and that was huge.”
The next time up, Abreu reminded everyone at Fenway Park who he really is.
Abreu’s go-ahead two-run double in the bottom of the eighth was the difference in Friday night’s 2-0 win over the Chicago Cubs. The right fielder stepped to the plate with two on and two outs in a scoreless game and crushed an opposite-field line drive high off the Green Monster.
That swing helped the Red Sox seal the doubleheader sweep, and the two clubs will now fly to St. Petersburg to get out ahead of the impending nor’easter to finish the regular season on Sunday at Tropicana Field.
In what was likely his final appearance of the regular season, Brayan Bello capped off his season of turbulence and redemption in style. The right-hander threw four-plus scoreless innings, held the Cubs to four hits and a walk and struck out two while throwing 39 of his 58 pitches for strikes.
Bello wraps up the year with a 4.33 ERA, a deceptively average mark for what was an extraordinarily unique journey. After earning himself a demotion following a disastrous first half that saw him lose his spot in the rotation, Bello finished the season with a 2.11 ERA over 55 1/3 innings in his last 14 appearances since being called back up just prior to the All-Star break.
Following the game Bello said he’s happy and grateful for the way his season ended, adding that the whole year was a big learning experience.
“I learned not to let bad moments dictate how the next one is going to be,” Bello said via interpreter Carlos Villoria Benítez. “Also I learned how to compete in the zone, I feel like in the second half I was able to compete in the zone and beat hitters in the zone, something that I wasn’t able to do in the first half.”
Bello gave way to rookie Jedixson Paez, who was called up between the two games and who has also endured an eventful first year in the majors. The 22-year-old had never pitched above Single-A prior to this season before he was poached by the Chicago White Sox in the Rule 5 Draft, and the right-hander made three uninspiring appearances for the White Sox before he was returned to Boston.
After spending most of the season in the Red Sox minor league system, he was called back up for a spot start on Sept. 1 and got shelled, allowing eight runs in 3 2/3 innings in a loss to the Seattle Mariners. But needing to cover some innings ahead of the club’s upcoming playoff run, Paez came through and gave the Red Sox five scoreless frames in what was by far the best outing of his MLB career so far.
“The first chance he got it didn’t probably go how he wanted and he gets another opportunity and goes out there and spins five scoreless innings and attacks the zone,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “It was awesome.”
Offensively the Red Sox were stymied by Cubs starter David Peterson, who held Boston to three hits and two walks over five shutout innings. The Red Sox had runners reach third base in both the third and fourth innings but couldn’t get the go-ahead runner home.
Boston didn’t fare much better against the Cubs bullpen, but the Red Sox finally got another chance in the bottom of the eighth when Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Jahmai Jones each walked to put two men on with two outs.
That brought Abreu to the plate to face left-hander Ryan Rolison, and the outfielder smoked an opposite-field line drive 100.5 mph off the bat high off the Green Monster. Kiner-Falefa and Jones both came around to score, and that was all she wrote.
Paez returned for the top of the ninth despite initially seeming to deal with a cramping issue while warming up, but after a brief visit by the trainer, he stayed in the game and sent the Cubs down 1-2-3 to end the game.
With this weekend’s finale relocated to St. Petersburg, Fla., Friday night marked the final regular season game at Fenway Park this season. The next time the Red Sox are back in Boston, it will either be for Game 3 of the American League Divisional Series against the Tampa Bay Rays, or for the end-of-the-season press conference should the club lose to the Yankees in the Wild Card round again.
Before they even knew when and where their last game would be, Tracy told his players to prepare to spend 11 days on the road, and Abreu said the team is determined to bring playoff baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021.
“I think the fans deserve it,” Abreu said. “It’s been five years that Boston hasn’t seen any playoff games, so I think we have to give them that opportunity to see playoff games again here at Fenway Park.”
In the meantime, the Red Sox and Cubs will play one more at Tropicana Field on Sunday starting at 3:05 p.m.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Star Sonny Gray Gets Big Free Agency Prediction Just Before Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Matt Levine
item.description: The Boston Red Sox are getting ready for the final few games of the regular season, with the postseason starting up next week. Boston has clinched a playoff spot, and they will be a wild-card team this season. The Red Sox battled back from a very slow start to the season, putting together a massive rally in the middle of the year. The goal is to win a World Series title, and they seem to have a decent shot at getting it done. But while the players are focused on the play on the field, the front
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are getting ready for the final few games of the regular season, with the postseason starting up next week.
Boston has clinched a playoff spot, and they will be a wild-card team this season. The Red Sox battled back from a very slow start to the season, putting together a massive rally in the middle of the year.
The goal is to win a World Series title, and they seem to have a decent shot at getting it done. But while the players are focused on the play on the field, the front office also has its sights set on the upcoming offseason.
Even with the impending lockout likely coming to baseball, teams all over the league could try to maneuver rosters before it happens. For the Red Sox, they do have a key free agent hitting the market in ace Sonny Gray.
The veteran right-hander has been excellent for the Red Sox this year, firing a 2.79 ERA over 29 innings. Gray has helped establish the Red Sox rotation as one of the best in baseball, and he has been a major reason why the team has made the playoffs.
The right-hander has a mutual option for next season, but there has also been some retirement talk. However, given how strong of a year he has seen, the right-hander may postpone that idea, looking to land one last big contract.
Boston would surely want him back, but that all remains to be seen. But his free agency will be something to watch for the Red Sox and other potentially interested teams out there.
Sonny Gray Gets Major Free Agency Prediction
analyst Zach Buckley of Bleacher Report looked ahead to some of the bigger stars hitting the free-agent market this winter, predicting some of the outcomes. In this, Buckley has predicted that Gray will indeed return to the Red Sox following a strong season.
"It sounds like everything is on the table for the 36-year-old. Per Mass Live's Chris Cotillo, Gray could fetch a similar deal to the three-year, $75 million deal Nathan Eovaldi inked with the Texas Rangers two years back. But Cotillo also noted that Gray relayed in a recent interview with The Boston Globe he would retire "in a heartbeat" if his family indicated any desire for him to do so.
"Only Gray knows what he's thinking, and since he doesn't need to make a decision right now, it's very possible even if he isn't sure. If he wants to keep playing, though, he has clearly set himself up to strike it rich in free agency," Buckley wrote.
Should Red Sox Resign Sonny Gray?
Given how dominant Gray has been, the Red Sox should try to sign him to a new deal. Even if this would be just for another year or two, having Gray around would help Boston heading into next season.
Gray has seen a lot of success with the Red Sox, and the team is a contender, so the two sides may come together. But for now, the focus will be on trying to win the World Series, with free agency in the back of everyone's mind.
This article was originally published on HEAVY

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox hoping investment in Ranger Suarez pays off again in the postseason - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: The Red Sox made their biggest investment of the offseason in January when they signed free agent lefthander Ranger Suarez for five years and $130 million. Eight months later, it’s fair to say Suarez did what was expected. He was 8-5 with a 3.22 earned run average over 28 starts and 148 innings. item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox made their biggest investment of the offseason in January when they signed free agent lefthander Ranger Suarez for five years and $130 million.
Eight months later, it’s fair to say Suarez did what was expected.
He was 8-5 with a 3.22 earned run average over 28 starts and 148 innings. Suarez was an All-Star, and the Sox were 17-11 in the games he started. Outside of missing three starts with a groin strain and a sore lower back, Suarez was a reliable rotation pillar.
He allowed one earned run or none in 16 starts. That’s right in line with how he pitched for the Phillies in 2024 and ’25.
Suarez allowed one run on three hits over five innings in a 1-0 loss against the Guardians on Thursday night. The one run came on a 319-foot Pesky Pole home run by Angel Martinez in the second inning.
Otherwise, Suarez stayed in control despite throwing 39 pitches over the first two innings.
“When you look at the body of work, especially coupled with the other guys in the rotation, he was fantastic,” manager Chad Tracy said. “He had a great year.”
Suarez wasn’t quite so complimentary of himself.
“In general, good,” he said via a translator. “Obviously I think I could have done better. But I was happy I was able to finish the season strong.”
Now comes the true test.
Suarez was 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 postseason games for the Phillies, eight of them as a starter. Philadelphia won eight of those games.
That includes Game 3 of the Division Series against the Dodgers last season when Suarez pitched five innings out of the bullpen and held the mighty Dodgers to one run at Dodger Stadium. That’s what he’s capable of in a big game.
Suarez is likely to start Game 3 in the Wild Card Series next week, which means he could have a huge say in whether this memorable season will continue.
“Being able to finish this month strong, I think, is going to be the key for the playoffs,” Suarez said.
Suarez was referring to the 1.09 ERA and 0.93 WHIP he posted over his final four starts.
His results against the Yankees this season were less encouraging. Suarez faced them three times and allowed 11 earned runs over 16 innings.
But he did have a strong start at Yankee Stadium on June 7, allowing one run over 6 innings against Cam Schlittler. It was 1-1 when Suarez left the game; then the bullpen allowed five runs.
Tracy has not revealed his rotation for the series. But if he stays in order, it would be Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Suarez.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone has held back that information, too.
Schlittler, who is a heavy favorite to win the Cy Young Award, would make sense to start Game 1. He dominated the Sox in four starts this season, allowing two earned runs over 24 innings and striking out 27.
A Tolle-Schlittler matchup would be must-viewing for even a casual baseball fan.
But there is speculation that the Yankees would save Schlittler for Game 2 and give Game 1 to lefthander Max Fried, who also has pitched well against the Sox this season.
That might be overthinking it, but it’s an option.
Based on the last few games, the Red Sox will need their pitchers to be close to perfect. Tracy has used the last 10 days to give his regulars rest while giving extra time off to players who have been dealing with injuries.
The Sox have scored only five runs over their last five games and hit .222. Willson Contreras, who was thought to be progressing well from a bruised right hand, said after the game he was concerned about being ready for the Yankees series.
“I’m doing everything that I can to come back and play with the boys and be with them,” Suarez said. “But sometimes you have to listen to your body.”
If Contreras can’t play, or is compromised, that would put even more pressure on the pitchers.
“This team can pitch,” Suarez said. “We’ll be ready for next week.”
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [NBC Boston] Red Sox legend Pedro Martinez launches coding program for kids in Lawrence
item.dc:creator: Malcolm Johnson
item.description: When Pedro Martinez was on the mound for the Boston Red Sox, he was a fan favorite. More than 20 years later, as schoolchildren cheered and swarmed around him for autographs Thursday in Lawrence, Massachusetts, it was clear that has not changed. The baseball Hall of Famer's childhood struggles continue to inspire his commitment to giving back. Martinez and his wife, Carolina, are launching a new afterschool coding program serving seven elementary schools in Lawrence. "I had to struggle for every
item.content:encoded:
When Pedro Martinez was on the mound for the Boston Red Sox, he was a fan favorite.
More than 20 years later, as schoolchildren cheered and swarmed around him for autographs Thursday in Lawrence, Massachusetts, it was clear that has not changed.
The baseball Hall of Famer's childhood struggles continue to inspire his commitment to giving back. Martinez and his wife, Carolina, are launching a new afterschool coding program serving seven elementary schools in Lawrence.
"I had to struggle for everything I achieved in life, and I just want to make it easier for others to get to where I got," Martinez said.
The program will give hundreds of third- and fourth-grade students access to modern technology and opportunities to develop coding and problem-solving skills.
"Maybe because it's something I was denied when I was younger," Martinez said when asked why the program is so important to him.
Martinez spoke with students at Lawrence schools as part of a back-to-school celebration, where children also received school supplies and gift bags.
The program is focused on reaching students early, Carolina Martinez said.
"Their age mattered to us in terms of the decision, because the earlier you get them, the more motivated they're going to be, but also, the more resourceful they're going to be later on," she said.
South Lawrence East Elementary School Principal Lori Butterfield said students are already immersed in technology, and the program will help them move from simply using technology to creating with it.
"They love playing games. They love using apps. They're using AI all the time. I want them to learn how to create those things, and I think this program will allow them to do that," Butterfield said.
For Martinez, the connection to Lawrence is personal.
"Why? Because in Lawrence, I quickly identified the need, I found my culture, I found my people here. I found my roots," he said.
Martinez also reflected on what can happen when young people are given even one opportunity.
"Remember, what you're seeing right now is the product of an opportunity. Only one, and that's all it took," he said.
Martinez seized his own opportunities on the mound, becoming one of baseball's most accomplished pitchers.
With the Red Sox preparing to face the Yankees in the postseason, Martinez was asked how he would feel about taking the mound today.
"I'll be ready from here, to give them all the knowledge and everything, all the experience I've done before — I'm ready to do that any day," he said. "But physically, to go pitch? I have Payton Tolle and I have Sonny Gray to go do it for me."
Martinez said he plans to continue coming back to Lawrence and contributing to the community — a place he now considers home.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox try Patrick Sandoval out of bullpen but bats go quiet as Guardians clinch playoff spot - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: In these waning days of the regular season, the Red Sox are trying something new: Patrick Sandoval, reliever. Sandoval tossed a scoreless sixth inning in a 1-0 loss to the Guardians on Thursday, his first appearance out of the bullpen since 2021. It was a successfully uneventful frame at Fenway Park: After José Ramírez grounded a single through the left side of the infield and stole second, Sandoval retired Chase DeLauter (strikeout looking), Jo Adell (ground out), and Angel Martínez (ground out
item.content:encoded:
In these waning days of the regular season, the Red Sox are trying something new: Patrick Sandoval, reliever.
Sandoval tossed a scoreless sixth inning in a 1-0 loss to the Guardians on Thursday, his first appearance out of the bullpen since 2021.
It was a successfully uneventful frame at Fenway Park: After José Ramírez grounded a single through the left side of the infield and stole second, Sandoval retired Chase DeLauter (strikeout looking), Jo Adell (ground out), and Angel Martínez (ground out). His velocity was down a tad in the small sample size of 12 pitches (10 strikes), but he was pitching just three days after his most recent start.
Ahead of the playoffs opening Tuesday, the Sandoval twist is of particular note because of his recent struggles as a starter and the Red Sox’ recent struggles looking for a reliable lefthanded reliever.
As a member of the rotation, Sandoval had a 5.15 ERA in 13 outings this year. That included a 7.32 mark in four starts this month. He has appeared unlikely to fit into the postseason plans in that role.
Also of late, Erik Miller, the team’s top lefty reliever, has had a bad time, entering the day with a 8.53 ERA in seven appearances this month. Of the 36 hitters he had faced, 17 had reached base: six hits, a whopping nine walks, and two batters hit by pitches.
Immediately after Sandoval departed, though, Miller entered — and maybe figured it out. He turned in a perfect seventh on just eight pitches, getting a strikeout of David Fry, a routine fly out from Travis Bazzana, and a 108-miles-per-hour line out from Patrick Bailey.
The loss dropped the Red Sox to 85-74 and — with three games to go — ensured that they will not match their 89 wins from last year.
They totaled two hits. Nick Sogard and Jarren Duran each had a single. It was the fourth game this month in which the Sox recorded four hits or fewer.
Lefthander Ranger Suarez finished a strong September — and strong regular season — with five innings of one-run ball. He held the Guardians to three hits and a walk and struck out five.
Cleveland’s lone run against him came on Martínez’s home run, tucked inside the Pesky Pole, an estimated 319 feet down the right-field line. It came off his bat at only 94 m.p.h. The batted ball had an expected batting average of .160.
At the end of the first season of a five-year, $130 million contract, Suarez owns a 3.22 ERA, third best in the Red Sox’ rotation behind righthander Sonny Gray (2.72) and lefthander Payton Tolle (3.03).
Suarez suffered from a midseason dip — a groin injury followed by mediocrity — but rebounded late, posting a 1.09 ERA over his final four starts.
The Sox mustered minimal offense against opener Daniel Espino (perfect first inning with two strikeouts) and lefthander Joey Cantillo (one hit and no runs in five innings).
For Cantillo, who entered the night with the most walks in the American League (79) but issued just two free passes against the Red Sox, it was his third consecutive scoreless appearance. In all three, he entered behind an opener.
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.content:encoded:
With the coming nor’easter hitting town this weekend, the Red Sox and Guardians have played with an October chill in the air this week.
The Red Sox halted their three-game slide with a 1-0 win on Wednesday. Andrew Monasterio’s RBI single in the bottom of the sixth held as the eventual winner after Sonny Gray dealt six shutout innings.
That came after the Guardians won Tuesday’s contest, 3-2, setting up Thursday’s game as the series rubber match.
Given his postgame comments, the Red Sox hope to have avoided a scare regarding center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, who left his first game back from the injured list with right hamstring tightness. A quad injury sent him to the IL on Sept. 3.
“Not even close,” Rafaela said of the severity comparison of the two injuries. “I think it was just a cramp.”
After the game, Tracy said Rafaela would have an MRI exam on Thursday.
Ranger Suarez will start for the Red Sox on Thursday. He’s 1-1 with a 4.00 ERA in four career appearances, including three starts, against Cleveland. On May 31, he struck out 10 and allowed four runs across five frames against Cleveland in Boston’s 9-4 win.
“He’s a very good competitor, a good pitcher that even when he gets traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it,” Tracy said of Suarez, whose ERA in three September starts is 0.92.
Daniel Espino will open for Cleveland before giving way to Joey Cantillo.
Here’s a preview of Thursday’s action.
Lineups
GUARDIANS (82-76): TBA
Pitching: RHP Daniel Espino (0-0, 4.73 ERA)
RED SOX (85-73): TBA
Pitching: LHP Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA)
Time: 6:45 p.m.
TV, radio: NESN, WEEI-FM 93.7
Guardians vs. Suarez: Jo Adell 2-5, Travis Bazzana 0-3, Chase DeLauter 2-3, David Fry 4-5, Austin Hedges 1-4, Steven Kwan 1-6, Nathaniel Lowe 1-6, Angel Martínez 0-2, José Ramírez 5-8, Brayan Rocchio 1-2
Red Sox vs. Espino: Has not faced any Boston batters
Stat of the day: The Red Sox have notched an American League-leading 17 shutouts this season.
Notes: The Guardians are on the verge of sealing their postseason berth. Cleveland’s magic number is just one, the same as their AL Central rival, the White Sox. If both win on Thursday, they both will earn a postseason berth. ... Cleveland, which had a six-game winning streak snapped on Wednesday, has a one-game lead over Chicago in the race for the division title. The White Sox own the division tiebreaker. ... “We know we control our own destiny still,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “So, I like where we are. We’ve got four games left, and we have a chance to get in. That’s all you can ask for.” ... Espino will serve as an opener for Cantillo, who will pitch in a bulk role. Cantillo is 10-9 with a 3.74 ERA this season. ... Cantillo is 1-0 with a 3.38 ERA in eight career innings against the Red Sox, and Espino has never faced Boston.
Cam Kerry can be reached at cam.kerry@globe.com.

item.title: [Spectrum News] Sonny Gray earns his 18th win as Red Sox beat Guardians 1-0
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: BOSTON (AP) — Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia's Cristopher Sánchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single, and the Boston Red Sox edged Cleveland 1-0 on Wednesday night to snap the Guardians' six-game winning streak. It was just the fifth win in 13 games for the Red Sox, who clinched a playoff spot on Sunday. The 36-year-old Gray (18-5) is in line to become the fourth Red Sox pitcher since 2000 to lea
item.content:encoded:
BOSTON (AP) — Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia's Cristopher Sánchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single, and the Boston Red Sox edged Cleveland 1-0 on Wednesday night to snap the Guardians' six-game winning streak.
It was just the fifth win in 13 games for the Red Sox, who clinched a playoff spot on Sunday.
The 36-year-old Gray (18-5) is in line to become the fourth Red Sox pitcher since 2000 to lead the AL in victories, joining Rick Porcello (2016), Josh Beckett ('07) and Curt Schilling ('04).
Gray allowed four singles, struck out three, walked one and lowered his ERA to 2.72.
Aroldis Chapman struck out the side in the ninth for his 35th save of the season.
Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) gave up a run on 10 hits with seven strikeouts.
The Guardians entered with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the AL Central after winning the series opener Tuesday, but needed a win Wednesday combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros to clinch a postseason berth.
The victory came with a price for the Red Sox when center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela left with right hamstring tightness after running out a single the same day he was activated from the injured list. He had been sidelined with a right a quad strain since Sept. 3 and made a diving headlong grab on Steven Kwan, the game's first batter.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Pedro Martinez on Game 7 in 2003, no regrets on calling the Yankees his daddy, and a mission to help - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Dan Shaughnessy
item.description: Many of us believe he’s the best pitcher we’ve ever seen. He’s a blue-chip, first-ballot Hall of Famer, part of the Red Sox team that broke the Curse, and seen on TBS after Sox playoff games in any given October. He’ll be 55 next month and spends every year shuttling between Boston and his native Dominican Republic, when he’s not working in Atlanta. He has no regrets about saying “The Yankees are my daddy,” all those years ago, and he thinks the Red Sox have a shot to beat the Yankees in New Yor
item.content:encoded:
Many of us believe he’s the best pitcher we’ve ever seen. He’s a blue-chip, first-ballot Hall of Famer, part of the Red Sox team that broke the Curse, and seen on TBS after Sox playoff games in any given October. He’ll be 55 next month and spends every year shuttling between Boston and his native Dominican Republic, when he’s not working in Atlanta. He has no regrets about saying “The Yankees are my daddy,” all those years ago, and he thinks the Red Sox have a shot to beat the Yankees in New York next week.
He is the one and only Pedro Martinez, and he’s spending Thursday in Lawrence with his wife, Carolina, launching an after-school coding program at South Lawrence East Elementary School, then engaging in a question-and-answer session with hundreds of students at Lawrence High School.
“Lawrence has been kind of forgotten a little bit,” said Martinez. “It has gotten kind of old in front of our eyes, but there is so much need. If there’s something I can really identify myself with, it is need. I grew up in those kind of needs. I’m just expressing the cry I had when I was a kid. I get excited every time I see a kid that has an opportunity to become someone.”
Martinez’s new program is designed to bridge resource gaps and enhance classroom learning for young students across Lawrence. His foundation, dedicated to transforming the lives of youth in the United States and the Dominican Republic, was started in 1998 when he joined the Sox after five-plus stellar seasons with the Dodgers and Expos.
“I got a very pleasant surprise when I got to Fenway as soon as I saw the drums and the people with the [Dominican] flag and the atmosphere kind of changing,” Martinez recalled. “Mayor [Thomas] Menino was kind enough to take me in his SUV to give me a tour around Boston, and right away I fell in love with the people … and the Latino community all over the place, and that’s when I landed in Lawrence, Lynn, Dorchester, and all those areas that continue to be linked to me.”
It was in those early Boston days that Martinez’s Fenway mound starts “became the curfew back home in the Dominican every time I pitched.”
A connection was made; an ongoing, lasting relationship because of the Pedro Martinez Foundation.
In 2026, Martinez and teammate/countryman David Ortiz are listed as “special assistants” in the fourth line of the the Red Sox’ official front office directory, just below chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. Martinez occasionally helps young Sox pitchers at spring training, but he was out of the loop when the decision was made to fire manager Alex Cora and six coaches just 27 games into the season.
“I was actually talking to Alex a couple of days before,” Martinez remembered. “When I found out, I wasn’t angry, I just couldn’t understand how everything snowballed to that point.”
Martinez’s beloved former teammate, catcher/captain Jason Varitek, was part of the purge. The Sox claimed Varitek was “reassigned,” but he hasn’t surfaced anywhere in the organization.
Does Martinez think the burned bridge will be repaired?
“I think it’s going to be OK with Jason,” said the three-time Cy Young Award winner. “Jason is a very professional person. He understands that business part, just like Alex Cora.”
What does Martinez think about the local demonization of Rafael Devers?
“This is a very misunderstood kid,” he said. “Devers is very shy. But he is legit. He’s a guy that doesn’t know how to express himself and has a hard time trusting anybody but his father. His father knows the actual truth … Devers is very respectful, a very lovely kid, but now it’s over and the team is on its way to success. … You have to learn to love Boston if you want to survive in Boston. Boston is 24/7 talking about their sports.”
Does Martinez want Payton Tolle or Sonny Gray starting Game 1?
“You don’t go wrong with either one,” he said. “Sonny is a true professional, a true competitor. I love, love Tolle. Just his amazing attitude. I love every single pitch he throws. I love everything about him.
“The Yankees are vulnerable, especially without [Aaron] Judge. I don’t think the Red Sox are intimidated by the Yankees. I think they can beat not only the Yankees but any team in baseball.”
The highlight of Martinez’s baseball career?
“Being part of the 25 that brought the trophy to Boston.”
Ever wish he never said, “The Yankees are my daddy”?
“No. I was being honest. That’s what you guys demand from all of us. The Yankees had my number at that point, and I expressed it. I will tell you in the most honest way, I got my ass kicked.”
Which brings us back to 2003, when Grady Little was fired (almost immediately) after failing to take Martinez out of the game when Pedro was past his pitch limit after seven innings of Game 7 of the ALCS at Yankee Stadium. Martinez had fanned Alfonso Soriano on his final pitch of the seventh, was at 100 pitches, and believed he was done for the night.
“[Red Sox pitching coach] Dave Wallace told me I was done after, so I didn’t put my jacket on,” said Martinez. “I had looked up in the sky and gave thanks to God for the seven innings I pitched. Our bullpen was lights out. All of a sudden Grady was like, ‘I don’t like [Alan] Embree against Nick Johnson in the eighth.’ He said, ‘You give me Nick Johnson and I got the rest of the bullpen for you.’ That’s the true story.”
Back on the mound, leading, 5-2, in the eighth, Martinez retired Johnson on a second-pitch popup to start the inning, then looked to the dugout. Nobody moved.
“Nothing happened,” recalled Martinez. “So I just kept going. I gave up a couple of line drives, and everything just snowballed after that. I thought I made a great pitch on [Jorge] Posada, but Posada blooped it [for a two-run double].”
All in all, it was four straight hits and a tie game before Little finally pulled Martinez after 23 disastrous eighth-inning pitches. Then Aaron Boone (now the Yankees’ manager) happened in the 11th.
Two summers ago, Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin wrote President Joe Biden a letter, imploring America’s tiring leader to end his reelection campaign. As part of his logic, Raskin compared Biden’s career to Martinez’s Game 7 performance, writing that there is “no shame in taking a well-deserved bow … when your arm is tired out.”
Days later, Biden pulled out of the race.
“I don’t know what to tell you about that,” chuckled Martinez. “Grady just told me, ‘Get one more out.’ That was Nick Johnson, right?”
Right.
All these years later, the wounds have healed and Martinez is on a greater mission, taking his message to Lawrence.
“I don’t have enough words to describe how grateful I am to have my opportunity through baseball and make a difference now,” said Martinez. “My message to these kids in Lawrence is that nothing in life is too far away if you have the will, if you have the passion.”
Dan Shaughnessy is a Globe columnist. He can be reached at daniel.shaughnessy@globe.com. Follow him @dan_shaughnessy.
