item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have scored 2.82 runs per game across their last 11 outings. The lineup is collectively batting .210 and posting a .621 OPS in that span. Wilyer Abreu, Adley Rutschman, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Nick Sogard have all gone cold at the wrong time.
With the Wild Card Series beginning September 29, the Red Sox need their bats to wake up before October arrives.
The cavalry is coming. And the timing could not be better.
The Latest on Rafaela
Ceddanne Rafaela is expected to return to the lineup on Tuesday when the Red Sox open a three-game series against the Guardians at Fenway Park.
The All-Star center fielder has been sidelined for 16 games since straining his right quadriceps.
Chad Tracy indicated over the weekend that Rafaela should come off the injured list for the homestand. The rotation is set up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez, a sequence that mirrors how the staff could be deployed in the Wild Card Series.
Getting Rafaela back before those games begin gives him a chance to find his timing and reintegrate into the lineup before the stakes get higher.
What Rafaela Brings Back
Rafaela's absence has been felt. On the season, he has produced 16 home runs, 70 RBIs, and a .282/.760 line. His combination of contact, power, and speed makes him one of the most complete players on the roster.
The defensive impact is equally significant. Rafaela's range in center field changes the way the pitching staff operates. Fly balls that fall for hits with other outfielders become outs when he is patrolling the middle of the outfield. His presence there tightens the entire defense.
The Red Sox have been using Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton to fill the void in center. Both have been serviceable, but neither provides the combination of offense and defense that Rafaela delivers on a daily basis.
The Red Sox Offense Needs a Spark
The numbers paint a clear picture of how badly the Red Sox have struggled at the plate.
Mickey Gasper is 4-for-25 over the recent stretch. Kiner-Falefa has managed just one hit in his last 20 at-bats. Sogard is 8-for-40. The lineup has lacked the consistent production that fueled the summer surge.
There have been bright spots. Roman Anthony broke out of a prolonged slump with a 5-for-13 weekend against the Rays that included two doubles and a homer. Trevor Story has been one of the hottest hitters on the roster since returning from the injured list, carrying a .338 average with an .869 OPS across 19 games.
Willson Contreras is also working his way back from a bruised right hand and could return this week. If both Contreras and Rafaela rejoin the lineup for the Guardians series, it would be the healthiest the Red Sox' batting order has looked in weeks.
Final Word for the Red Sox
The Red Sox have six games left before the playoffs begin.
Rafaela's return gives the lineup a jolt it needs. What he provides on both sides of the ball is invaluable for Boston.
Fenway awaits.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox Get Ceddanne Rafaela Update Ahead of Guardians Series appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Ranger Suarez’s antics cement his perfect playoff mentality after Red Sox clinch
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: Ranger Suarez is back to having fun after clinching the playoffs. Despite losing on Sunday, the Boston Red Sox clinched their spot in the postseason due to other teams' losses. The Sox took a team picture on the field at Tropicana Field before heading into the clubhouse for the usual champagne showers and beer. In the team photo, Suarez clearly sticks out. Standing right in the middle, the lefty starter had bright red shorts pulled up well above his waist, and his celebratory shirt tucked in. He
item.content:encoded:
Ranger Suarez is back to having fun after clinching the playoffs. Despite losing on Sunday, the Boston Red Sox clinched their spot in the postseason due to other teams' losses. The Sox took a team picture on the field at Tropicana Field before heading into the clubhouse for the usual champagne showers and beer.
In the team photo, Suarez clearly sticks out. Standing right in the middle, the lefty starter had bright red shorts pulled up well above his waist, and his celebratory shirt tucked in. He was also the only player in the picture with his goggles already covering his eyes. Suarez was known as a fun celebration guy with the Philadelphia Phillies, and it was something the fans there loved about him; Red Sox Nation was just waiting to see in Boston.
While Suarez is all fun and games with good spirits during a celebration, he does a complete 180 once the playoffs start. He's been one of the best playoff pitchers ever. His 1.48 ERA is the sixth-lowest of all time among pitchers with at least 40 innings pitched in the playoffs.
The 31-year-old has pitched in each of the last four postseasons. In 2023, he allowed just two earned runs in 14 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed four earned runs in 18 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed no runs in 4 1/3 innings. In 2025, he allowed one earned run in five innings. In the regular season, the lefty has a career 8.4 K/9; in the playoffs, it's 9.3
Ranger Suarez's playoff pedigree should excite fans after last season's playoff rotation
His playoff excellence was part of the reason the Red Sox signed him. While Suarez has been a very solid regular-season pitcher, it was his success in the playoffs that really made him stand out in last season's free-agent pool. After Garrett Crochet, the Red Sox ended up relying on Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. The Sox knew they needed another playoff-tested arm for the postseason and made the splash signing of the lefty to do so.
The Red Sox now head into the 2026 playoffs with a projected Wild Card round rotation that will consist of Suarez, Sonny Gray, and Payton Tolle. While the exact order is yet to be determined, those three arms will instill much more confidence than the three who started the games last year.
Suarez likes to have his fun. He did so in Philly and is doing so again here in Boston. That doesn't mean that opponents should take him lightly. Come playoff time, Suarez turns it on and shuts down the other teams.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Decisions, decisions: Five questions for Red Sox to answer before playoffs
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand. But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday. Who starts Game 1? When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultim
item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Risky business: In 2026, Craig Breslow and the Red Sox defied expectations with bold in-season risks - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Alex Speier
item.description: Even with the Red Sox having secured their second straight postseason berth, the magnitude of Craig Breslow’s gamble five months ago remains startling. There have been times when teams reacted to slow starts with a managerial or coaching staff change. But longtime members of the industry could not recall anything like the shakeup enacted by Breslow in April, when he fired manager Alex Cora and replaced six other members of the coaching staff. It was a move that departed from convention both for
item.content:encoded:
Even with the Red Sox having secured their second straight postseason berth, the magnitude of Craig Breslow’s gamble five months ago remains startling.
There have been times when teams reacted to slow starts with a managerial or coaching staff change. But longtime members of the industry could not recall anything like the shakeup enacted by Breslow in April, when he fired manager Alex Cora and replaced six other members of the coaching staff.
It was a move that departed from convention both for when it happened (barely a month into the season) and the extent of the change. It also pointed to an emerging theme of Breslow’s time as chief baseball officer: The willingness of the Sox to take significant in-season risks.
The firing of Cora and the staff members (with replacements plucked from the minors with little big league clubhouse experience), the mid-June trade of Rafael Devers in 2025, and the acquisition of catcher Adley Rutschman in exchange for a package of young talent (four of the Sox’ top 10 prospects, as well as catcher Carlos Narváez) that exceeded any in-season move by the Sox this century all pointed to an organization making massive bets on in-season changes.
“I always try to be guided by what I believe to be right and best for the organization,” Breslow said of his in-season risk tolerance. “Oftentimes, most people in these jobs would say their initial read or inclination of a situation was largely a correct one, but friction and inertia and emotion prevented you from acting on that. Then, you look back and say I wish I would have done whatever it was you were thinking at the time more often than you say that was probably not the right decision, and I wish I hadn’t.
“When you evaluate decisions through that lens, I think I default to, when you reach a certain level of conviction, you have to act.”
That sounds straightforward, but given baseball’s 162-game schedule, there’s often a willingness by heads of baseball operations to let situations play out over larger samples rather than intervene quickly. On both a personal and organizational level, a major in-season shakeup is uncomfortable.
“I certainly don’t sleep well [after a major change] for a few reasons, mostly because these are people that you have relationships with, and it’s not the outcome that you were looking for,” said Breslow. “These decisions are incredibly difficult. We’re talking about people’s lives, their families, children … there are a lot of implications to making these changes. So, it is wildly uncomfortable.”
Still, in a view perhaps informed by his playing career, Breslow has learned to remain open to uncomfortable in-season change — not for its own sake, but instead as a course correction when he sees a path to improving the club.
“I try to balance my [playing] experiences with what more information is telling me,” Breslow said. “I don’t think if I were only looking through things as I had experienced them that that would necessarily position us to make better decisions. But I think ignoring them would be ignoring valuable insights that I’ve learned.
“I was a lefthanded reliever that bounced around, who didn’t find success early on, pretty consistently evaluated the information that my performance was telling me, and tried to make adjustments as quickly as possible. I didn’t have the luxury of infinite runway in front of me to figure things out over time. If that’s an attitude or approach that I take to this job, then I think that’s OK.”
Breslow’s playing career may also inform his approach to in-season risks in another way: The way he values the chance to contend for a title.
It certainly would have been understandable if the Sox had decided by mid-June — around their 32-46 nadir — that they were open for business in a sell-off. Indeed, the Sox were at least starting to prepare for such an eventuality, with some of their pro scouts assigned to organizations who might be interested in short-term veterans, particularly Sonny Gray (who will be a free agent after 2026).
That said, Breslow had experience as a player of a long-shot team emerging as a champion. And so, even though there were few precedents for a team such as the Sox to overcome their long odds, based on his belief in the talent of the group, Breslow wanted to give the team as much time as possible to compete, respecting what he referred to as “the sanctity of a season.”
“Maybe that is born out of my playing career and the fact that the Red Sox won the World Series in 2013 as an improbable group going into the season,” he said. “Fundamentally, my confidence and belief in the players that we had on our roster [in 2026] had not changed. Players didn’t become meaningfully less talented. My belief in the roster was consistent.”
“But it’s interesting. Everybody who sits in my seat is going to talk about sustainability and the ability to compete for championships every single year. I think it’s very important to balance that with acknowledging the importance of every individual season. Otherwise, you talk about windows and about how maybe this isn’t the year, but that’s OK because next year we’ll still have the core of a really good team.
“I have learned that sometimes really good teams don’t have the seasons that they want. Sometimes teams that you don’t have maybe the highest expectations far outperform them for a season’s length. So you don’t want to dismiss what is immediately in front of you in exchange for this idea of lumping seasons together and just kind of thinking about being in the midst of a window.”
And so, the Sox ended up doing the opposite of what everyone forecast. A team for whom a veteran sell-off seemed almost inevitable instead ended up — thanks to one of the great runs in franchise history from late June to mid-August — taking big swings for deadline upgrades with moves to add infielder Curtis Mead and Rutschman.
In different ways, both moves stunned the industry given what the Sox gave up (Connelly Early for Mead; prospects Anthony Eyanson, Kyson Witherspoon, Enddy Azocar, and Harold Rivas, as well as Narváez for Rutschman). But from afar, Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young — like Breslow, a former player — could appreciate what his colleague did.
“In general, careers are short, and I want every player that puts on our uniform to have a chance to compete for a World Series. That should be our goal as an organization,” said Young. “When you have a team that’s in a win cycle, you need to be bold at times to go for it.
“It doesn’t mean necessarily you’re going to sustain success, but the goal is not to just make the playoffs. The goal is to win championships. And for me, especially in 2023 when we made very bold moves, it led to [a championship]. It easily could not have, but I know that if we didn’t make those moves, we wouldn’t have won. [And] there’s no doubt the player in me is influenced by the opportunity to win.”
Breslow’s deadline deals were motivated by a similar hunger. Now that the Red Sox have qualified for the playoffs, the ultimate impact of the bets made by Breslow in what he repeatedly described as a “difficult” season will gain greater definition in the postseason tournament.
But regardless of what happens, the path to get to the playoffs represented a fascinating shift in how the Red Sox conducted business, in a fashion that defied expectations at numerous turns on and off the field.
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Yankees' rotation vs. Rays is setting up a potential Wild Card Series mistake
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: The New York Yankees are almost guaranteed to face the Boston Red Sox in an upcoming best-of-three Wild Card series, and can lock up homefield advantage with either a singular win in their final seven games or one Boston loss. The time is now for forecasting and getting your ducks in a row, and the Yankees have acknowledged as such; resetting Brent Headrick, for example, is more important than going all out to embarrass the Tampa Bay Rays this week. That makes every rotation decision or perceive
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are almost guaranteed to face the Boston Red Sox in an upcoming best-of-three Wild Card series, and can lock up homefield advantage with either a singular win in their final seven games or one Boston loss. The time is now for forecasting and getting your ducks in a row, and the Yankees have acknowledged as such; resetting Brent Headrick, for example, is more important than going all out to embarrass the Tampa Bay Rays this week.
That makes every rotation decision or perceived pattern seem magnified, especially after Boston lined up their starters for their upcoming series with the Cleveland Guardians: Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, Ranger Suárez. Is that the chips falling where they may, or is that foreshadowing? Either way, while winking and nodding, it's probably time to read similarly into the way the Yankees are handlng things.
That's why our eyebrows raised on Sunday when the Yanks revealed that Cam Schlittler and Gerrit Cole will stay on turn in the Rays series (for now), with Schlittler closing the four-game set and Cole pitching Game 3, both staying out of the doubleheader. That will leave Cole with an extra day of rest ahead of the WIld Card opener and Schlittler on normal rest. You're not saying ... ?
All the love in the world to Gerrit Cole, who got closer to securing an all-important Wild Card Series start with his strong appearance in the desert on Friday night. But given that his spot in the rotation in general has been rightly questioned, there is no world where he should start Game 1 over Schlittler. That is not even something that should be rolling around in the canals of my addled gray brain. And yet!
Yankees giving Gerrit Cole the rest he needs ahead of Wild Card Series. Will Cam Schlittler even start vs. Rays?
For now, this is all hypothetical, but ... Cole has always seemed like a candidate for a deciding Game 3, but nothing before it. Would the Yankees really dare to use him in a deciding game with three extra days of rest building up on his right arm?
And, if the Rays clinch the AL East this week and the Yankees lock down their positioning, will they use Schlittler at all in this series? Will he make a perfunctory three-inning cameo just to keep his sea legs ahead of the Sox showdown and prevent overthrowing/overcompensating? The Cy Young race between he and Dylan Cease is informally over, and Cease may not even be healthy enough to make another start. If positioning gets more solidified throughout the week, these decisions only become more fascinating.
As of now, though, before any adjustments ... it seems like there's at least a chance the Yankees are lining up Cole for Game 1 - or working him out of the picture entirely.

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] Who matters most for Red Sox in playoffs? We ranked the top 10
item.dc:creator: Justin Leger
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history. But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way. It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes raz
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.

item.title: [morningjournal.com] Guardians can make it simple for clinching a 2026 postseason berth: Keep winning
item.dc:creator: Justin Lada
item.description: Baseball season’s marathon is coming down to its final sprint this week, and the Guardians are going to find out if they have enough figurative speed to finish on the podium. The Guardians did the hard work over the weekend by sweeping the Oakland/Sacramento/not-yet Las Vegas Athletics — though they had to come back on Sept. 18 and 19 — and squeaking out a 1-0 win. But style points don’t matter. Plus-one in the win column is all that counts. The Detroit Tigers begrudgingly gave Cleveland the sli
item.content:encoded:
Baseball season’s marathon is coming down to its final sprint this week, and the Guardians are going to find out if they have enough figurative speed to finish on the podium.
The Guardians did the hard work over the weekend by sweeping the Oakland/Sacramento/not-yet Las Vegas Athletics — though they had to come back on Sept. 18 and 19 — and squeaking out a 1-0 win. But style points don’t matter. Plus-one in the win column is all that counts.
The Detroit Tigers begrudgingly gave Cleveland the slightest bit of help by overcoming a six-run first inning to beat the Chicago White Sox on Sept. 18, 11-8. Unfortunately, their offense didn’t make much noise after that comeback, but it gave the Guardians just enough to climb back atop the AL Central alone.
Now, Cleveland takes its one-game lead in the AL Central and a five-game winning streak to Boston to face the freshly playoff-clinched Red Sox for three games. A series at Boston vs. the Red Sox is almost inarguably the toughest series left for Cleveland, the White Sox, and the rest of the wild card orbit of Texas, Toronto and Houston.
The White Sox will head to Kansas City this week, where the Royals are above .500 at home. Then they come back home to host the Colorado Rockies to end the regular season.
Unfortunately for the Guardians, they don’t have the safety net of any tiebreakers against teams in their orbit. A sweep of the Red Sox would give them the tiebreaker over Boston, but that wouldn’t matter as it would keep them in first place in the division going into the final weekend anyway.
The Red Sox also have their rotation lined up for the wild card Series, likely with the Yankees, since they’re close to having that locked in. Meaning Cleveland gets to face Boston’s best starting arms in Peyton Tolle, ace Sonny Gray, and another lefty in Ranger Suarez. So they all have six days of rest lined up into their starts in three-game wild card series.
Boston is six games back in the loss column of the New York Yankees, so catching them is highly improbable. Will that mean the Red Sox will get some players to rest? Possibly. They might be unlikely to push their starters too hard. But then that’s up to the Guardians’ offense to put them in that position to decide.
By virtue of holding Williams back to pitch last week in the opener vs. the White Sox, he’s not scheduled to pitch again until at least September 25 or 26. Cleveland has Parker Messick going vs. Boston in the opener, which also lines him up for regular rest on the final day of the season on Sept. 27, should Cleveland still need to win that game to get in the postseason.
The division title would be the most advantageous path for Cleveland. It would get a bye to the ALDS and host it at home, though the Guardians just did get their at-home record one game above .500 thanks to a 5-1 home stand to wrap up the regular season at Progressive Field. There is also a scenario in which Texas catches fire this week and clinches the second seed as the AL West champ and relegates Cleveland to a wild-card series no matter what. But for the Guardians, everything right now is about being one game better.
If they manage to win the division, then they can line the rotation up how they want for the ALDS.
If they are still fighting for a wild-card spot heading into the weekend in Kansas City, they would need to decide how they need to use Williams and Messick. If WIlliams starts on September 25, he could go in Game 2 of the wild card series on Sept. 30. If Messick has to pitch for the wild-card spot on Sept. 27, that takes him out of the wild-card round rotation at least on regular rest. At the very least, Cleveland needs the wild card spot wrapped up by Sept. 26, so it can skip Messick on Sept. 27, push him to Sept. 29 and have Messick and Williams lined up for Games 1 and 2.
The Guardians will either finish with another AL Central title, the franchise’s third in a row and the 14th in the history of the division, dating to its first in 1995, the last wild card spot, sending them to the worst division winner, possibly Houston or Texas, and then onto the White Sox IF they get past the wild card round. That means this final road trip could be a four-city, two-week tour to play the most meaningful and stressful baseball all year.
Or: They could miss the playoffs entirely. Thinking about some of those losses earlier in the year at St. Louis and Juan Brito’s error and one of the few Cade Smith blown saves. Or another one of his blown saves during the sweep by the Mets with two outs at home after the trade deadline.
Without having any tiebreakers over teams competing for playoff spots with them, the Guardians have to be one game better than any of them for a playoff spot. Be it the division or the wild card. That means winning one game at a time and just needing to be one run and one game better.

item.title: [bostonglobe.com] Red Sox offense has been running on fumes down the stretch - The Boston Globe

item.content:encoded:
Call it a product of injuries or just a slump, but the Red Sox are staggering into the final week of the regular season offensively.
They have averaged 2.82 runs over the last 11 games, hitting .210 with a .621 OPS.
Wilyer Abreu (7 for 36), Mickey Gasper (4 for 25), Jahmai Jones (2 for 18), Isiah Kiner-Falefa (1 for 20), Adley Rutschman (6 for 30), and Nick Sogard (8 for 40) have all gone cold.
Roman Anthony was 5 for 13 with two doubles and a home run over the weekend against the Rays after hitting .137 in his 12 prior games.
The Sox are eighth in the American League in runs scored (678, 4.35 per game). They were third last season at 4.85.
“Just got to stay with it,” interim manager Chad Tracy said after a 5-1 loss against the Rays on Sunday. “Obviously we’ve got to hit and score runs. But we’re getting our way back to health, and we’ll get there.”
The return of two of the team’s top hitters, Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela, should help.
Contreras has played only four games this month because of a strained left hamstring and a bruised right hand. He started swinging a bat Sunday and hopes to return this week after missing the Rays series.
“It’s getting better every day,” Contreras said Sunday. “We’ll see.”
Contreras leads the team in home runs (27), RBIs (81), and OPS (.905).
Rafaela should be back in the lineup Tuesday after missing 16 games with a right quadriceps strain. He has hit .282 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, and 70 RBIs.
Caleb Durbin has reached base in 13 consecutive games, raising his on-base percentage from .324 to .338.
Trevor Story has been another positive, hitting .338 with an .869 OPS and 10 RBIs over 19 games since returning from the injured list.
Tests this week
The postseason doesn’t start until Sept. 29, but the Red Sox will get a taste of what’s to come this week at Fenway Park.
They start a three-game series against the Guardians on Tuesday before the Cubs arrive Friday.
The 81-75 Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox in the American League Central. The 87-69 Cubs are tied with the Padres atop the National League wild-card race.
The Guardians have All-Star lefthander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57) starting Tuesday with Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67) on Wednesday. Messick faced the Sox in Cleveland on May 30 and allowed one run over five innings.
The Sox have Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez lined up in the series, which could be how they approach the Wild Card Series next week.
Honor for Arias
Shortstop Franklin Arias was named the Eastern League’s Most Valuable Player and Top Prospect by Minor League Baseball. The 20-year-old from Venezuela hit .318 with a .993 OPS in 75 games for Portland before he was promoted to Triple-A Worcester. Sea Dogs first baseman Brooks Bannon also was named to the Eastern All-Star team. The Pitcher of the Year was righthander Anthony Eyanson, who was 4-0 with a 1.69 ERA in 11 games for Portland before going to the Orioles organization in the trade for Rutschman . . . The Sox finished 46-35 on the road, a five-game improvement on last season . . . Assistant general managers Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith interviewed with the Athletics, who are searching for a head of baseball operations after firing David Forst in August. Longtime assistant GM Billy Owens also is a candidate, along with former Nationals GM Mike Rizzo and former Astros GM James Click, who now works for the Blue Jays.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Red Sox-Cubs weather nightmare could give Yankees a surprising playoff edge
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: Fans of the Boston Red Sox are about to become bigger fans of the Philadelphia Phillies and San Diego Padres than they've ever been. And fans of the New York Yankees are about to get a renewed interest in destructive weather systems. item.content:encoded:
Fans of the Boston Red Sox are about to become bigger fans of the Philadelphia Phillies and San Diego Padres than they've ever been. And fans of the New York Yankees are about to get a renewed interest in destructive weather systems.
With Boston and New York all but fated to meet next week in a best-of-three Wild Card Series, the Yankees are suddenly invested in a chaotic super storm that might interfere with the Sox's meaningful weekend series with the Chicago Cubs. If the Cubs' playoff positioning is at stake - right now, they're tied atop the Wild Card standings with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies - these games will need to be completed, whether or not they have any significance to the Sox. Bostonians probably hope the Cubs slip up before they ever arrive at Fenway while the Pads and Phils surge.
It seems very likely these games will need to be completed, though. It also seems very likely these games will be washed out, leading to either a baseball game (or two!) taking up Boston's lone off day before the start of the postseason, or an emergency roadtrip to Chicago disrupting things in a different way.
Will Red Sox insane weather weekend against Cubs hurt their chances against Yankees in playoffs?
Now, counterpoint, we know how much the Red Sox tend to excel when faced with plane trauma or travel trouble of any kind. Does extreme weather also make them superhuman? I, for one, do not want to find out.
Objectively, though, even if they rest all their starters and even if they have zero members of the playoff rotation penciled into this Cubs series, all lined up for the previous showdown with the Cleveland Guardians ... this has to have an effect, doesn't it? It's in MLB's absolute best interest to avoid any nonsense here. Cram a doubleheader into Friday. Tell John Henry he's about to lose some gate receipts and push this whole series to Chicago. The impact on the Wild Card Series is too great.
And you thought this weekend of baseball was meaningless, didn't you, Yankees fans? Joke's on you.
Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez will all be out of commission either way, but any undue duress that removes a clean reset point from the Sox while allowing the Yankees to veg out and get in the right mindset can certainly swing things a bit. And if this series is crucial to the Cubs, MLB won't love Boston trying to rest their starters and back away from the competition either. This is about to be fascinating, strange, and a potentially damaging wrinkle in any playoff preview.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox' Payton Tolle Can Make Franchise History in Postseason
item.dc:creator: Matthew Singer
item.description: The Boston Red Sox are set for a pivotal playoff matchup, likely with the New York Yankees in the first round of the postseason. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are set for a pivotal playoff matchup, likely with the New York Yankees in the first round of the postseason.
It’s been a whirlwind of a season for Boston fans after their horrible start under manager Alex Cora and subsequent hot streak under interim manager Chad Tracy. Part of this hot streak has been the emergence of an elite rotation led by rookies and veterans alike.
Their rotation is so good, in fact, that it’s a real discussion of who will start Game 1 and Game 2 between Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez. And it’s a good problem to have!
Rob Bradford of WEEI shared that Tolle has a “good shot” at taking the mound in the first game of the series. If he gets the ball in Game 1 or Game 2, he will make franchise history as the youngest pitcher to start the first or second game of a playoff series since Babe Ruth in the 1918 World Series, per former Red Sox director of baseball communications and media relations JP Long.
Should Boston Red Sox Phenom Payton Tolle Start Game 1 or 2?
The Red Sox drafted Tolle in the second round of the 2024 MLB Draft out of Texas Christian University. Teams quickly saw that Tolle had the tools to succeed, as he sprinted through the minors.
He would soon have an elite year in the minors in his first professional season, making it all the way to the majors in 2025. However, it was rough sledding for Tolle as he sported a 6.06 ERA in 16.1 major league innings.
Going into 2o26, he was a top-20 prospect. From the start of the season, he has not disappointed. In 25 starts during 20026 (143 innings), Tolle has a 3.02 ERA with 166 strikeouts and just 38 walks.
He has the second-lowest ERA among qualified starters on the team, just behind Sonny Gray. While you could definitely make an argument that the veteran Gray should start Game 1, Tolle has been a monster against the Yankees this season.
In his season debut on April 23, Tolle went six innings, allowing just three hits, one walk, one run and striking out 11 batters. On June 26, he would face New York again, going seven innings and allowing just one hit and two walks with seven strikeouts.
Gray has the regular-season production, postseason experience and fuel, being a former Yankees castoff. However, Tolle seems to be at his best when playing against New York and other AL East teams.
Either way, Tolle will likely be making history not seen since the Great Bambino in over a century.
What About Game 3 and Moving Forward?
Suárez should be locked in for a top-3 start, if necessary. In 27 starts, Suárez has a 3.27 ERA in 143.1 innings with 135 strikeouts. The two-time All-Star is also a formidable playoff pitcher, with a minuscule 1.48 ERA in 11 postseason games.
After him, it gets a bit murkier. While you don’t need a full five-man rotation in the playoffs, it’s likely necessary to have a fourth dependable starter.
Rookie Jake Bennett was cruising through his first dozen career starts. However, in his last seven starts, he has a 5.40 ERA. He may be unlikely to shoulder such a burden in his first postseason. It also complicates things that 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet has been out since late April and will likely be a bullpen arm if and when he returns in 2026.
And perhaps the most shocking positive development has been the improvement of Brayan Bello. In his first 10 games, Bello was a disaster. In his last 15, he has been borderline elite with a 2.98 ERA. This was highlighted by an eight-inning performance on Saturday. If needed, Bello could likely be a starter or bulk reliever in the playoffs.
Whatever the case may be, the Boston Red Sox could be a dangerous team in October, with their monster pitching staff at the head of it all.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] Ben Clemens FanGraphs Chat - 9/21/26
item.dc:creator: Ben Clemens
item.description: Ben Clemens Hey everybody, welcome to the chat. We're testing out a new chat interface today, one that we'll hopefully roll out more broadly in the weeks to come. So come on, let's run it through its paces. Kevin In a weekly transactions H2H league, would you risk rolling with Aroldis this week? I don't see why the Bosox would rush him back into action. Ben Clemens Yeah, I would not. For exactly the reason you said. It just feels like you're opening yourself up to some risk without enough upside
item.content:encoded:
Ben Clemens
Hey everybody, welcome to the chat. We're testing out a new chat interface today, one that we'll hopefully roll out more broadly in the weeks to come. So come on, let's run it through its paces.
Kevin
In a weekly transactions H2H league, would you risk rolling with Aroldis this week? I don't see why the Bosox would rush him back into action.
Ben Clemens
Yeah, I would not. For exactly the reason you said. It just feels like you're opening yourself up to some risk without enough upside back for it. You're going to feel REALLY bad if they ease him back in and you're playing him. And on the flip side, what if he's not right immediately? Can't have a 0% chance of that.
SPArn
Any favorite random MLBers as we wind down the stretch, or little hopeful glimpses? I still don't believe Scott Bandura is real, even though Mo'Ne Davis went to his debut, and I nearly shed a tear during Josiah Gray's return
Ben Clemens
I mean, this guy is definitely very real, but David Freese is my all-time favorite good but not great guy who stuck around long enough for me to have fond memories of them.
Ben Clemens
Many of mine are Cardinals themed because that's when I was most strongly a fan of a single team. Pete Kozma. Bo Hart.
Ben Clemens
If we're talking current guys, well, how about Trent Harris, who I've grown inordinately fond of very quickly this year
SPArn
Your piece(s) on Cade Cavalli are excellent, much more thorough and better reasoned than this. But, I think the extension boils down to: 4/47 is low risk enough it doesn't hurt if he regresses or breaks, and if it turns into 5/70, it must have worked out great for the Nats. All reporting seems like he's a truly excellent leader too. We came a long way from "sit down, boy" and we can all be grateful for that
Ben Clemens
Yeah, I think that's basically the risk management part of mine. It's a good bet even if you know he gets hurt some of the time, because on average you get a nice amount of value out of signing him. I leave the leadership stuff aside – I agree with you that it's widely reported that way, I just think that those types of things are extremely subjective and don't hold over long periods of time anyway.
aldrinbatistarocks
A while ago, I remember listening to a BP podcast in which they were talking about christopher morel, the gist of the discussion being "it's okay to acknowledge when a guy is probably having their career year." Are there any candidates in 2026 for guys you think hit their apex production this season?
Ben Clemens
Love this one. Some easy ones for me: Otto Lopez. PCA. Gabriel Moreno. Randy Arozarena. Jake Bauers.
Ben Clemens
I don't mean any of them ill by that. But I just think a ton of stuff broke well for those players in their years, and that it feels hard to have all of that plus more hit right in a future year for them to eclipse it. You can still be a very good player after hitting your apex production
smoothio
Does Tatis have an MVP season in him?
Ben Clemens
Whether he actually wins one? who can say. Whether he has the capability to? Clearly yes. He's played at an MVP level for half of this year, for example. The talent is definitely there. Winning an MVP is tough because you have to have it hit for a whole year when no one else hits their even better outcome.
oaktownblues
Think the A's can hold onto a winning record against every AL west team this season? Just need to not lose series vs Angels and Astros
Ben Clemens
I do. I think that'd be a pretty cool footnote on what was just a real bummer of a season. Kind of a hilarious one, too. The AL is a mess this year.
bosoxforlife
The Red Sox should start Tolle in game 1 in The Bronx. The reality is that the Red Sox look outmatched and his personality fits the occasion perfectly and a few quick K's could change the mood.
Ben Clemens
I like the idea of starting Tolle game one. I feel crazy saying this, but I kind of like the idea of just starting three lefties and daring the Yankees to play their righty platoon bats, kind of gambling on Judge being less than 100%
Anonymous Member #46
Holy crap, I dig the new chat interface so far. No login issues!
Ben Clemens
Great to hear. Sean and team are still working on adding functionality (polls, images, that kinda thing) but I have been liking the clean look and it gives us more flexibility on our end
Ben Clemens
a little more legible and the scroll bars are nicer. Setting up the chat has more options. Basically this just has more options across the board. Oh, and I love the little FanGraphs icon by my name, so fun
oaktownblues
How does the new chat interface differ on your end? Are questions organized differently than before?
Ben Clemens
so, there's something I'm still getting used to, published those two out of order
riceball
where does Yordan rank among unlikely batting title winners? (assuming he holds on)
Ben Clemens
Nowhere near the top. He has a career .300 batting average! Among big league regulars, only Luis Arraez, Chandler Simpson (small-ish sample), and Jose Altuve are better
bosoxforlife
I can't get over the fact that either the Guardians or the White Sox will, most likely, receive a bye in the first round while whoever wins the AL West plays the team that finishes second but gets the home field against a team with a better record. I don't want to pour cold water on the new interface but the submission box is too small to handle more than two lines of copy.
Ben Clemens
Great feedback on the submission box. That sounds like an easy fix to me, I'll let Sean know.
As to the playoff system, yeah, I agree that this is a problem. I really like the bye system we have at current. It gives a reward for teams that have great regular seasons. But I agree that the divisional system interacts awkwardly with it. What if they handed out playoff spots the way they do now but pre-reseeded, ordering teams by record? I'm totally with you that it's a good idea that feels obviuosly unfair in practice.
SPArn
Pitchers having their best year: Nick Martinez, Luzardo, Messick, Louis Varland, Martin Perez some candidates that leap to mind. (Don't say the Miz, don't say the Miz, don't say the Miz)
Ben Clemens
I don't think the Miz counts. Like, yes, he's having an extremely good year. But he could throw more innings. the strikeouts don't look crazy unsustainable. it COULD be a career year but it doesn't feel like a blow-off top (a finance term I love and have been trying to use more of late) in the way that, say, Otto Lopez does
didace
Submission box – The default seems small, but click/hold and drag the little thing in the bottom right corner and you can make it very large.
Sean Dolinar
We are going to fix that once this chat is over. Thanks everyone for the feedback! – Sean
Ben Clemens
Martinez doesn't count because this isn't even his best year! He had his career year in 2024 in Cincy. Luzardo, same kinda deal, he's basically repeating last season. probably not 'career year' territory. I definitely agree with you on Varland, don't think Messick is really fair since he's a rookie, and Martin Perez got a qualifying offer once!
Ben Clemens
My own list would have: Reid Detmers, who I think is good but not this good. Sean Burke, though without much conviction there. And Foster Griffin.
Michael De Vivo
will spencer jones be overmatched by playoff level pitching?
Ben Clemens
If by overwhelmed you mean he'll strike out a lot, absolutely yes. He's a high-strikeout guy and the octane of pitchers ramps up int he playoffs. But it's not like he hasn't faced hard pitches in the regular season or in the minors. His game is tons of strikeouts and sometimes the ball leaves the yard. One playoff homer or so and we'llb e like man, this guy has it. And since homers are pretty rare events, it feels like Jones could be basically the same hitter and based on whether he happens to run into one or not we'll say he just didn't have it or performed as expected.
ado64
Who do you think starts Brewers playoff game 3, and how many innings do they get? 3 innings of Gasser or Drohan, maybe? Does May ever start a game with his recent inconsistency?
Ben Clemens
I think that some kind of piggyback situation is reasonable here. Like, three of Drohan with May backing him up? Or some other lefty/righty switch of that style. I'm extremely curious to see how they deploy Harrison.
Ben Clemens
I really don't know what you do with Harrison. Like, he's been so bad recently! But he has such high highs. The test in relief hasn't gone all that well so far. It's not like they can afford to just not have him pithc, he was a big part of their run prevention this year.
Ben Clemens
Sorry, I missed an answer before messing around iwth the interface. I meant to say that Harrison is the highest-unceratinty question in the entire playoff picture for me. The Brewers were the best team in baseball this year and Kyle Harrison was a ton of that. What are they going to look like with less good pitching? Can they figure out what ails him in time? I have no clue but I'm very excited to find out.
Anon21
Maybe dumb question. When Team A is one game ahead of Team B in the standings and also holds the tiebreaker on Team B, it's often said that they effectively have a two-game lead. But is there a similar way of describing the situations of the Astros and White Sox, who are one game back in the standings but hold the tiebreaker over the team ahead? Like are they effectively 0.8 (or something) games back, rather than one? (I know this is accounted for by magic numbers, just wondering if there's a simple way to describe this situation.)
Ben Clemens
I'd say they're one back with the tiebreaker. Or alternately that they're 'effectively only a half game back' because of the breaker. I agree with you that the wording is kind of tricky, though. You can't say they're 'effectively tied', that's not true. If they hvae the same records they won't make the playoffs
Nomar6666666
No question really. Just a frustrated fan with few places to vent. If the owners lock out the players next season, and we miss one single game, I will not go to a single game next year, nor will I buy the MLB TV package. I Wii continue to support this site
Ben Clemens
Nomar, we appreciate your continued support, of course. That's very kind. And honestly, I feel pretty similar. I think the owners are more to blame than the players for the upcoming fight we're sure to have. I don't feel great about anyone's role in this though. There's so much freaking money in baseball. Work it out between yourselves like adults so that we the fans, who pay a ton of money to enjoy your product, can still get it. No one is on our side in this negotiation, and that makes it feel bad
Braydon Roberts
Thoughts on the NL RoY race? Seems like everyone gave it to Sal Stewart when JJ went on the IL, but Stewart has had a rough September. fWAR is 4.4 to 2.2 in JJ's favor.
Ben Clemens
So, I've had JJ all along. I just don't really buy the arguments that some counting numbers matter so much that they're more important than the overall picture. I'm not saying Stewart's homers don't matter or anything. Obviously they do. But eh, the RBI's, I'm not as convinced by, because a stat like RE24 (which cares about driving in runs, but also cares about how many opportunities you had to drive in runs) says Stewart was about 10 runs better with the bat than Wetherholt this year so far.
Ben Clemens
That's not a ton of runs better. And again, that accounts for the RBI and the homers and all. And if you care about win probability – as in how important those RBIs were – Wetherholt actually has a BETTER bat than Stewart
Ben Clemens
Also he's a plus defender at an important position instead of a first baseman who defensive metrics aren't fond of
Ben Clemens
Like, I get the sentiment. And I get wanting to push back against WAR and be like 'no the old stats we love still matter'
Ben Clemens
There are times where I think that's true! I'd vote for Yordan by a mile for AL MVP, and it's because I think that his offensive value is so high that WAR is overly penalizing him for his defense. no one cares when you hit that well. BUt that's not Sal Stewart's case.
war2d2
Don’t like the new interface, all my questions are still poorly thought out and badly edited. Thought it would have fixed that.
Ben Clemens
That's coming in FanGraphs 2.0 🙂
Greg Simons
Regarding last week's lack of any questions about lunch, I think we all figured someone else would ask. Of course, when that happens, you make a "fig" out of "u" and "re," or something like that. Whatever the case, I hope you have a good lunch planned today.
Ben Clemens
Why thank you. It's like House said once, I think: That's what happens when you make a presumption. You make a pres out of you and some guy named umption.
As for lunch, leftovers from a very nice salmon dish that a friend of ours cooked this weekend.
WonderWall
Piggybacking on Nomar's comments, why do you think that both the owners and the Union seem to pretty much refuse to let the situation continue. Why do both sides feel like something needs to change?
Ben Clemens
Many possible answers to this. I think the most important, for me, is that they'd act this way even if they thought that 'no change' was acceptable, because that's how bargaining well in advance of a deadline works. So I'm hopeful that when the rubber meets the road, both sides will cave simultaneously.
Barbaro Garbey
Thank you for the chat Ben. The Tigers have to feel good about former top prospects Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark thriving in their first big league action this year. Wondering though if you have any thoughts on any of the "other" Tigers rookies who have been getting run down the stretch? Personally, I have loved watching the energy guys like Hao-Yu Lee and Eduardo Valencia have brought; and Ben Malgeri and Brett Callahan have at least looked like quality defensive outfielders (at least compared to some of the butchers the Tigers have put out there). Do you think any of this group could succeed/thrive in closer to a full time role next year?
Ben Clemens
Truthfully I don't think I've seen enough of any of them to be all that sure, but I do think that they did enough that if I'm the Tigers, I'm interested in leaving some space for the minor leaguers to have bigger roles next year. Like, leave an outfield hole perhaps?
Phil
Are we sure the Sox' best option, with Rafaela back, isn't Anthony in right and Gasper/Jones at DH? I'm not really believing in Duran right now.
Ben Clemens
This seems like possibly the best option, but their behavior year to date basically tells me they won't be doing this. Or, well, assuming you mean Anthony in left, I like Abreu in right.
PC1970
Would you even put Harrison on the roster if you were Milwaukee? He looks unplayable at the moment. Maybe overreaction, but, you also can't just punt a playoff game like they can a regular season game.
Ben Clemens
I mean, I would. If I thought playing Harrison was punting a game, I wouldn't put him on there. But I kind of think that you need to give yourself chances to have your best possible team. And c'mon, if he's awful for two innings and you yank him, I think that's short of punting the game. I think that not rostering him would basically be playing too conservative. You should try to hit your high-upside outcomes to win in the playoffs, imo
Anon21
Following up more on the lockout question…I think implicitly I'm assigning the probability of missing any games to be low, definitely less than 10%. Commentators throwing around the possibility of losing the whole season seem nuts to me–isn't that obviously suicidal from a business perspective? Where do you stand on probabilities of losing any games/a significant number of games/the whole season?
Ben Clemens
I'm at least close to you on this one. I think I have the odds of missing games very low and the odds of missing a season at pretty close to zero. I just don't think the owners have the collective will. I don't think the players do either, when push comes to shove.
Robert Stewart
After the Bregman injury, should MLB enforce the rule that on deck hitters should be in the on deck circle? I remember a few years ago when they did that and the batter (I think it was Beltre) moved the actual circle to where he was standing. He may have been ejected.
Ben Clemens
No, because clearly this enforcement wouldn't stick and no one likes feeling either like a nanny or like they're being nanny stated by the umpires. The Beltre thing was a while ago at this point I think? But a specific umpire told him to get back in the circle so he moved it. It wasn't at the same time as an enforcement push or anything, if I'm remembering correctly.
wheelhouse
Boston’s about to sail to the WS, no? Easy opponent after easy opponent ahead of them
Ben Clemens
A jinx? A stealth insult? Who knows, let's hit publish.
Vee
i would be very happy if this is not Pete's peak. I dream of 12 war PCA.
Ben Clemens
Haha right? That one was kind of a gimme just because it's SO hard to imagine a better season.
HappyFunBall
Is Kyle Harrison at risk of not even making the playoff roster?
Ben Clemens
Didn't realize that this was less of a fringe opinion and more of a 'thing people are thinking'. I guess that I underestimated it. I don't really think that it's likely because he's good! Clearly capable of dominance. But the Brewers have a lot more granular data and maybe they really do think he's cooked for the moment. I just…. c'mon, the guy was so good earlier this year, and if you leave him off the playoff roster in the NLDS, you're never bringing him back on, you're accepting that you're just playing without this big important piece. I just hate settling like that.
Tim Tebow's Thunder Thighs
Dider Fuentes is rolling as a mid-reliever, but do you think the Braves should stretch him back out into a starting role next year a la Strider?
Ben Clemens
I think they'll try, realize that he's better in this current role, and move him back. They should try even if they don't think it'll work. The odds of it working are obviously not zero and he'd be more valuable by a lot if it stuck
appayipyip
If you had to sit down and name every baseball player you can think of how many names could you get to?
Ben Clemens
Oh man. Hundreds. Probably a thousand? I think I'd get tired before I ran out of names. Playing OOTP for many years, and Perfect Team in particular (Paul Sporer curates the sets over there and does an incredible job of finding fun old players) has given me a big memory bank of names
Tim Tebow's Thunder Thighs
Holy crap, am I able to submit a question as a logged in FG member? That's the first time in months.
What you do suspect the Braves will do with Profar's contract after two long term suspensions with one year remaining (which isn't far off from a qualifying offer)? I can't imagine AA getting much of anything for him
Ben Clemens
Oh yeah…. I think they'll either cut him or trade him eating all the money for a lottery ticket.
Ben Clemens
Tebow sighting yesterday btw! At the Broncos Jags game. Florida man with Denver connections, makes sense.
Phil
Yes, by right I meant left, sorry, and thanks. Also, Sean, can we bring back the thing where your own question is blue? That was both pleasurable and, particulalry when illicitly following the chat on a phone at work, useful.
Ben Clemens
putting this in the log so Sean can see it too. I didn't even know about that feature. See, this is why it's good to test things.
jonmberra
Do you think the Mariners can fix their defense this offseason? Seems like they hit a little worse than expected, and the team imploded because their defense is terrible.
Ben Clemens
I do think this is fixable. I think it might kind of fix itself, to be honest. Their worst defenders by FRV are Crawford and Arozarena, both FA's. Luke Raley was bad in right before he got hurt, but he was also just not great overall, they're surely looking for better options. TO me, it looks like they're set up to improve on defense without even focusing on it specifically, just from the change in team composition.
draftdingers
Do the Cardinals test the trade market for Herrera this offseason and could they even get a good return? Burleson seems to be the First Basemen for the next few years and I can't see Herrera staying behind the plate with his subpar defense and the glut at catcher coming through the system.
Ben Clemens
I think that they'll test the trade market, and I think they will definitely get a good return if they decide to trade him. I think that zero-ish other teams see him as a catcher, though. I see him as a 1B/DH who can maybe be an emergency catcher, I didn't like the way the Cards kept tring him at catcher even after the writing was on the wall, at least to me.
Ben Clemens
But when I was bouncing players off of my sources this summer and talking about Herrera as a fringy name, probably not top 50 trade value but surely top 100, people didn't have much to say about that eitehr way, which suggests to me that it's roughly right. Good plus bat, might benefit from not having to play catcher so often, cost controlled for a while. Teams would be interested in this for sure. He has a batting line 20% above average for his career and doesnt' cost much; the pitch sells itself.
kingkash7788
how much has nimmala rose post trade deadline
Ben Clemens
This is really more of a question for the prospect guys than for me but his stock is clearly up, impressive performance in Double-A at 20. I am not sure he's their starting shortstop on opening day next year because Neto is awesome and I'm not sold on a move to third base being inevitable. But I think that he's clearly arrow up from what we thought of him at the deadline. Good trade for the Angels. Might be a win-win, I think Soriano is gonna play well in Toronto next year, but the Angels have 100% done well there.
HappyFunBall
re: Dider Fuentes. The question to ask is not whether or not he'll be better as a reliever. MOST pitchers are. That's why they get put there in the first place. The question to ask is will Fuentes be able to thrive in a 5+ innings role or not.
Ben Clemens
Concur with this. And my thinking there is that if you're being honest with yourself, it's not certain whether he'll thrive in a 5+ inning role but he certainly hasn't ruled it out with his performance. Particularly if the Braves feel good about his feel for the splitter, which he's basically been able to mothball in relief but would surely need to add back in as a starter, I think it'd be crazy NOT to try. He's 21 and destroying major league hitting and came up as a starter.
sloejoe
Thanks for the chat! Is Robert Gasser a starter next year? According to Roster Resource he is their 5th starter. Has he shown to have the stuff to move up?
Ben Clemens
Yeah, the Brewers always use a bunch of starters interchangeably throughout the year but I have no reason to think he won't be one of them.
appayipyip
If you were the Jays would you try to extend Soriano?
Ben Clemens
I would. The weird part is the timing – like, if they haven't started on it now, I doubt they're getting it done before the lockout unless both sides really want it. So is it a next year post lockout kinda thing? Maybe. But I am generally a fan of trying to sign contract extensions when it makes even a little sense, and this one clearyl makes some sense.
fincampbell05
What are the Red Sox going to do? They're going to have some money to spend, but there really isn't a clear hole on the roster except for SS, where they surely would not sign someone that blocks Arias, if there were even any good free agent shortstops.
Ben Clemens
This isn't a great year to spend money, it's looking like. But that suits them just fine – like you said, there isn't a super clear hole on the roster aside from shortstop. And for me, backup at 3B because I dno't quite believe Durbin's torrid stretch. But I think I'd just be willing to keep some powder dry, basically. I think we've discussed their payroll situation some in recent weeks; it's really well set-up for next year, very few players leaving. Maybe they try to work out another year of Sonny Gray, maybe they just top up on pitching, but this is a great year to not need a bunch of players in FA, because the FA class is not good. I don't think they need to overcomplicate things too much – they went hard last winter, they can cool it this winter.
Rayball
Who do you have emerging in this final week between TEX and HOU?
Ben Clemens
Houston because they're like the bogeyman, they always seem to keep coming even when you think they're done. But no strong lean
drplantwrench
Also another note: it would be nice to make `Your questions awaiting the host` collapsible
Ben Clemens
Noted.
randomname1234
If you're the Red Sox, do you tank this week and hope to get WC#3 instead of WC#2? Almost certainly not catching NY for WC#1, and road games against AL West and AL Central winners sound much better than road games against Yankees and Tampa.
Ben Clemens
A few people asked versions of this earlier, I happened to like this phrasing most. But I'm answering all of your questions. No. I'd be happy if that happened, but I would not mess with wanting my good players to play well a week before the playoffs, for marginal gain. Matchups matter, but only so much, and there's no guarantee.
bosoxforlife
I do not understand why teams don't see players like Herrera as a potential career DH and as a very valuable third catcher. Mickey Gasper is presently showing just how valuable that type of player is even if doesn't keep hitting at this level. When a team has two catchers it really only has one but with three all can be used freely.
Ben Clemens
Oh I 100% agree. I think this is a leak among teams. And Herrera hits well enough, or at least projects to hit well enough, that you're not sacrificing offense anywhere, it's just free-ish value.
Phillip Denny
Do you think Luzardo's injury means he's just a glorified opener (or maybe gives you 2-3) in the WC/DS? If so, is there an argument for turning him into a late inning fireman instead?
Ben Clemens
I am unsure, but I am leaning towards him having very short starts, at which case yes, I'd prefer him as an impact reliever. I don't know if he is ready to warm up and play in that role, though, and given his at-times-injured past and his contract, if I'm the Phillies, I want him to give me a strong sign that he's interested in this role and thinks he'd do well at it
Ben Clemens
Okay everyone, this was a wonderful chat, but now I'm going to go have that aforementioned salmon and start working on an article for tomorrow.
Ben Clemens
Thanks for all the great questions, and for helping us test out the new chat interface. May the last week of the regular season be delightful for you, and let's get ready for the playoffs.
Ben is a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @benclemens.

item.title: [mlb.com] Postseason FAQ: What's next for the Red Sox?
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne
