item.content:encoded:
Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

item.title: [FanSided] Yankees can deliver Sonny Gray the ultimate karma in potential final game
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: Having owned a Coonhound named “Karma” for 13 years, I’m well familiar of the idea that what goes around comes around. Even the dog who would stare at the wall during thunderstorms would join us in being amused by veteran Boston Red Sox pitcher Sonny Gray’s upcoming predicament. As things stand entering the regular season’s final week, the 36-year-old right-hander would likely start next Wednesday’s second game of the Wild Card Series. Fittingly, Gray would make his Red Sox playoff debut against
item.content:encoded:
Having owned a Coonhound named “Karma” for 13 years, I’m well familiar of the idea that what goes around comes around.
Even the dog who would stare at the wall during thunderstorms would join us in being amused by veteran Boston Red Sox pitcher Sonny Gray’s upcoming predicament. As things stand entering the regular season’s final week, the 36-year-old right-hander would likely start next Wednesday’s second game of the Wild Card Series.
Fittingly, Gray would make his Red Sox playoff debut against a Yankees team he’s publicly admitted to despising. The three-time All-Star pitched in 41 games for the Yankees from 2017-18, a stint that resulted in him being demoted to the bullpen midway through that second season.
“It feels good to me to go to a place where it’s easy to hate the Yankees,” Gray said this past offseason. “I never wanted to go there in the first place.”
Good news, Sonny: Your next trip to the Bronx could also mark the last start of your impressive 14-year career.
Could Boston Red Sox pitcher Sonny Gray retire after the 2026 season?
We’ve done plenty of speculating about players’ futures lately, but this isn’t one of those instances. Gray recently told the Boston Globe that he’d retire in a “heartbeat” if his family wanted him to, and the organization is reportedly preparing for the possibility that he won’t return in 2027.
Gray turns 37 in November and has a $30 million mutual option for 2027, though he can opt out and forfeit a $5 million buyout. Assuming that he wants to return next year, it’s difficult to envision the Red Sox passing on his option given his performance and his outspoken love of pitching in Boston.
Garrett Crochet gets all of the attention, but don’t sleep on Gray’s impact. He climbed the 2,000-strikeout threshold earlier this year, and he's already recorded a career-high 17 wins. The journeyman starter’s 2.82 ERA and 4.0 bWAR both mark his best since 2023, his final year with the Twins.
The only thing left on Gray’s to-do list is pitching in the World Series, which is far easier said than done. Boston is all but locked into the AL’s No. 5 seed, and the Red Sox would play the entire Wild Card Series on the road. If they were to knock off the Yankees, the Red Sox would start the ALDS away from Fenway Park, and the only way they’d have home-field advantage in the ALCS is if the No. 6 seed — currently the White Sox — embarks on a miracle run.
Hey, we’ve seen stranger things. Who else is old enough to remember the 2007 Rockies going from a controversial Game 163 win to sweeping the NLDS and NLCS as a Wild Card team? Of course, they suffered their own sweep at the hands of the Red Sox. It’s like poetry.
And what would be more poetic than Gray either exacting revenge on the Yankees or seeing his career end against that same team?
"We’ll see what the future holds for me," Gray said. "But if this is it, no better way to go out and try to do something special here the next couple months."

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Payton Tolle Can Make Red Sox Playoff History 108 Years After Babe Ruth
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown

Boston is very likely going to face the New York Yankees in the first round of the playoffs and Tolle has had success against the Red Sox's biggest rival this season. Saturday, Rob B
item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox kick off postseason action, if they turn to red-hot rookie Payton Tolle in either Game 1 or Game 2 on the mound, he will make a bit of absurd team history.
It's a real discussion right now about where to slot in Tolle. Boston's top three starters clearly are him, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez. Boston is very likely going to face the New York Yankees in the first round of the playoffs and Tolle has had success against the Red Sox's biggest rival this season. Saturday, Rob Bradford of WEEI shared that Tolle has a "good shot" at being the team's Game 1 starter in a playoff series, which would've been a shocking statement a few months ago. If Tolle does get the ball in Game 1 — or Game 2 — he'll become the youngest pitcher to start the first or second game of a playoff series for Boston since Babe Ruth back in 1918, per former Red Sox director of baseball communications and media relations JP Long.
"At 23 years old, Payton Tolle could become the youngest pitcher to start Game 1 or Game 2 of a Postseason series for the Red Sox since Babe Ruth (1918 World Series Game 1),"
How crazy is that? It's been over 100 years since Ruth took the mound in Game 1 of the 1918 World Series and no one has been able to start a Game 1 or Game 2 for Boston in a playoff series since.
Payton Tolle Has A Shot At History
Tolle is 23 years old and 324 days old. So far this season, the big lefty has a 3.02 ERA and a 166-to-38 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 143 innings pitched for Boston. For as good as Tolle has been, it's easy to forget that he actually didn't make Boston's Opening Day roster out of Spring Training.
The Red Sox promoted the lefty on April 23 and he has been incredible ever since. He should get votes in the American League Rookie of the Year race, despite the fact that it's seemingly a foregone conclusion that Kevin McGonigle is going to win the award.
When it comes to Boston's playoff rotation, you can't go wrong with any of these three guys, at least on paper. Tolle, Gray and Suárez are all pitching very well right now, to the point that any could realistically be the Game 1 starter. Tolle has done the best specifically against the Yankees this season and New York struggles against lefties, that should work in the rookie's favor. Gray has been Boston's ace all season and Suárez has plenty of playoff success and is also a lefty.
On paper, any of these three would be a good choice. When it comes to Tolle, it would be historic.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox SP Payton Tolle Explains the Difference Between 2025 and 2026 For Him
item.dc:creator: Dan Morrison
item.description: For the second season in a row, the Boston Red Sox have clinched a trip to the MLB postseason. In many respects, 2025 and 2026 look very similar, with the Red Sox heading for a Wild Card matchup and a likely opening-round series against the New York Yankees in the Bronx. Of course, the team itself is completely different. It's a new manager and largely a new coaching staff. Injuries, trades, and free agency have changed the faces of the team itself. Even for faces that were there a season ago, l
item.content:encoded:
For the second season in a row, the Boston Red Sox have clinched a trip to the MLB postseason. In many respects, 2025 and 2026 look very similar, with the Red Sox heading for a Wild Card matchup and a likely opening-round series against the New York Yankees in the Bronx.
Of course, the team itself is completely different. It's a new manager and largely a new coaching staff. Injuries, trades, and free agency have changed the faces of the team itself. Even for faces that were there a season ago, like Payton Tolle, they've seen their roles completely change.
Boston Red Sox SP Payton Tolle on the Difference a Year Can Make
Going into the 2025 playoffs, the Boston Red Sox weren't confident in Payton Tolle. He had been called up midseason to deal with rotation injuries, and while he flashed success with his fastball, that's all he had in his arsenal at that point.
When the playoffs rolled around, he wasn't a part of a three-man rotation. Instead, he only pitched 0.1 playoff innings in relief.
2026 saw Tolle start in the minors, working on his arsenal. When injuries hit the rotation, he got called up to the Red Sox again, and this time he didn't give up his spot in the rotation for anything. He's quickly become a dominant starter and, for many, a fan favorite. In 25 starts and 143.0 innings, Tolle has a 3.02 ERA, 1.070 WHIP, and 10.4 strikeouts per nine.
Tolle would also be among the biggest celebrators when the Red Sox clinched their playoff spot in Tropicana Field on Sunday. When he did take a break from partying, he took some time to hilariously explain the difference a season can make for him.
"Last year," Tolle said. "It kind of felt like I got an A on the group project and didn't do anything… I'm super proud to be a part of this group, just excited to keep going."
This season, the Red Sox need Tolle to become a dominant playoff pitcher. Without that, there is a good chance that Boston doesn't have enough to get past that first round, which would still be a major letdown for many fans.
Payton Tolle May Be the Game 1 Starter for Boston
With Garrett Crochet still injured and not able to start even once he's healthy, the Boston Red Sox have a problem. Who's the Game 1 starter? Right now, it seems like there are two options. They could either pitch Sonny Gray, a veteran. They could also turn to Payton Tolle and trust a young pitcher who has been excellent this season.
It seems like they're in the process of lining Tolle up to start, too. Red Sox writer Rob Bradford looked ahead at the playoffs. There, he noticed it looked like Tolle is being positioned for that Game 1 start.
"It sure looking like Tolle has a good shot at pitching Game 1 the way they are lining things up," Bradford wrote.
That is, obviously, speculation and not evidence at this point. Gray has also been excellent and deserves a long look at the start. Regardless, the Red Sox need to start out on the right foot in October.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox SP Payton Tolle Explains the Difference Between 2025 and 2026 For Him appeared first on HEAVY.

If they can beat those teams, they will have to play the Cleveland Guardians, Chicago White Sox, Texas Range
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox secured a spot in the postseason on Sunday, but the real work is only beginning.
The Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in a best-of-three Wild Card series in a couple of weeks. That will be the first team standing between the Red Sox and a trip to the fall classic. If they win that series, they will play another American League East team, the Tampa Bay Rays.
If they can beat those teams, they will have to play the Cleveland Guardians, Chicago White Sox, Texas Rangers or Houston Astros.
The path to the World series is loaded with taolent, but so are the Red Sox. They are on the side of the bracket that features the three best records in the American League. They know they have their work cut out for them, but they are confident. Breakout pitcher Payton Tolle, who could start Game 1 against the Yankees, thinks the team has everything it needs to go deep into October.
"I think we could make a run," said Tolle, per The Athletic's Jen McCaffrey. "I think we got the guys. I think we can get hot. We're just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we've been having. I'm really just excited to be in this moment again with these guys."
The Red Sox have enough stars to compete with anyone. Roman Anthony is back and healthy. How he performs in October could dictate how far the Red Sox go. On the pitching side of things, Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez will be asked to carry the load. They could have Garrett Crochet back as a reliever as well.
More MLB: Craig Breslow Reflects On Firing Alex Cora After Red Sox Clinch Postseason Berth

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Get Garrett Crochet News After Clinching Playoff Berth
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. The clinch became official Sunday when the Braves beat the Astros, guaranteeing Boston a spot in the Wild Card Series starting on September 29. The roster is not yet complete. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. The clinch became official Sunday when the Braves beat the Astros, guaranteeing Boston a spot in the Wild Card Series starting on September 29.
The roster is not yet complete. Several key arms are still working their way back from injuries, and the next six games at Fenway Park will determine how the pitching staff looks when October arrives.
One of the biggest names on that list took a step forward this week.
Tracy Provides Update on Crochet
Garrett Crochet is closing in on a significant milestone in his comeback. Interim manager Chad Tracy said the plan is for Crochet to throw a live bullpen session against hitters early next week, with Tuesday as the hopeful target.
"Maybe early next week, a potential IBP dependent on how he feels over the next couple days," Tracy said. "Maybe early next week we'll be able to face some hitters. But yeah, tentative."
Crochet's ramp-up has been deliberate at every stage, and the Red Sox are not going to rush the left-hander into a situation he is not ready for.
Facing live hitters would represent the most significant test of Crochet's rehab to this point. He threw 30 pitches over two simulated innings earlier this month, and Tracy said at the time that everything went well. A live session against hitters is the next level up.
What Crochet Would Mean for October
Crochet's potential availability changes the shape of Boston's postseason pitching plans.
The rotation is lining up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as the likely starters for the Wild Card Series. Tolle has posted a 2.44 ERA across his last eight starts. Gray has been one of the best starters in the American League this season, carrying a 2.76 ERA.
Adding Crochet would give Tracy another weapon to deploy, albeit from the bullpen.
Tyron Guerrero returned from the injured list Sunday and looked sharp. Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, and Erik Miller round out a late-inning group that has carried the pitching staff down the stretch. Tanner Houck continues to progress through minor league rehab and remains a potential option.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Garrett Crochet is not back yet. The live bullpen is tentative. The timeline is still dependent on how his body responds day to day.
The Red Sox have been patient with this process, and that patience could pay off at exactly the right time.
Tuesday will tell the story. If Crochet gets through a live session clean, Boston's pitching picture for the postseason gets significantly deeper.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox Get Garrett Crochet News After Clinching Playoff Berth appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Craig Breslow proved the critics wrong, and deserves credit for the Red Sox clinching a playoff spot - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Craig Breslow stood in a puddle of beer in his stocking feet on Sunday, watching the team he assembled celebrate having clinched its spot in the postseason.
That’s when he realized he still had his phone in his pocket. The Red Sox chief baseball officer carefully picked his way down the hallway to put it out of harm’s way before he got even more soaked.
“Smart move,” Breslow was told.
“It might be too late,” he said, laughing.
You can always get a new phone. But how often can you enjoy the satisfaction of proving that an entire city, if not an entire industry, was wrong?
Breslow made what still remains the most stunning move of this baseball season when he fired Alex Cora and six of his coaches on April 25 after only 27 games.
He was convinced the team had potential it would not realize under Cora and needed a change.
“I believed in the players that we had, and I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded,” he said.
“And, while there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered.”
Some people? How about most of us?
It was not a straight line to success. The Sox were 13-16 in the first 29 games under interim manager Chad Tracy, and I wrote in late May that it was time to start rebuilding by getting a jump on the trade deadline.
With Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet on the injured list, it seemed obvious the Sox weren’t going to contend. There were loud “sell the team” chants at Fenway Park.
Tracy’s record was 22-29 three weeks later, and even the players had started to question what was going on at Fenway Park.
“We’re not good. We’re just not a good team right now. That’s just a fact,” righthander Sonny Gray said after a 3-2 loss against the Blue Jays on June 18.
I wrote the next day that it felt inevitable the Sox would be sellers and could well finish the season with 95 losses. Some executives from other teams believed Breslow could only save his job by turning veterans into prospects.
You know what happened next. The Sox went on a season-saving 32-6 run and are now a threat to make a deep run into October. They are the first team in history to lose 44 of their first 75 games and make the playoffs.
“You stared impossible in the face with the position we were in,” Tracy told his players on Sunday.
Breslow did not see any particular series or moment as a turning point.
“I think the turnaround was the result of incremental change, incremental improvement, changes to the way that we practice, the ways that we trained, the way that we delivered information to our players, the way that we supported our players,” he said.
“So I think when you put all those things together, they compound, and then ultimately the performance on the field by way of wins and losses was the last thing to catch up.”
Breslow spent 12 seasons pitching in the majors and grew a beard with the rest of the wild bunch Red Sox of 2013. He appeared in 10 of the 16 playoff games that season and got three huge outs in the eighth inning of Game 6 in the ALCS.
His job now is giving others that opportunity. But in the end, you’re standing in the same puddle of beer with a big smile.
“The obvious difference is I didn’t have a direct impact on the outcomes of games in this role, whereas I did as a player,” Breslow said. “But I think there’s a different sense of gratification when you’re kind of part of this massive effort to identify players and bring them in and help support the coaching staff.
“It’s very different, and in some ways it’s maybe a couple of layers removed. But it’s certainly as satisfying.”
Breslow has earned that satisfaction. The job’s not over, but he had it right about this team.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] The moments that marked the Red Sox’ path back to the postseason: ‘Oh, now it’s our turn’ - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: In their darkest moments, when they were running out of time, all the Red Sox had was faith. item.content:encoded:
In their darkest moments, when they were running out of time, all the Red Sox had was faith.
Nearly halfway through the season, at the bottom of a bad American League, in a sport dominated by data and measurables, virtually all available evidence led to a consistent conclusion: The 2026 Red Sox were just not good. They fired the manager a month in. They lost key players to long-term injuries. They showed little life.
And so they were left with mere belief. Belief in themselves, belief that they could salvage it, belief that how could it possibly stay like this forever?
“We all still had faith in each other,” Garrett Whitlock said. “Human beings still do the thing. All the numbers and data would have counted us out and all that kind of stuff. And the players in this clubhouse were like, hey, we can stick with this.”
Or, at least, that’s what they said.
“We wouldn’t have said it if we didn’t believe it,” Caleb Durbin said.
Improbably, incredibly, here they are. They clinched a spot in the postseason Sunday, allowing aspirations of late October in a season that felt over in June.
The moments that marked their ascent were many, an almost endless series of sliding doors and what ifs, minor-turned-monumental plays. Recently, in a series of interviews, some of these Sox reflected on their favorites.
“The fun thing about a season,” Durbin said, “is that there’s a whole lot of moments you can look back on that tell the story.”
The Schlitt Show
The date: June 25
The playoff odds (via FanGraphs): 10.6 percent
The moment: Caleb Durbin homers off Cam Schlittler
Remember how dire it felt on June 25. In the end, it was the start of the Red Sox’ run.
When Boston had last played at Fenway Park, it got swept by the Blue Jays, including a gut-wrenching finale in which the Sox rallied for a late tie only to lose. Emanating from the stands were loud boos and chants of “sell the team,” sentiments and sounds burned into the players’ psyche.
Just before they returned, the Sox dramatically dropped two of three to the Rockies. Durbin partially dislocated his left pinkie finger sliding head-first into first base. On the way back from Colorado, plane problems delayed their Boston arrival to 5 a.m., about 14 hours before the first pitch of a four-game series against the Yankees.
“And,” Isiah Kiner-Falefa said, “Schlittler.”
On the mound that night was righthander Cam Schlittler, the Walpole native and emerging Yankees ace, who ended the Red Sox’ season last year.
The weekend was ripe for misery. And it was the beginning of everything.
“It’s a very discernible line in the sand: the Yankees series at home,” interim manager Chad Tracy said.
The Red Sox were hitting like they had barely slept the night before, so Schlittler cruised into the fifth inning. But when a Yankees fielding error prolonged the frame, the Sox managed to tie it. Up came Durbin with the go-ahead run on base.
Durbin, back in the lineup a day after popping that pinkie back into place, homered to left field — just high enough and just far enough, off the lip of the Green Monster.
The dirt dog Durbin? Against that team, off that pitcher, after that travel and those losses?
“That was the big defining moment of the year,” Kiner-Falefa said. “Turned the whole attitude of the team around.”
The Red Sox trailed for half of an inning the rest of the series, sweeping all four games.
Still in a huge hole, they were 10 games under .500 at 36-46. But for the first time, they had something tangible to build on, not just blind belief.
“Right there is when it changed,” Tracy said. “Oh my God, that was awesome. But like, was that a blip? That’s what people think.”
The comeback
The date: July 12
The playoff odds: 40.5 percent
The moment: Francisco Lindor’s error leads to ninth consecutive win
Against the Angels, against the White Sox, after an overnight flight delay trying to escape Chicago, despite rolling up to Citi Field just two hours before scheduled first pitch, the Red Sox won eight consecutive games to take them into mid-July.
It was a significant accomplishment, especially considering it took them three months to win more than three in a row.
Unfortunately for the Sox, that is where the win streak was going to end. The Red Sox had one hit heading into the ninth inning against the Mets.
With a runner on first base and one out in the ninth, Romy Gonzalez hit a hard ground ball right at Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor. It was a ready-made double play. The game was over, and so was the streak … until it wasn’t.
“The guy has a Platinum Glove,” Whitlock said.
“Oh, now it’s our turn,” Connor Wong said. “Everything was going wrong for us, and then the one thing kind of went right for us.”
“He makes that play, we lose. And we somehow win that game,” Durbin said. “That was probably our biggest game of the year. Not because of who we beat, but because of the way we won that game.”
Lindor failed to turn the double play. He failed to get even one out. The ball ricocheted off his chest, everybody was safe, Devin Williams lost the strike zone, Durbin walked to load the bases, Andruw Monasterio walked to force in a run, and Jarren Duran singled to bring in the tying run. The Red Sox won in 10 innings.
Opportunity knocked, and the Red Sox kicked the door down. It was the difference between an 8-1 road trip, a solid week-plus with a total dud of a loss heading into the break ... and a stunning 9-0, feeling great going into four days off, with a chance to bring the momentum home.
If the win streak had ended at eight, would the Sox have won the next six after the break? Would they have grabbed such a strong hold on a wild-card spot? Would they have known what it felt like to stage late comebacks — the theme of their summer surge?
“Even that ninth inning, though, we needed five people to do the job, and they all did. That was the first time that happened,” Durbin said. “That kind of sparked the feeling of OK, we’re a team that if we need to get something going, we can.”
Tracy said: “Two weeks ago, we were pretty entrenched as the worst team in the American League. Now, we were holding a spot or were really close. I felt like that was — for the whole group — all right, we have turned this around and we have a legitimate chance now.”
The homecoming
The date: July 17-22
The playoff odds: 50.3 percent to 61 percent
The moment: “There’s so many,” Tracy said, leading to six more wins
Upon returning from the All-Star break, the Red Sox reached the chaotic, fever dream, how-is-this-possible portion of their turnaround.
Every game — four more wins against the Rays, then two against the Orioles — seemed to bring out a more electric version of Fenway Park than the one before.
For the Red Sox, that was the most gratifying. Their lowest low, several players said, wasn’t getting dumped in Denver. It was struggling in Boston and hearing it from the home crowds. They went 17-27 at Fenway in the first half.
How to pick just one moment?
For win No. 10, the first game back from the break, the Red Sox beat Tampa Bay, 10-0. It was resounding.
“That was like an important statement game for us,” Greg Weissert said.
For No. 11, the second game of a doubleheader, the Rays scored two runs in the top of the first and the Red Sox came right back with three in the bottom half. That got them back to .500 and into a tie for a playoff spot.
“Relentlessness,” Trevor Story said.
For No. 12, Wilyer Abreu’s fourth homer in two games was a go-ahead shot off Garrett Cleavinger, capping a four-run rally in the seventh for the Sox’ first lead of the day.
“When you win that many games in a row, there’s usually three or four of them that you’re probably not supposed to win,” Tracy said.
For No. 13, Sonny Gray tossed a quality start in an actual low-stress afternoon.
“It’s hard to remember everything,” Wong said.
For No. 14, Durbin went deep again, in the eighth against Tyler Wells to break a tie. Fourth-string shortstop Tsung-Che Cheng recorded the final out with a leaping catch of a line drive to save two runs.
Even for the Red Sox, the believers, it strained belief.
“It comes off the bat and you’re like, ‘Oh no.’ And [Cheng] out of nowhere snares it,” Tracy said. “Everybody’s fired up in the coach’s room and you fist bump. You shake your head like: ‘Holy [expletive]. We did it again.’ There were plenty of those for sure behind the scenes.”
For No. 15, they scored four runs in the first inning, leaving no doubt and matching the franchise record win streak set in 1946.
Later that day, July 22, the Red Sox lost the second game of a doubleheader. The streak was over — for real this time. The season is not.
That 15-0 run was part of 27-3 and 32-5 stretches, some of the wildest in franchise history.
“It was maybe the beginning of August, I think, when someone was like, ‘Hey, you realize we’re six games up in the wild card, right?’” said Whitlock, not a standings tracker. “Wait, what?”
“That’s a testament to the people that we have,” Durbin said. “As a player, we have talent. We have a lot of talent to do the job. But [after] the start we had, it takes the person to continue to push forward and come out of it the way we did.”
“I never doubted it, our ability to come together at some point and turn this thing around,” interim bench coach José David Flores said. “To be honest with you, it was kind of shocking the way we did it.”
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.content:encoded:
By The Associated Press
NEW YORK — Cristopher Sánchez earned his major league-leading 18th win Sunday, leading the Phillies to a 7-2 victory over the New York Mets.
The Phillies (86-70), who salvaged a split of the four-game series, entered Sunday in the third National League wild-card spot, one game behind the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four games clear of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Sánchez surrendered six hits, including Bo Bichette’s sixth-inning homer, and struck out six over 6 1/3 innings as he snapped a tie with the Boston Red Sox’s Sonny Gray for the big league lead in wins. The last Phillies pitcher to lead the majors in wins was Steve Carlton with 23 in 1982.
Justin Crawford hit a three-run triple, and Luis Arraez finished with two RBIs. Alec Bohm and Trea Turner each had run-scoring hits. Kyle Schwarber tied a career high with four walks.
Rookie Jonah Tong (2-2) gave up four runs and struck out five in 4 2/3 innings for the last-place Mets, who finished 36-45 at home, their worst record at Citi Field since the 2013 team went 33-48.
The Mets drew 2,712,120 fans this season, a drop of 5,870 fans per game from last season. It’s the steepest decline in the majors.
Brett Baty added a pinch-hit RBI single.
Despite a rainy forecast and the postponement of a ceremony honoring retiring Mets radio broadcaster Howie Rose, the game began on time and wasn’t interrupted. The crowd of 33,611 cheered and chanted Rose’s name after “Hello, Goodbye” by The Beatles played in the eighth.
Up next
Phillies: Open their final homestand Tuesday, when RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 2.99 ERA) starts against the NL Central champion Milwaukee Brewers, who haven’t announced a starter.

item.title: [98.5 The Sports Hub] Red Sox punch playoff ticket in Tampa
item.dc:creator: Alex Barth
item.description: ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – SEPTEMBER 20: Sonny Gray #54 of the Boston Red Sox and Adley Rutschman #31 of the Boston Red Sox celebrate clinching an AL wild card spot following a loss to the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field on September 20, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida. Mark Taylor/Getty Images The massive turnaround of the 2026 Boston Red Sox hit a major milestone on Sunday afternoon. With results around the league, the Sox clinched a spot in the MLB Playoffs. Entering Sunday, the Red Sox didn't
item.content:encoded:
ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – SEPTEMBER 20: Sonny Gray #54 of the Boston Red Sox and Adley Rutschman #31 of the Boston Red Sox celebrate clinching an AL wild card spot following a loss to the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field on September 20, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida.
Mark Taylor/Getty Images
The massive turnaround of the 2026 Boston Red Sox hit a major milestone on Sunday afternoon. With results around the league, the Sox clinched a spot in the MLB Playoffs.
Entering Sunday, the Red Sox didn't even need a win of their own to clinch. That was good news because they failed to get one, falling 5-1 to the American East-leading Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field.
Instead, all eyes turned to Texas, where the Houston Astros were hosting the Atlanta Braves. There, they got the help they needed from some familiar names. Former Red Sox starting pitcher Martin Perez allowed just one run in 4.1 innings, and Mike Yastrzemski, the grandson of Red Sox legend Carl Yastrzemski, drove in three runs in Atlanta's 4-2 victory.
After their game ended, the Red Sox watched the Braves and Astros from their locker room in Tampa. As soon as the final out happened the team kicked off a champagne celebration.
Earlier this season, this seemed like an improbable achievement for the Red Sox. On June 24 the team had a 32-46 record and sat in last place in the entire American League. Since then they're 52-26. According to ESPN, they're the fourth team to make the MLB playoffs after being 14-plus games under .500 in a season in the World Series Era.
Now at 84-72 with six games to go, all that's left to determine is seeding - although there's not much wiggle room there. The Red Sox are five and a half games behind the Yankees, who also own the tiebreaker. On the other end the Sox are four and a half games up on the third Wild Card team, which is currently the Chicago White Sox. However Chicago hasn't clinched yet, with a two and a half game lead on both the Astros and Toronto Blue Jays.
The Red Sox will wrap up the season at home before most likely visiting the Yankees in the Wild Card round. For their final week of the regular season the Sox are off on Monday before hosting the Cleveland Guardians, and then the Chicago Cubs.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] The Red Sox should take advantage of Garrett Whitlock's desire to start in 2027
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello

item.content:encoded:
Garrett Whitlock is looking to make a career pivot and transition into the starting rotation. For the Boston Red Sox, it's a strange proposition. The right-hander is one of the best setup men in the league, and that has tremendous value.
Of course, starting pitchers have even more value, hence the higher salaries, but the transition is a risk. Not only does a hurler need to reserve something in the tank rather than just air it out for an inning, but he also needs to have enough variation in his arsenal to turn over a lineup multiple times.
Some Red Sox beat writers don't believe the transition is the best idea. The biggest concern is whether or not Whitlock's health can hold up under a starter's workload. The 30-year-old's past forays into starting have resulted in injuries, making this a serious concern and not just some folks crying wolf.
However, there are still reasons to give it a try. Not now, of course. But in 2027, Whitlock in the rotation could make a lot of sense for a few distinct reasons.
The Red Sox should roll the dice on Garrett Whitlock as a starter in 2027
Presumably, the reason Whitlock would like to try his hand again in the rotation is monetary. On the free-agent market, mid-rotation starters can get upwards of $15 million per season. Look at guys like Chris Bassit and Merrill Kelly, for example, who are making $18.5 million and $18 million this season, respectively.
However, Boston holds options for 2027 and 2028 on Whitlock. If exercised, the Red Sox will pay him $8.25 million next year and $10.5 million in 2028. If he works out as a starter, that's an incredible value.
The next reason to give this a go is the fact that Whitlock has the repertoire to work in the rotation. While the majority of relievers are one-or-two-pitch pitchers, Whitlock has three quality offerings. His sinker is the cornerstone, which he throws 56% of the time, but he has a slider and changeup, too.
The slider he uses at a 26% rate, and it generates a ton of whiffs, coming in at 46.7%. The change gets broken out at an 18% clip, is a weapon against lefties, and also has a healthy 35.6% whiff rate. You might like to see a fourth pitch, just to have a show-me offering, but that's a solid foundation for a starter.
The next point is about righty-lefty balance. The Red Sox have an extreme imbalance towards southpaws. Theoretically, if everyone is healthy, you have Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle, and Jake Bennett all throwing from the left side. If Sonny Gray retires, Boston will have to find a righty to avoid skewing entirely left-handed.
Finally, the risk is minimal. As long as he doesn't suffer a catastrophic injury, the Red Sox can always stick Whitlock back in the bullpen and have a dominant high-leverage reliever should he struggle as a starter. In that regard, they're playing with house money. They control his future for the next two years, and he's paid a reasonable rate for a setup man, and what would be a steal for a No. 3 or No. 4 starter. At that point, why not take the plunge?

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox appear to be getting rotation in line for Wild Card Series - The Boston Globe

item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park.
That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each.
“Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.”
True. But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Yankees twice this season and allowed one run on four hits over 13 innings with three walks and 18 strikeouts.
Gray allowed three runs on nine hits over 13⅔ innings in two starts against the Yankees. He struck out 12 and walked three.
Guerrero returns
Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero returned from a 19-day stint on the injured list with shoulder inflammation. Righthanded reliever Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero pitched a perfect eighth inning, striking out two.
“Felt good to be out there,” Guerrero said. “If I get a few more games I’ll be fine [for the postseason].”
Guerrero, 35, was called up in May for his first major league stint since 2019. He emerged as a reliable late-inning option, posting a 3.18 ERA over 39 games.
“He’s obviously a very important piece to this puzzle in our bullpen,” Tracy said.
Olds deserved a better fate. The 27-year-old has a 1.20 ERA and 1.20 WHIP in 13 games since making his major league debut on Aug. 17.
“Very tough. He’s thrown the ball great. He’s got big stuff,” Tracy said. “We had to make a roster decision.”
Contreras doing better
Willson Contreras took some swings in the batting cage to test his bruised right hand and came through fine. He said he hopes to be able to do more on Tuesday. “Step in the right direction,” Tracy said … There was no update on Garrett Crochet, who has yet to face hitters. That could come in the next few days … Tanner Houck had a 3.38 ERA over eight innings in four minor league games. Tracy suggested he would face hitters in a simulated game early this week. “Figuring out the next steps at home — and want to figure that out — but no plans for the next outing,” Tracy said. Could Houck be activated? “It’s possible,” Tracy said. “At this point, it’s going to depend very much on where’s the roster at, what are the needs, and then go from there.”… Rays shortstop Taylor Walls showed his baseball acumen in the first inning. With Roman Anthony on first and one out, he allowed Adley Rutschman’s popup to drop. Walls picked up the ball and flipped to second to get the force on Anthony. That left the Sox with a slower runner on first. It ultimately didn’t matter as Trevor Story struck out … Worcester, as Double-A Portland also did last weekend, had its final game rained out. The WooSox finished 76-67. Kutter Crawford was at Polar Park, and the plan was to have him start what would have been a bullpen game. Crawford has not appeared in a major league game since Sept. 28, 2024. He missed the 2025 season because of an injured right knee. He injured his right wrist in August of that season doing yard work at his home in Florida. Crawford pitched three innings in a rehab game for Worcester on April 11 but had a setback and wasn’t cleared for a game until Sunday. “He got to a point where he wanted to go out there and throw one,” Tracy said.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox right-hander Kutter Crawford was set to make a rehab start with Triple-A Worcester. But with the game being cancelled due to rain, per the Worcester Telegram-Gazette's Tommy Cassell, the club faces a tough roster decision on the 30-year-old starter.
The cancellation also ends Worcester's season. That means the Red Sox will have to decide if they want to roster Crawford during the final seven games of the regular season, and possibly the postseason.
Crawford is currently on the 60-day injured list after suffering a major setback in his recovery from wrist surgery. After a rehab start in April, he experienced issues in his right elbow and has been shelved since. This appearance would have been his first outing in five months.
Red Sox Face Tough Roster Decision on Kutter Crawford
With nowhere to get a rehab outing, the Red Sox will have to decide the next steps for Kutter Crawford. They certainly had some contingency in place if the game was affected by weather.
The first question the Red Sox have to answer is whether Crawford is an option for the postseason. If not, they will likely just shut him down. Otherwise, they have to clear a 40-man roster spot to activate him from the injured list.
If Boston does roster the 30-year-old, it will likely be in a relief role. The Red Sox will likely go into the Wild Card Series with a three-man rotation of Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, and Payton Tolle. If they advance further, they could turn to either Jake Bennett or Brayan Bello as their fourth starter.
Given the postseason in general, there could be some need for an innings-eater for the bullpen. But Bello and Bennett are further stretched out than Crawford at this point in the season.
If Crawford is done for the year, it will mark the second straight season the right-hander has not thrown a pitch for the Red Sox. That could make him a non-tender candidate in November. But if they do tender him, he won't see much of a raise from his $2.75 million salary for 2026.
It's quite possible that Crawford has thrown his last pitch for the Red Sox.
Red Sox Right Now
The Red Sox aim to clinch a postseason berth in their series finale against the Tampa Bay Rays. They'll send left-hander Patrick Sandoval to the mound.
Boston needs a win or a loss by the Houston Astros to officially clinch. They've already been eliminated from American League East contention, so they would be locked into a Wild Card spot.
The Red Sox have a five-game lead for the AL's second Wild Card spot. So they should lock in their postseason seeding in the next couple of days. That would allow them to set up their rotation for the Wild Card Series. Their likely first opponent in the postseason will be the New York Yankees.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox Face Tough Kutter Crawford Roster Decision After Rehab Start Cancelled appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Just Baseball] Payton Tolle’s Case To Be the Red Sox's Game 1 Starter | Just Baseball
item.dc:creator: Jordan Leandre
item.description: They haven’t clinched a postseason berth yet, but it looks more likely by the day that the Boston Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round again. This will be the third matchup between these two arch rivals in the Wild Card round since 2021, with each organization winning once. item.content:encoded:
They haven’t clinched a postseason berth yet, but it looks more likely by the day that the Boston Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round again.
This will be the third matchup between these two arch rivals in the Wild Card round since 2021, with each organization winning once. The Red Sox got the best of Gerrit Cole in 2021 at Fenway Park, while the Yankees won two straight elimination games to knock off Boston in the Bronx last year.
This series promises to be low-scoring. These two teams are top three in baseball in staff earned run average. The Yankees have nearly three-quarters of a run lead on the Red Sox among starters, while the two bullpens are separated by 0.01 earned runs per nine.
A lot will be made of how these two staffs line up in a couple of weeks. The first two games for the Yankees, as deep as their pitching staff is, seem destined to be Cam Schlittler in Game 1 and Max Fried in Game 2. However, the Red Sox have serious questions to answer about how they want to line up.
Preparing for this series to go the distance is difficult. If you sweep, you line yourselves up well for Game 1 of the American League Division Series. However, if you get swept, one of your best pitchers may never see the hill.
The conundrum is as follows: Sonny Gray has been their best arm wire-to-wire. Payton Tolle is by far their hottest arm, seeming to get stronger as the season wears on. Ranger Suárez is riding two great starts in a row and is their high-priced free agent with elite postseason pedigree.
But of the three, there’s no question who should pitch opposite Schlittler in Game 1: Tolle.
Stats updated prior to games on September 19.
Game 1 Is a Tone-Setter
The dialogue surrounding Game 1 is that it’s almost a “scheduled loss.” To be frank, it’s hard to argue against the logic. In four starts against Boston this year, Schlittler has a 0.74 ERA, a .174 batting average against, and a 27.3% strikeout rate across 24.1 innings.
Let us not forget the sheer domination he exhibited in Game 3 against the Red Sox last year, either. Across eight innings, he allowed five hits, no runs, and struck out 12.
But the mindset for Boston can’t be that it has no chance of winning. Sure, they’ve been one of the league’s best road teams this year, but the Yankees have the best pitching staff in baseball this year for a reason. By comparison, sure, it’s easier to win against someone not in the Cy Young race. But Max Fried habitually finds himself in the discussion for a reason.
The Red Sox’s mindset should be that runs will be at a premium, so matching the Yankees ace zero-for-zero is paramount. Of the three options, Tolle presents the best opportunity to do so. While Gray has Tolle beat overall in ERA, the Red Sox rookie southpaw is, by far, the hottest arm on the staff.
Since the All-Star break, Tolle has a 2.90 ERA with a 28.2% strikeout-to-walk rate. That ERA drops to 2.53 over his last nine starts. That 2.90 ERA, however, is nearly a third of a run better than Gray’s, and over half a run better than Suárez’s.
Sheer run prevention is the name of the game in this series. Tolle is their best option.
Tolle’s Attitude Is Perfect for the Moment
Every time Tolle speaks, he endears himself to the baseball world even more. But as goofy as he can be in media sessions, he’s all business on the field. Furthermore, he can appreciate the moment he’s in at any given time.
Look no further than his recent start against the Kansas City Royals. Eight pitches, eight strikes, six whiffs, all fastballs. He had the wherewithal to glance at pitching coach Andrew Bailey, grin, lock back in and pick up the final strike of an immaculate inning.
Sure, it’s one pitch in the first inning against a team out of postseason contention, but talk to anybody who’s played, and they’ll tell you how aware they are of when they’re on the brink of something cool. Tolle said as much after the game.
But that moment should tell the world he’s unafraid of going into the Bronx, facing off against Schlittler, and going band-for-band with the likely AL Cy Young.
Tolle clearly cares about what he does, but it’s that somewhat unserious attitude that makes him perfect for the high stakes of setting the tone in a postseason series.
This moment, honestly, seemed set in stone the moment he made his MLB debut last season against Paul Skenes. While any postseason start is high leverage, he’s always finding himself making big starts against the game’s best. He’s always met the moment, and the Red Sox should let him continue that trend this postseason.
The Yankees Struggle Against Hard Fastballs
The Yankees are a deep, talented team even if not all players are at full strength or potential going into October. One area where they struggle, however, is against hard fastballs.
This season, the Yankees have the highest strikeout rate on fastballs 95 mph or harder, to go with the second-worst expected batting average. Only the Chicago White Sox are worse against such fastballs.
They’re even worse this season on hard fastballs thrown by left-handers. Their 33% strikeout rate is the second-highest behind the 61-93 Athletics, while their .191 expected batting average ranks only higher than the Cleveland Guardians.
Tolle isn’t positioned with an elite-level fastball from a velocity standpoint, but it’s comfortably above average. This season, he’s in the 71st percentile with an average fastball of 95.7 mph. Opponents struggle mightily against it as well, hitting just .190 with a .248 expected wOBA and a 30.4% whiff rate.
Tolle throws his four-seam and sinker a combined 68.4% of the time. While that leaves him susceptible to predictability, he varies that look with a cutter that comes in at 88.6 mph on average. He throws that offering at a 19.4% clip.
His strength is his fastball, along with 98th percentile extension. That plays directly into the weaknesses of the Yankees lineup. With Game 1 very much being a tone-setter, there’s no question who the Red Sox should send out there.
Lining It Up After Tolle
Following Tolle, the Red Sox have their two veterans waiting in the wings. Win Game 1, you’ve got two proven performers to help you win one more game to advance. Lose Game 1, you’ve got two experienced professionals tasked with staving off elimination.
The order after Tolle almost doesn’t matter. Could they vary looks and go to Gray to keep the Yankees off the lefty scent? Maybe, but then you potentially run into the same problem of playing with your food. That said, Suárez is much craftier than Tolle, and prone to the hanging breaking ball.
The Yankees have a 99 wRC+ as a team against right-handed pitching, and a 107 against lefties. Gray also took a no-hitter into the eighth inning against the Yankees back in late June, while Suárez was touched up in his last start against them.
What can be said either way is that having two accomplished veterans to follow the rookie gunslinger is a good position for the Red Sox to be in.

item.title: [Audacy] Brayan Bello has suddenly become a potential key postseason piece
item.dc:creator: Rob Bradford
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - There was no celebration, but there was a revelation. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - There was no celebration, but there was a revelation.
The Red Sox couldn't close the deal in securing a postseason berth, succumbing to a Rays 2-1 walk-off win at Tropicana Field on Saturday. But an interesting development emerged along the way. Brayan Bello is suddenly a potential huge part of the postseason solution.
The almost out-of-nowhere conversation about Bello's importance was given an enormous boost by one of the pitcher's best outings of his career. Not only did Bello hold the Rays to just one run over eight innings, but he also struck out 11 and walked no one.
Why was this even more impressive than simply the end-of-day box score? Because Bello managed all those punchouts, along with 17 whiffs, against a Rays team that has struck out fewer times than any club in baseball. No starting pitcher had managed double-digit strikeouts against Tampa Bay, with Toronto's Dylan Cease coming the closest with nine.
Bello matches his career high with 11 strikeouts! pic.twitter.com/NA2a2pDcAy
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 19, 2026
The dominance was just what the doctor ordered for Bello and the Red Sox, even if starting a postseason game isn't in the righty's immediate future.
While there has been no announcement, it appears the Red Sox are lining up their wild-card rotation with Payton Tolle to pitch Game 1 against the Yankees, followed by Sonny Gray and then Ranger Suarez if Game 3 is needed in the best-of-three series. But that doesn't mean Bello can't have an impact on outcomes from late September into October.
Bello's fastball routinely sat at 97 mph, almost two mph above his season-average velocity. It was a fastball that got nine whiffs, with the Rays coming away with just four hard-hit balls all day.
"That was exceptional," Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. "By far and away, his best outing of the year, as good as I've seen him, so, I don't know what else to say, he was awesome. Really awesome."
Bello's appearance allowed for thoughts on what might be in store for his effectiveness out of the bullpen in high-leverage situations come Sept. 29. It has been well-documented what he can do as a reliever, posting a 1.98 ERA in 15 games out of the bullpen this season. But now we're not just talking about bulk roles or giving the Red Sox some length.
This version of Bello can absolutely be a late-inning, high-leverage weapon.
For instance, while we aren't sure of Aaron Judge's health heading into the postseason, if the Yankees' slugger does play, this might not be a bad reminder to put in your statistical back pocket: Judge is just 2-for-21 with eight strikeouts against Bello.
While some naysayers might point to the less-than-inspiring appearances Bello has turned in at Yankee Stadium as of late, including maybe his worst relief outing of the season at the end of August when he allowed four runs over 4 1/3 innings, or the 2 1/3-inning start in Game 2 of last season's wild card round. But before those two, the pitcher had been absolutely nails in the Bronx, totaling a 1.44 ERA in five starts.
Assuming their health is OK, the Red Sox will have Aroldis Chapman and Garrett Whitlock at the ready to help close out games. But with a week to go in the regular season, there is some uncertainty regarding the late-inning options. Saturday, Bello sure seemed like he was ready to help with that.
“For me, it's just showing the team that I'm ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.”

item.title: [bostonherald.com] Red Sox mailbag: Should Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck be on playoff roster?
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store. But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag. Tanner Houck and Gar
item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Garrett Crochet isn't Red Sox's only looming bullpen savior after Justin Slaten injury
item.dc:creator: Anthony Ranaudo
item.description: There's a version of this continuous Boston Red Sox news saga that could have sent fans into a real panic, and I get why.
