item.content:encoded:
There's a version of this continuous Boston Red Sox news saga that could have sent fans into a real panic, and I get why. Justin Slaten had quietly turned into one of the more trustworthy arms in this bullpen, working to a 2.84 ERA over his final two months of availability before elbow trouble sidelined him in August.
Now we know the full picture: an evaluation revealed degenerative changes in the flexor mass of his right elbow, and rather than push for a return with the postseason approaching, the Red Sox are having him get a PRP injection and start planning for 2027 instead.
On the year, he had thirty-six appearances, a 4.60 ERA overall, but provided a real chunk of high-leverage relief work, which is now gone for the stretch run. That's a real hole, absolutely. It's also not the whole story right now, and it's worth taking a breath before assuming the bullpen just got worse.
Garrett Crochet was the AL Cy Young runner-up last season, an 18-5, 2.59 ERA workhorse who threw 205.1 innings and struck out 255 batters. What a lot of people forget is that before all of that, Crochet broke into pro ball as a reliever with the Chicago White Sox, sitting comfortably in the upper 90s and regularly touching triple digits in short bursts. That's exactly the version the Red Sox may get back down the stretch.
He hasn't pitched in a game since throwing six scoreless innings on April 25, and after months sidelined with a shoulder issue that turned into more of a lingering problem, he just threw his first bullpen sessions in nearly three months. There isn't time left to stretch him back out as a starter, but a Crochet who can air it out for one to three innings at a time is exactly the profile that's thrived in October before.
Pair that with a Payton Tolle start going five or six innings, Crochet bridging the seventh and eighth, and Aroldis Chapman closing it out, and that's a real, dangerous alignment behind Sonny Gray in a Game 1.
Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo are trending toward returns to Red Sox bullpen alongside Garrett Crochet
Crochet isn't walking through that door alone, either. Tanner Houck is further along than anyone, working back from UCL surgery and already up to three innings and 48 pitches in a rehab outing for Double-A Portland, allowing just one run with four strikeouts, before moving on to Triple-A Worcester to keep building and facing some better competition.
Johan Oviedo, who Boston acquired from the Pittsburgh Pirates over the winter, finally made his own rehab appearance with Worcester this week after missing more than five months with a flexor strain, which is a sign he could factor into the bullpen picture before the year is out. Kutter Crawford is the longer shot of the group, hasn't pitched for the big club since 2024, and there are only unconfirmed "rumblings" he could get a look at Worcester this week. Even if that goes nowhere in 2026, he's still under team control for two more seasons.
Losing Slaten hurts, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But between Crochet, Houck, and Oviedo all trending in the right direction at the same time, Boston may be walking into the stretch run with more usable, high-upside arms than it's had healthy at any single point all season.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox's Game 1 Playoff Starter May Not Be Who You Expect
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: We're just over one week away from the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season coming to a close. Then, the entire focus around the league will turn to the playoffs. When it comes to the Boston Red Sox, they will be in the mix. The Red Sox haven't officially clinched yet, although that could happen as soon as Saturday. As the playoffs have inched closer and closer, one topic that has lingered around Boston is the starting rotation. The rotation is loaded and it's a real question of how the clu
item.content:encoded:
We're just over one week away from the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season coming to a close. Then, the entire focus around the league will turn to the playoffs. When it comes to the Boston Red Sox, they will be in the mix.
The Red Sox haven't officially clinched yet, although that could happen as soon as Saturday. As the playoffs have inched closer and closer, one topic that has lingered around Boston is the starting rotation. The rotation is loaded and it's a real question of how the club will sort it out ahead of a Wild Card round series, very likely against the New York Yankees. Sonny Gray has seemed like the likely choice, but that may not be the case.
Could Boston Turn To The Rookie?
Do you roll with the veteran in Game 1? He has been among the best pitchers in the league in general all season to this point. Ranger Suárez has been red-hot recently and was brought to town because of the fact that he has been electric in the playoffs throughout his career to this point. Also, of course, there's Payton Tolle, who is also red-hot right now. On Saturday, Rob Bradford of WEEI shared on X that Tolle actually has a "good shot" at nabbing the Game 1 spot.
"It sure looking like Tolle has a good shot at pitching Game 1 the way they are lining things up," Bradford wrote on X.
Gray has been among the best pitchers in baseball this season. He has a 2.82 ERA and a 146-to-45 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 163 innings pitched this season. Gray also is leading the league with 17 wins. He has been Boston's ace all season. Since Aug. 15, Gray has a 2.89 ERA and a 3-2 record. Since Sep. 4, Suárez has a 0.92 ERA and a 3-0 record. Since Aug. 13, Tolle has a 2.50 ERA and a 42-to-9 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 36 innings pitched across six starts.
Frankly, Boston would be in a good position with any of these three starting Game 1. But in a three-game series, there are even more reasons to get the decision right.
Tolle has made two starts against New York this season and has allowed one run in 13 innings pitched (0.69 ERA) with 18 strikeouts. Gray has made two starts against New York and has allowed three runs in 13 2/3 innings pitched (1.98 ERA) with 12 strikeouts.
Suárez has made three starts against New York and has allowed 11 runs in 16 1/3 innings pitched (5.94 ERA. Of the three, Tolle has fared the best against New York, so the fact that he has a "good shot" at starting Game 1 actually makes a lot of sense.
All three of these guys are red-hot at the moment. Slotting in Tolle for a Game 1, the righty Gray for a Game 2 and then back to a lefty in Suárez for Game 3 — if necessary — arguably is the best bet for a New York series.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com
Follow patmcavoy

item.title: [roundtable.io] How Should Boston Red Sox Set Playoff Rotation?
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe
item.description: Sonny Gray? Ranger Suarez? Payton Tolle? Who should get the ball in game one in the Bronx for the Red Sox? To manage the starting rotation workload and line up the rotation for the playoffs, the Boston Red Sox are turning to Brayan Bello to start Saturday's game against the Tampa Bay Rays. Whether the Red Sox go with Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, or Payton Tolle, the team will feel very good about its chances of winning. However, if the team gets swept, it risks leaving an incredible arm on the ben
item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray? Ranger Suarez? Payton Tolle? Who should get the ball in game one in the Bronx for the Red Sox?
To manage the starting rotation workload and line up the rotation for the playoffs, the Boston Red Sox are turning to Brayan Bello to start Saturday's game against the Tampa Bay Rays. Whether the Red Sox go with Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, or Payton Tolle, the team will feel very good about its chances of winning. However, if the team gets swept, it risks leaving an incredible arm on the bench.
Let's take a look at the argument for each of the trio to get the ball in game one:
Gray
The 36-year-old veteran has inarguably been the Red Sox' best starter in 2026. After entering the season with questions about how effective he could be late in his career, Gray has passed every test with flying colors. In 28 starts, Gray has posted a 2.82 ERA, the eighth-lowest mark in the league, while the Red Sox have gone 20-8 on his start days.
Most importantly, even when he doesn't have his best stuff, he has done well to limit damage; of his 28 starts, he has allowed more than three runs on four occasions. In two starts against the New York Yankees in 2026, Gray has allowed only three earned runs on nine hits, while striking out 12 and walking only four. In his career, Gray has a solid record of playoff success, posting a 3.26 ERA in 30.1 innings.
However, when it comes to elite strikeout stuff that can completely shut down a lineup, Gray lacks that, posting a rather pedestrian strikeouts per nine innings of 8.06, which ranks 30th out of 48 qualified starters.
Still though, Gray appears to be the most obvious choice to get the start in game one.
Suarez
The Red Sox' most difficult decision with their postseason rotation may be the one they have to make with Suarez. The 30-year-old All-Star signed a five-year, $130-million deal with the Red Sox in the offseason, in part because he posted an impressive 1.48 ERA over 42.2 innings with the Philadelphia Phillies.
However, of the trio in consideration, Suarez has been the shakiest since the All-Star break, posting a 3.46 ERA in his last 10 starts. However, the three-time All-Star has been better lately, allowing only two earned runs in 19.2 innings across three starts. Suarez has struggled against the Yankees in three starts in 2026, allowing 11 runs on 20 hits for a 6.06 ERA.
Still, it seems unlikely the team would risk leaving its $130 million investment on the sidelines for a playoff series.
Tolle
The 23-year-old rookie has been Boston's best starter since the All-Star break. In his last 10 starts, Tolle has posted a 2.90 ERA while striking out 12.05 batters per nine innings, the fifth-highest mark among 93 pitchers with at least 50 innings pitched.
Tolle has also performed incredibly well against the Yankees, allowing only one earned run on four hits while striking out 18 and walking only four. Tolle is also the only pitcher on the Boston staff with the electric stuff that could match New York ace Cam Schlittler in shutting down the lineup.
While it certainly may seem risky to some to give a 23-year-old rookie the ball in game one in Yankee Stadium, how can you risk not throwing him at all?
Up next for the Sox
With their magic number down to two, the Red Sox will look to win a series against the likely American League East champion Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday afternoon. Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.74 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) will start for Tampa. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 4:10 p.m. ET.

item.title: [New York Post] Red Sox believe Sonny Gray could retire after this season — and Yankees could be final game

Asked recently about the possibility of retirement, Gray declined to say muc
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season could end up being Sonny Gray’s last.
The veteran right-hander, who turns 37 in November, has not committed to pitching in 2027 and recently told The Boston Globe he would retire “in a heartbeat” if his family wanted him to do so.
Boston reportedly is taking the possibility seriously, according to the outlet, with some in the organization believing retirement is on the table despite Gray’s strong season.
Asked recently about the possibility of retirement, Gray declined to say much.
“We can get into that at another time but not right now,” he said, per the Globe.
If 2026 is, indeed, his final big league season, Gray’s final start could come in the increasingly likely matchup against the rival Yankees during the wild-card round of the postseason.
Gray spent a season and a half in pinstripes after coming over before the 2017 trade deadline, and it didn’t go exactly as planned for either him or the team.
The three-time All-Star posted a 4.51 ERA across 41 games (34 starts) with the Yankees before being traded to Cincinnati before the 2019 season, during which he posted a Cy Young-caliber season with the Reds.
Gray ripped the Yankees during his introductory press conference with the Red Sox over the winter.
“It feels good to me to go to a place where it’s easy to hate the Yankees,” Gray said.
“I never wanted to go there in the first place.”
Gray is enjoying one of the best seasons of his 14-year MLB career in Beantown, posting a 2.82 ERA in 163 innings.
“I’ve very, very much so enjoyed Boston. Enjoyed the guys. Fenway has been, and is, a very special place,” Gray said.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Ranger Suarez may not have been at his best, but the Red Sox lefthander still showed he had enough fight - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tara Sullivan
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter. This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week fro
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter.
This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week from Tuesday and once again in the Bronx, the pitching plans look nothing like they did back then.
Which is good news for the Red Sox.
Even with Crochet sidelined all season by injury, the pitching rotation has been, in the words of interim manager Chad Tracy, “pivotal” to the drastic midseason turnaround that lifted this team from the depths of the American League standings and into the playoff race.
A trade for Sonny Gray. The continued development of Payton Tolle. And the free agent signing of Ranger Suarez. Three big moves, three likely starters for one more entry in the ongoing Boston/New York postseason clash of baseball titans.
Friday night in Florida, it was Suarez’s turn to prove his readiness. Facing the first-place Rays presented an obvious test, but for Suarez, it also was a chance to build on his two previous starts, in which he allowed only one run in 14 innings. As Tracy pointed out before the game, there is no mystery into what makes a good Suarez outing. Control the tempo, get ahead in the count, and locate pitches. When the lefthander does those three things, he can be pretty hard to beat.
But, as the Rays learned Friday, even if he doesn’t quite do those three things as well as he wants to, he can still find a way to battle through.
So there he was at the end of a decidedly mixed bag of a night, leading the Sox to a 4-2 win, improving his record to 8-4 after giving up just one run in 5⅔ innings. On the upside, he struck out five and consistently got key outs in key moments.
On the downside, he had to labor mightily to get there, walking a career-high five batters, throwing just 56 of his 98 pitches for strikes. He got away with it this time, but come the playoffs, that’s playing with fire, whether against the Yankees or perhaps the Rays again, with Tampa Bay in line to host the wild-card winners.
The Sox chose to take the positive out of the night.
“When I issued those walks, I think that the game was taking me to a place that wasn’t the right one. So I just tried to take a deep breath and slow it down, and I was able to then take it from there,” Suarez said.
He struck out Yandy Díaz to end the second inning, stranding two runners on base. He got out of another jam in the third, a Chandler Simpson hard-hit line out to right and a strikeout of Jonny DeLuca to strand two more runners.
Suarez did it again in the fourth, helping his own cause by starting a nifty inning-ending double play, snaring Taylor Walls’s line drive to the mound and then throwing to first to double off Nick Fortes.
A clean fifth ended on a called third strike to Junior Caminero, but gave way to a messier sixth, with a leadoff walk to Ryan Vilade eventually leading Tracy to pull the plug as Suarez approached 100 pitches. But not before he struck out DeLuca to get the first out.
“He’s a very good competitor and a really good pitcher,” Tracy said, “that even when he’s got traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it. . . . He walked five, but still almost completed six innings. He was very competitive with men on base.”
“I got traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today, and that was part of it,” Suarez said. “It was one of those nights that you didn’t have the command, but I was able to turn the page quickly and was able to get outs when I needed.”
Good as the escape act was, it’s all just staging for what comes next, a playoff berth the Red Sox could clinch on Saturday. Suarez was signed in part because of his experience in the postseason, earned across eight seasons with the Phillies. Suarez is 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 playoff appearances, which includes eight starts. He was the winner of Game 3 of the 2022 World Series, beating the eventual champion Astros with five shutout innings.
The Phillies also called on him to come out of the bullpen in Game 5 of the NLCS, and all he did was earn his first postseason save by getting two outs on two pitches, stranding the winning run and clinching the Series berth.
“When you get to this part of the season, not every outing is going to go perfectly. But he’s been there and done that as far as navigating his way through an outing and finding a way to strand base runners,” Tracy said. “The game’s not going to speed up on him. You know, even if he’s walked some and there’s some people on base, he doesn’t ever look like he speeds up. He just keeps making his pitches.”
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox’ Ranger Suarez sets a career high in walks, but navigates tightrope in win

There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings. But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough. "I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all.
There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings.
But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough.
"I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today and that was part of it."
Suarez had difficulty explaining how the walks piled up on him. It wasn't mechanical, and it wasn't the result of nibbling around the strike zone.
"I think it was one of those nights when I didn't have the command," he said. "But I was able to get outs when I needed."
The latter has always been his calling card. In an era when most starters unleash fastballs at 95 mph or better, Suarez thrives by mixing pitches, keeping hitters off balance and inducing soft contact.
On nights when he can't locate with precision, the margin for error slips further. But again, knowing how to get out of trouble is a mound skill in and of itself.
Suarez has used that talent particularly well in the postseason before, which is part of what motivated the Red Sox to offer him $130 million over five years last winter. Suarez isn't about to come unglued in Yankee Stadium in two weeks — or any other time he gets the ball in the postseason. His career ERA of 1.48 in the playoffs virtually guarantees that.
"He was very competitive with men on base," said interim manager Chad Tracy. "He lost some counts, was behind more counts today, but he wa able to really good pitches with people on base."
Even as he labored, Suarez was adding to a September resumé which has him 3-0 with 0.92 ERA in his last three outings while limiting opposing hitters to a .186 batting average.
No one knows exactly how or when Suarez will fit into Boston's postseason rotation. The assumption is that Sonny Gray will pitch Game 1, with either Payton Tolle or Suarez slotted for Game 2, and the remaining choice available for a winner-take-all Game 3.
Of course, the risk there is that a team may never get to its third starter if it doesn't win at least one of the first two games. That's part of the difficult decision the Red Sox will have to make before their wild card round gets underway.
Even with his history of success in October, Suarez isn't thinking too much about the postseason — not yet anyway.
"No, no,'' he said with a chuckle. "When we clinch, I'll be able to do that. But mathematically, we're not there yet, so I'm not thinking about that."
Suarez has one more start in the regular season, which he can treat as both a tuneup for himself and an audition for Game 2 in the best-of-three wild card round.,
"He's a very good competitor, a good pitcher that even when he gets traffic, you trust that he's going to find his way through it. He does that at times this year, so that's never a concern with him."

item.content:encoded:
Alec Gamboa, who played for the Lotte Giants in the KBO League last year. He failed to re-sign with Lotte, but a year later he debuted in the major leagues and is aiming to make the postseason roster.
On the 18th (Korean time) at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, in the game against the Texas Rangers, Gamboa came in with one out in the eighth inning and no runners on, recorded 2/3 of an inning, allowed one hit and no runs, and earned a hold. It was his second hold of the season.
That day Gamboa entered the game after Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run homer in the top of the eighth to put them up 4-3. Starter Sonny Gray pitched well with 6 1/3 innings, three hits (one home run), three walks, six strikeouts and three runs, and second pitcher Wyatt Alls recorded one inning, one strikeout and no runs.
Gamboa came in to face a left-handed batting lineup of Corey Seager and Josh Young. He gave up a single to the first batter, Seager, to right field. Later, he fell behind Josh Young 3-1 in the count but induced a shortstop grounder with a low 95.6-mph sinker, producing a double play to end the inning.
After recording his first hold in his debut by getting Lee Jung-hoo and others out in the Aug. 22 game against the San Francisco Giants, he recorded his second hold of the season. Gamboa's season performance is excellent. In 19 appearances he pitched 29 2/3 innings with 1 win, 2 holds, 1 save, a 1.21 ERA, a .216 batting average against and a 1.04 WHIP.
That day closer Aroldis Chapman could not take the mound because of trapezius muscle stiffness, and another lefty in the high-leverage group, Eric Miller, had earlier shown instability on the 17th against Texas by allowing three runs on 22 pitches in one inning. As a result, rookie right-hander Wyatt Alls and left-hander Gamboa had to take on the high-leverage roles, and setup man Garrett Whitlock had to assume the closer role. All of them then held the one-run lead.
Acting manager Chad Tracy praised Alls and Gamboa's high-leverage performances, saying, "They were really great. They were inserted suddenly into important situations. At times they had to take the mound with the lead, and they did really well."
Gamboa once again successfully passed a high-leverage test for the high-leverage group. Now the question is whether he can join Boston's postseason journey. Boston has a 83-70 record and sits second in the wild-card standings. They are five games ahead of the third-place Cleveland Guardians, so barring an upset they are all but certain to secure the 5 seed.
Over the Monster, which reports on Boston news, listed Gamboa in the "pitchers who need to prove themselves" spot while predicting the postseason roster. The outlet said, "He is a player who had a pleasantly surprising performance this year. He even made two starts as an opener. In recent weeks the bullpen has had injuries, and combined with his own performance, he has risen to the point of being used in higher-stakes, high-leverage situations."
Closers Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Eric Miller, Tyrone Guerrero and Garrett Crochet are confirmed. It is likely that one more left-handed reliever will be added and the rest filled with right-handers.
They went on to say, "If Aroldis Chapman, Eric Miller and Garrett Crochet are the confirmed left-handed bullpen pieces, the final left-handed spot could be a competition between Hobani Moran and Gamboa," and added, "If I had to pick the final four now, I would choose Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Moran and Gamboa," predicting they would make the postseason roster.
Boston regional outlet MassLive also highlighted the performances of Gamboa and Alls on the 17th, saying, "He seized an unexpected opportunity this year, expanded his standing, and his entry into the postseason roster race—which would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago—is worthy of high praise," introducing that Gamboa has performed well enough to be included on the postseason roster.
Gamboa was drafted by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the ninth round, 281st overall, in the 2019 draft. But he couldn't break through the Dodgers' deep minor league system, and last year he joined the KBO League's Lotte Giants as a replacement player and delivered a sensational performance.
He had an especially strong performance, including being named player of the month for June, but fatigue accumulated late in the season and elbow pain caused him to miss several turns in the rotation, preventing a smooth finish. His KBO League stats were 19 games, 108 innings, 7 wins, 8 losses and a 3.58 ERA.
Although Gamboa failed to re-sign with Lotte, he said of going to Lotte, "It was a good opportunity to show myself elsewhere. I wanted to experience a bigger and new environment than Triple-A in the U.S. I believed I would show good pitching there, return to the U.S. and seize another opportunity," and added, "Before going to Korea I had never been abroad. Experiencing another country, seeing how polite the people there are and how much they love baseball, and seeing what style of baseball they play was really fun," saying it was an opportunity that lifted his spirits.
Was failing to re-sign with Lotte a blessing in disguise? After signing a minor league deal with Boston he made an emotional big league debut and now stands on the verge of making the postseason roster. Gamboa is becoming a symbol of a life turnaround.
[OSEN]

Sonny Gray allowed three earned runs on three hits and three walks while striking out six over 6 1/3 innings in Thursday’s win over the Rangers.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox open up a three-game series against AL East rival Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, September 18, at Tropicana Field.
Ranger Suarez will get the ball for Boston tonight. After that, the pitching plans are unclear. The Red Sox have listed TBDs for their starting pitcher spot on Saturday and Sunday, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. Payton Tolle and Patrick Sandoval were lined up to start this weekend, but that is now in doubt.
Probable pitchers for Red Sox-Rays this weekend…
* Friday: Ranger Suarez vs. Ian Seymour* Saturday: TBD vs. Freddy Peralta* Sunday: TBD vs. Griffin Jax
Saturday would be Payton Tolle's day, if the Red Sox stay on turn. We'll see how they handle it.
— Tim Healey (@timbhealey) September 17, 2026
Tolle has already zoomed past his previous career high in innings as a pro. The lefty tossed 108 frames between the minors and majors in 2025. Tolle has thrown 158 innings across both levels this season.
Boston Red Sox May Skip Payton Tolle Against the Tampa Bay Rays
Tolle has been a fixture in Boston's rotation for much of the season. He's posted a 3.03 ERA across 25 starts with the big-league club. The young lefty opened the season in the minors, but was promoted to the majors in April. Tolle has solidified a pitching staff that has dealt with injuries and underperformance at times in 2026.
While he won't win AL Rookie of the Year, Tolle has put together a solid case. He's right up there with Cleveland Guardians left-hander Parker Messick as the top rookie starter in the American League. Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers and Munetaka Murakami of the Chicago White Sox are the betting favorites, but Tolle and Messick will receive some down-ballot votes.
Tolle struggled to a 6.06 ERA in his first taste of the big leagues last year. He missed bats at a decent 25.7% clip, but notched a 10.8% walk rate. The lefty has improved in both departments this season. Tolle pushed his strikeout rate to 28.9% and trimmed his walk rate to 6.6% in his first full campaign as a major league starter.
Red Sox Lining Up Postseason Rotation
Moving Tolle's next start could be an effort to align the playoff rotation. The pitching staff will likely be headlined by Sonny Gray, but the second and third slots are up for grabs. Suarez has a solid case to pitch the second game of the Wild Card round. The gig could also go to Tolle.
Sandoval and Jake Bennett are likely looking at long relief roles in the first round of the playoffs. Both have had decent stretches this season, but faded recently. Bennett has permitted a dozen runs in three September starts. Sandoval has a 7.82 ERA this month.
Brayan Bello is the question mark among the unit. He's struggled as a starter and been tremendous out of the bullpen. Bello could operate in tandem with one of Boston's many left-handed starters.

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses starter Sonny Gray joining Red Sox Hall of Famer Tim Wakefield in franchise history. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
The Boston Red Sox avoided a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers on Thursday night thanks to a 4-3 win that was powered by an eighth-inning, go-ahead, three-run home run off the bat of shortstop Trevor Story. While Story's big swing was undoubtedly the story of the game, Boston was in position to win because of Sonny Gray's fantastic start, a start that saw him join Red Sox Hall of Famer Tim Wakefield in the history books.
Gray tossed 6.1 innings, allowing just three earned runs on three hits while striking out six and walking three. According to Red Sox Nation Stats on Twitter/X, Gray became the first pitcher aged 36 or older to log 21 or more starts of six or more innings pitched since Wakefield did so in 2008.
Gray has been nothing short of a revelation since arriving in Boston on an offseason deal with the St. Louis Cardinals. The 36-year-old veteran was brought in, in part, to be the "Robin" to Garrett Crochet's "Batman." However, because of the shoulder injury that has kept Crochet out of the rotation since late April, Gray has served as "Batman" just as well as the 2025 American League Cy Young Award runner-up could have.
In Crochet's absence, Gray has posted a 2.57 ERA in 23 starts, spanning 140 innings pitched. The team has gone 17-6 in those starts. Not only has Gray been Boston's best starter since the Crochet injury, but he's also been one of the best arms in baseball in the stretch, with his ERA ranking as the sixth-lowest mark over that time.
Overall, Gray has posted a 2.82 ERA that ranks fifth best among all American League starters, doing it in 163 innings with an fWAR of 3.2 that sits just outside the top 10 at No. 11. Perhaps most importantly, even when the 36-year-old veteran doesn't have his best stuff, he keeps the team in a position to win, as was evident on Thursday night.
When Gray was first acquired, many questioned whether he could still be a top of the rotation arm. Now, after answering those questions with a season that'll likely see him finish top five in American League Cy Young Award voting, the only question that remains is whether he'll return for 2027 and beyond.
Up next for the Sox
After dropping two of three in Texas, the Red Sox' final regular-season road trip rolls on as they open a three-game series at Tropicana Field against the likely American League East champion Tampa Bay Rays on Friday night. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for Tampa Bay. First pitch is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are expected to have to pay up to keep a star pitcher beyond 2026. At the moment, Sonny Gray’s future in Beantown is very much in the air. The three-time All-Star is currently in his final year under contract. The two sides do, however, have a $30 million mutual option to extend his stay in Boston another year.
Despite this substantial salary, Gray would likely receive more money in the long term if he hit free agency. It was previously pointed out that the star would receive $10 million from the Red Sox if he declined the option. He could very well opt to collect the $10 million and then look for a lucrative multi-year deal elsewhere. If so, just how much money could the ace get in the winter?
Mass Live’s Chris Cotillo believes Gray could receive at least $75 million in the open market. “As a free agent, Gray’s renaissance season may position him to receive a lucrative deal that some in the industry expect to match or exceed the three-year, $75 million deal the Rangers gave to Nathan Eovaldi two winters ago,” writes Cotillo.
As the beat writer alludes to, Gray is experiencing a stellar campaign in his first season with the Boston Red Sox. The starter currently leads the American League with 17 wins and has posted a minuscule 2.82 ERA and 1.16 WHIP. Boston previously acquired the veteran in an offseason trade with the St. Louis Cardinals.
Boston Red Sox Hopeful Sonny Gray Returns to Team in 2027
While Gray could very well become a free agent, he has also recently admitted he is willing to return to the Boston Red Sox in 2027. As Cotillo reported, the pitcher claimed he was “definitely” open to signing an extension with the club. Craig Breslow, Boston’s president of baseball operations, will surely be looking to extend the star’s stay.
There is, however, a major wild card in all of this. Gray has recently hinted that he could very well retire soon. During a recent interview with The Boston Globe, the ace claimed that he would “be done in a heartbeat” if his family asked him to step away from the game.
Assuming the Boston Red Sox pitcher returns for his 15th MLB season and declines the mutual option, he should be positioned well in free agency, though. The upcoming starting pitching free agent class is not exactly super strong. Tarik Skubal is there, but Kevin Gausman and Freddy Peralta have seemingly hurt their values recently.
Boston Needs Star to Lead Team During Playoffs
For now, the Boston Red Sox will head towards the playoffs with Gray leading the way. Boston is currently in the fifth spot in the American League postseason standings. At the moment, they are projected to play against their bitter rivals, the New York Yankees, in the first round of the playoffs.
The veteran is likely to be the Boston Red Sox’s top starting pitcher during the upcoming postseason. The star leads the team’s rotation in wins, starts, innings, WAR, and ERA. He most recently allowed just three earned runs in six and a third innings during Boston’s victory on September 17.

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray has been one of the best hurlers in baseball this season, entering the weekend in the mix to win the American League Cy Young Award. While he’ll likely be pitching in October for Boston, keeping him long-term reportedly could be an issue.
MassLive.com‘s Chris Cotillo reports that Gray could command a three-year contract this winter, potentially in the range of $75 million total. It would be closely aligned to what Nathan Eovaldi received in December 2024 with the Texas Rangers.
The project salary for Gray is fairly reasonable given how well he’s performed on the mound this season. At a $25 million average annual value, he would be tied for 17th among the highest-paid starting pitchers in MLB.
Given the financial flexibility that Boston has, it should be a reasonable price to tack onto the Red Sox payroll in 2027. However, Cotillo also wrote that Gray disclosed in an interview with The Boston Globe that the 36-year-old will retire “in a heartbeat” if his family wants him to step away from baseball and be around them more.
Gray will turn 37 years old in November and he’s already pulled in more than $125 million in career MLB earnings, according to Spotrac.com. The Tennessee native has a home in Nashville, where his wife and their two children reside. He’s reportedly spent his off days visiting them and, per Cotillo, the Red Sox organization believes retirement is a real possibility.
If Gray retires, that creates an immediate void in the Red Sox rotation ahead of an MLB free agency class that is not particularly deep when it comes to proven starting pitchers. Assuming Tarik Skubal is outside of Boston’s price range, Trevor Rogers and Freddy Peralta are the top options expected to be available.

item.title: [MassLive.com] Why was Aroldis Chapman unavailable for Red Sox in win? Chad Tracy explains injury

That’s because one of them was unavailable due to a nagging — and previously undisclosed — injury. item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — When Trevor Story hit his clutch three-run homer to flip a two-run deficit into a one-run lead Thursday against the Rangers, interim manager Chad Tracy didn’t rush to get his two highest-leverage bullpen arms instantly ready. That’s because one of them was unavailable due to a nagging — and previously undisclosed — injury.
With Boston suddenly up, 4-3, Tracy used a pair of rookies (righty Wyatt Olds and lefty Alec Gamboa) to pitch the eighth, then turned things over to righty Garrett Whitlock in the ninth. For at least one night, Whitlock took the job of closer Aroldis Chapman, who has a tight lat muscle.
“He’s just dealing with some lat tightness we’re going to be conservative with,” Tracy said. “It’s getting better, but we’ve got to make sure it gets there. That’s why he wasn’t available tonight.”
Tracy said Chapman — who last pitched Saturday against the Royals — has been dealing with the injury for “a couple of days.” Asked if an injured list stint was possible for the All-Star, Tracy said: “We’re not doing that right now.”
“We’re just going to keep monitoring it and see where he’s at each day,” Tracy said. “Obviously, you know how diligent he is about his prep and getting in and getting treatment, so we’re just monitoring day-to-day.”
Chapman, 38, has had another stellar season in Boston, tallying 34 saves to go along with a 1.95 ERA and 68 strikeouts in 50 ⅔ innings over 52 games. He was one of two key Red Sox players with an injury concern Thursday; first baseman Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit on top of his right hand with a pitch.
Olds, who has a 1.23 ERA and 19 strikeouts in his first 12 MLB appearances since debuting last month, relieved Sonny Gray with one out in the seventh inning and the Sox trailing by two. He got two quick outs before Story’s three-run blast put Boston up 4-3. Olds got Ezequiel Duran to pop out to start the eighth before Gamboa entered for the left-on-left matchup against Corey Seager. Seager singled but Gamboa got Josh Jung to ground into an inning-ending double play five pitches later.
“They were awesome,” Tracy said. “Getting thrust into a big spot, going back out anyways, and then all of the sudden you’re going out with a lead. They did an amazing job.”
Whitlock then recorded his fourth save of the year, needing 12 pitches and getting a similar 6-4-3 double play to end the game.
“He’s great,” Tracy said. “He’s reliable. He’s done it before if Chappy’s down.”

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox removed first baseman Willson Contreras from Thursday’s 4-3 win against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, after he was hit in the hand by a 92.3 mph sinker from Jakob Junis in the eighth inning.
Following the game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said that Contreras suffered a bruised right hand and is day to day.
From Tim Healy of the Boston Globe on X: Willson Contreras has a bruised right hand, Chad Tracy said. He is day to day. X-rays were negative.
Contreras was asked about the injury after the game.
Boston Red Sox 1B Willson Contreras Makes Statement on Injury Following Win Over Rangers
Via Chris Cotillo on X: Willson Contreras: “Sore. Painful. My hand was numb for like five minutes. That was the reason I came out of the game. I have fractured, before, the same hand. It felt like a fracture. Thankfully, it’s not a fracture on the top of the bone. I’m just frustrated.”
Contreras went 1-for-3 with a single and a strikeout in Thursday’s win.
The Red Sox acquired Contreras from the St. Louis Cardinals over the offseason. He is under contract through 2027 and has a 2028 club option worth $20 million.
Contreras, 34, is having a spectacular first season with Boston, slashing .276/.387/.518 with 27 home runs and 81 RBI over 129 games.
Recapping Boston’s 4-3 Win Over Rangers
Trevor Story hit a three-run home run in the eighth inning as the Red Sox beat the Rangers 4-3 on Thursday.
Sonny Gray allowed three earned runs on three hits and three walks while striking out six over 6 1/3 innings.
Rangers designated hitter Josh Jung hit a solo home run in the first inning, giving Texas a 1-0 lead.
Danny Jansen hit an RBI single in the second inning. Evan Carter followed with an RBI sac bunt, increasing the Rangers’ lead to 3-0.
The Red Sox scored their first run of the game on a throwing error from Nicky Lopez in the second inning. Then Story delivered the big hit in the eighth inning.
The Rangers used seven pitchers in the game. Cody Bradford pitched the most of any of them, hurling 4 1/3 scoreless innings.

Josh Jung hit a solo home run for Texas (76-77), which fell a game behind the Houston Astros (77-76) at the top of
item.content:encoded:
Trevor Story hit a three-run homer in the eighth inning as the Boston Red Sox overcame a three-run deficit to defeat the Texas Rangers 4-3 on Thursday in Arlington, Texas.
Story’s blast came against Texas closer Jacob Latz (3-3) and erased a 3-1 deficit.
The victory allowed Boston (83-70) to avoid being swept in the three-game series and ended the Rangers’ four-game winning streak. Josh Jung hit a solo home run for Texas (76-77), which fell a game behind the Houston Astros (77-76) at the top of the American League West.
Wyatt Olds (2-0) earned the win by tossing one scoreless inning. Boston starter Sonny Gray allowed three runs on three hits in 6 1/3 innings. He struck out six and walked three.
Texas had the tying run on first with one out in the ninth, but Garrett Whitlock got Jake Burger to ground into a game-ending double play for his fourth save.
Danny Jansen had two of the Rangers’ four hits, including an RBI single.
Boston’s Willson Contreras left the game after he was hit by a pitch on his right hand in the eighth inning. Contreras leads the Red Sox with 27 home runs.
Jung hit a solo shot in the first inning to open the scoring. It was his 10th homer of the season.
Texas extended its lead to 3-0 in the third. After two walks and a sacrifice bunt, Jansen singled home Wyatt Langford, and Burger scored on Evan Carter’s sacrifice bunt.
The Red Sox got on the scoreboard in the seventh. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin walked, and Eaton took third on a flyout. A throwing error by second baseman Nicky Lopez on Roman Anthony’s grounder brought in Eaton.
In the eighth, Boston’s Wilyer Abreu walked and Contreras was hit by a Jakob Junis pitch. Latz entered and got Adley Rutschman to foul out before Story belted a 2-2 curveball to left-center, handing Boston a 4-3 lead. It was Story’s fourth homer of the year.
The Boston offense struggled in the first two games of the series. The Red Sox struck out 15 times as the Rangers won 4-2 on Tuesday, and the visitors were held to three hits in a 7-3 loss on Wednesday.
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Story reaparece con jonrón y completa remontada de los Medias Rojas
This browser does not support the video element.
ARLINGTON -- Trevor Story esperó más de cuatro meses para conectar su siguiente jonrón. Y llegó justo a tiempo para los Medias Rojas.
Story finalmente despertó con un cuadrangular de tres carreras que puso a Boston al frente en el octavo inning la noche del jueves, impulsando a los Medias Rojas a una victoria por 4-3 sobre los Rangers en el Globe Life Field y ayudándolos a evitar su primera barrida desde julio.
Wilyer Abreu abrió el octavo episodio con una base por bolas antes de que Willson Contreras fuera golpeado por un lanzamiento y saliera del juego, con Isiah Kiner-Falefa ingresando como corredor emergente. Story entonces atacó una curva de 80.3 mph y la mandó en línea entre los jardines izquierdo y central para su primer vuelacercas desde el 13 de mayo y su cuarto de la temporada.
Boston había comenzado a reducir la desventaja un capítulo antes. Después de boletos consecutivos a Caleb Durbin y Nate Eaton, Roman Anthony bateó un rodado para una jugada forzada que permitió anotar a Eaton. Un error en tiro del segunda base Nicky López en la jugada permitió que Anthony avanzara a la intermedia.
La remontada en las últimas entradas llegó después de que Sonny Gray mantuviera a los Medias Rojas a una distancia alcanzable pese a un complicado comienzo de su apertura.
El derecho de 36 años lanzó 6.1 entradas, permitiendo tres carreras y tres hits, con seis ponches y tres bases por bolas en 102 pitcheos, su mayor cantidad de la temporada, de los cuales 67 fueron strikes.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Trevor Story hit a three-run home run off All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning, capping a comeback from a three-run deficit as the Boston Red Sox beat Texas 4-3 on Thursday night and dropped the Rangers out of the AL West lead.
Texas (76-77) had won four straight games to gain a share of the lead but dropped one game behind Houston (77-76), which holds the tiebreaker. The Rangers trail by two games for the last AL wild card.
Boston (83-70) has a five-game lead for the top AL wild card and improved to 8-59 when trailing after seven innings. Texas dropped to 63-2 when leading after seven innings.
Latz (3-3) entered after Wilyer Abreu walked starting the eighth and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch from Jakob Junis.
Latz struck out Adley Rutschman and Story, who is from nearby Irving, reached down for Latz's second straight low curveball and drove the ball over the left-field wall for his fourth home run this season.
Boston’s Wyatt Olds (2-0) got three outs and Garrett Whitlock pitched the ninth for his fourth save in eight chances, getting Jake Burger to ground into a game-ending double play.
Josh Jung hit a first-inning homer off Sonny Gray, and Texas opened a 3-0 lead in the second on Danny Jansen's RBI single and Evan Carter's safety squeeze bunt.
Roman Anthony hit into a run-scoring forceout in the seventh.
Texas’ Cody Bradford followed a one-inning opener with 4 1/3 shutout innings, seeking his first major league since Sept. 18, 2024. He missed last season following elbow surgery.
Gray gave up three hits in 6 1/3 innings, throwing a season-high 102 pitches.
Up Next
Red Sox: LHP Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33) will go against LHP Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27) on Friday at Tampa Bay.
Rangers: RHP Kumar Rocker (5-11, 4.54) starts Friday against visiting Toronto and RHP Dylan Cease (11-5, 2.38).

item.content:encoded:
Trevor Story Saves Red Sox From Crushing Sweep With One Swing originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
For seven innings, the Boston Red Sox appeared headed toward a disastrous conclusion to their stay in Texas.
Trevor Story changed everything with one swing.
Story crushed a three-run home run in the eighth inning Thursday night, lifting Boston to a dramatic 4-3 victory over the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field. The comeback allowed the Red Sox to avoid a three-game sweep and improve to 83-70. Boston entered the seventh inning without a run and trailed 3-0. The Red Sox had managed only three hits through six innings and continued to waste the few scoring opportunities they generated.
Then the game suddenly flipped.
The Red Sox pushed across their first run in the seventh when Nate Eaton scored on a throwing error by Rangers second baseman Nicky Lopez. That cut the deficit to 3-1, but Boston still needed a much bigger response.
Story supplied it one inning later.
Trevor Story Delivers Red Sox's Biggest Swing
Wilyer Abreu opened the eighth with a single before Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch. Isiah Kiner-Falefa entered as a pinch runner, placing two runners aboard with one out.
Story then hammered Jacob Latz's offering 394 feet to left-center field.
The three-run blast turned a 3-1 deficit into a 4-3 advantage. It was Story's fourth home run of the season and accounted for three of Boston's four runs.
Story finished 2-for-4 and produced the Red Sox's only hit in seven at-bats with runners in scoring position. Boston recorded only five hits all night, making Story's timely power even more important.
The late rally rewarded starter Sonny Gray for keeping Boston close after a difficult beginning.
Texas scored once in the first inning on Josh Jung's solo home run before adding two more in the second. Gray settled down from there and held the Rangers scoreless over his final 4 1/3 innings. The veteran right-hander allowed three runs on three hits over 6 1/3 innings. He struck out six and walked three while throwing 102 pitches.
Red Sox Bullpen Protects One-Run Lead
Wyatt Olds recorded the final two outs of the seventh and returned for a scoreless eighth, earning his second victory of the season. Angel Gamboa completed the eighth before Garrett Whitlock handled the ninth. Whitlock issued a walk but did not allow a hit, securing his fourth save.
Boston's defense also turned two double plays, helping its pitching staff hold Texas to four hits.
The victory did not erase the disappointment of losing the first two games of the series. Texas still won the set after taking Monday's opener 4-2 and Tuesday's game 7-3.
It did, however, keep a frustrating trip from becoming a sweep at a critical point in the season.
For most of Thursday night, the Red Sox looked lifeless. Story needed only one pitch to completely rewrite the ending.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Trevor Story’s late home run helps Red Sox flip script on Rangers
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time. Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence wil
item.content:encoded:
This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time.
Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence will loom over the club in the days to come, Trevor Story once again proved that you can never count this Red Sox team out.
The veteran shortstop came through with a go-ahead three-run home run in the top of the eighth inning, flipping the script and giving the Red Sox a badly needed 4-3 win to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers.
Story’s shot came with one out against Rangers closer Jacob Latz, completing a three-run comeback and cutting Boston’s magic number to clinch a playoff spot to three with nine games remaining.
“To steal that last one is huge,” Story told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “It’s momentum we can ride out into Tampa.”
Prior to Story’s home run, Thursday was shaping up to be among the club’s worst losses of the season.
A hallmark of the offense’s struggles early in the year was a lot of empty, uncompetitive at-bats, tons of swing and miss and a general inability to make good contact. Even with the Rangers opting for a bullpen game led by Cody Bradford, whose fastball averages just 88.6 mph, the Red Sox couldn’t square anything up.
The Red Sox only managed two hits through the first five innings, both singles in the fourth inning. That put runners at the corners with two outs, but Jarren Duran grounded out to squander the opportunity.
It was a similar story in the sixth, when Wilyer Abreu singled and Adley Rutschman finally did some damage with a ground-rule double into the left-field gap. Had the ball stayed in play, Abreu probably would have scored, but instead the Red Sox had two men in scoring position for Story, who worked a full count and struck out to end the threat.
The offense did nothing to pick up Sonny Gray, who wasn’t perfect but did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
The veteran right-hander allowed a solo home run to Josh Jung with two outs in the first, and in the second he walked the first two batters of the inning, both of whom came around to score on an RBI bloop single by Danny Jansen and a run-scoring squeeze bunt by Evan Carter.
Gray settled down afterward and retired 14 of the last 16 batters he faced from the second inning into the seventh. He was charged with three runs over 6 1/3 innings and limited the Rangers to three hits and three walks with six strikeouts.
“I thought he was awesome,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. “The only blemish was the two walks, we kind of walked ourselves into the part of their lineup where they can play baseball a little bit with bunts and they drop a flare into center and there’s a safety squeeze, outside of that, that was a really, really good effort.”
Even when the Red Sox finally scored in the top of the seventh, they did so without recording a hit. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin led off with consecutive walks and Eaton advanced to third after Nick Sogard hit a rocket of a fly out to the center field wall. But with one out and a chance to fight back into the game, Roman Anthony grounded into a run-scoring fielder’s choice to make it 3-1. He advanced to second after the Rangers threw away the double-play attempt, but Mickey Gasper grounded out to end the inning.
Then came the eighth.
Once again the Red Sox got two men on base right away, with Abreu drawing a leadoff walk before Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch. He immediately left the game with the trainer and was replaced at first by Isiah Kiner-Falefa, but while the Red Sox worried about their slugger, the Rangers pulled Jakob Junis for their closer Latz, who has been among the most dominant closers in the American League this year.
Latz drew a pop out from Rutschman, but then Story stepped up to the plate and everything changed.
“You see one of our guys keeled over holding his hand and you’re down in the dumps seeing that and moments later the whole dugout erupts,” Tracy said. “We haven’t been doing much offensively for a few days and to get a swing right there and feel like you steal a game, it was enormous. Big emotion swing.”
With the lead in hand, Wyatt Olds and Alec Gamboa pitched a scoreless eighth, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable, Garrett Whitlock came on for the ninth and locked down the save for the win. Story and Sogard turned inning-ending double plays in both the eighth and the ninth to ensure the Rangers couldn’t mount one last comeback.
“Good teams find a way to win and we’ve been doing that in the second half and that’s kind of who you become,” Story said. “And you feel that momentum, you feel that vibe around the game and we never give up.”
X-rays negative, Chapman day-to-day
The Red Sox got some good news postgame when X-rays on Contreras’ hand came back negative.
“He’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “So we’ll just take it day to day and see how he is.”
Tracy also confirmed that Chapman has been dealing with some lat tightness for the past few days and they are taking a conservative approach.
“It’s getting better but have to make sure it gets there, that’s why he wasn’t available tonight,” Tracy said, adding that an IL stint isn’t being considered for Chapman right now.

item.dc:creator: Darryn Albert

item.content:encoded:
Instead of securing the bag this offseason, Sonny Gray might potentially be walking away from the bag.
The Boston Red Sox pitcher Gray could possibly retire after this season, Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com reported on Thursday. Cotillo notes that Gray has touched on the potential of retirement in recent interviews and adds that the Red Sox do not believe that Gray is making an empty threat.
However, Cotillo does add that some in the industry believe that Gray’s strong 2026 campaign could put him in a position to receive a new contract in the range of three years and $75 million (if Gray decides to keep pitching). You can read Cotillo’s full report on the situation here.
Gray is 36 years old now but is still very much at the top of his game. A three-time MLB All-Star, Gray has enjoyed a big-time resurgence this season, leading Major League Baseball with 17 wins to go along with a 2.76 ERA and a 1.17 WHIP through 27 starts.
As it stands right now, Gray has a $30 million mutual option with the Red Sox for the 2027 campaign. But with a $10 million buyout clause, Gray can easily decide to opt out and test free agency.
Gray is a 14-year veteran in an MLB landscape where pitchers can sometimes last into their early 40s. The right-hander also drew trade interest from some prominent teams at this year’s deadline, but he may stunningly be considering the possibility of walking away after the season.

item.content:encoded:
New Red Sox Rumors on Sonny Gray's Potential MLB FA Contract Amid Retirement Speculation
Sonny Gray is enjoying one of the best seasons of his career at 36 years old, and it could lead to a big payday in free agency — if he continues playing beyond the 2026 campaign.
According to Mass Live's Chris Cotillo, the Boston Red Sox's ace could command a deal similar to the three-year, $75 million deal the Texas Rangers gave Nathan Eovaldi two years ago.
But Gray isn't fully set on returning to baseball.
Cotillo noted that Gray said in an interview with The Boston Globe recently that he would retire "in a heartbeat" if his family gave any indication that they wanted him to be home year-round.
Cotillo added that those within the organization take Gray's talks of retirement seriously. He has spent off days this season visiting his family's home in Nashville, regardless of where the team is playing.
"We can get into that at another time but not right now," Gray said when asked about retirement, per Cotillo.
Whether Gray will call it quits after this year remains to be seen, but he'll look to finish off his renaissance season strong. He's tied for the best record in baseball at 17-5, notching a 2.76 ERA and 1.17 WHIP with 140 strikeouts.
With Gray's help, the Red Sox turned their season around and are now on the precipice of securing the second wild-card spot at 82-70.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Sonny Gray's Rumored Price Tag Shouldn't Scare Red Sox Off

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox made one of the very best moves in baseball for the 2026 season, despite the fact that some fans didn't initially believe in the deal.
While searching for a No. 2 starter last offseason, Boston turned to the St. Louis Cardinals and swung a deal for three-time All-Star Sonny Gray. With the Red Sox searching for another elite starter, some wondered if Gray was better suited for a mid-to-back of the rotation spot, rather than the No. 2 spot for a club with World Series aspirations. He has more than delivered and has been Boston's best starter all season. Gray's going to get Cy Young Award votes and Boston should do what it can to try to keep him in town beyond the 2026 season. If he plays, he'll cost a pretty penny. MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo reported that some in the industry believe Gray will get a deal in the range of three years and $75 million — or more — if he continues his career.
"As a free agent, Gray’s renaissance season may position him to receive a lucrative deal that some in the industry expect to match or exceed the three-year, $75 million deal the Rangers gave to Nathan Eovaldi two winters ago," Cotillo wrote. "Interestingly, though, Gray has not committed to pitching again in 2027. In a recent interview with The Boston Globe, Gray said he would retire 'in a heartbeat' if his family signaled that he was wanted back home year-round, even if that meant retiring after the end of this year."
The Red Sox Should Do Everything To Keep Sonny Gray
That's actually also the same deal that the Cardinals gave Gray before the 2024 season as well. He inked a three-year, $75 million pact that he's currently in the final year of. After the season, Gray has a $30 million mutual option for the 2027 season with a $10 million buyout. If Boston picks up its end of the buyout and Gray opts out, then the buyout would be forfeited.
Gray has pitched well enough in a Red Sox uniform to get paid again — if he keeps pitching. So far this season, he has a 17-5 record, 2.76 ERA and 4.0 wins above replacement in 156 2/3 innings pitched. When it comes to Gray, his age stands out at 36 years old. But it hasn't stopped him yet. The price of pitching has gone up in a big way. A deal with a $25 million annual value, as Cotillo pointed out, would be in the range of guys like Michael King, Sean Manaea, and Eovaldi. It would be just above guys like Aaron Nola, Seth Lugo, Robbie Ray and Luis Severino. Gray has been better than all of these guys so far this season.
When it comes to the Red Sox, there isn't as much pitching depth down in the minors as there once was. Over the last year, Boston has traded guys like Hunter Dobbins, Richard Fitts, Brandon Clarke, Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon, among others. Plus, Connelly Early was traded as well.
Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, and Jake Bennett are locks for the 2027 rotation. Johan Oviedo is someone who could play a role. Tanner Houck is another guy who could as well. We've seen all season how impactful injuries are to the rotation. You never have enough arms. A dependable veteran like Gray for the next few years should be a necessity. It's no guarantee that he pitches beyond the 2026 season, but if he does, it should be in a Boston uniform.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox magic number has been stubbornly stuck at five for the last couple of days, and while there's no real concern about them ultimately getting in, it would be nice to win tonight and knock that down to three (Red Sox win + Rangers loss).
Another reason it would be nice to win this game is because Sonny Gray is starting, and this is his second to last start before the postseason. Ideally, he'll be locking in for an excellent outing at the end of the month. Despite the loss last time out against the Royals, he still boasts a 17-5 person record, which is 12 games over .500, and also the exact number of games the team is over .500 at 82-70. (Make of that what you will.)
Lineup wise, Nick Sogard is back at second base after Isiah Kiner-Falefa got a start there last night. Also, with Texas throwing lefty Cody Bradford, Jahmai Jones is at DH instead of Mickey Gasper. As usual, we'll probably see a pinch hit to switch the platoon advantage there at some point in the game.

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox need something to change Thursday night. Putting Jarren Duran back in the lineup is a start.
Boston will turn to Duran in center field for Thursday's series finale against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field after he did not start Wednesday's 7-3 loss. The Red Sox have dropped the first two games of the series and enter Thursday at 82-70 with only 10 games remaining in the regular season.
Roman Anthony will remain in the leadoff spot and start in left field, while Jahmai Jones gets another opportunity at designated hitter. Wilyer Abreu, Willson Contreras and Adley Rutschman make up the middle of the order.
Christopher Smith of MassLive shared Boston's lineup shortly after it was released Thursday.
The complete Red Sox lineup:
- Roman Anthony, LF
- Jahmai Jones, DH
- Wilyer Abreu, RF
- Willson Contreras, 1B
- Adley Rutschman, C
- Trevor Story, SS
- Jarren Duran, CF
- Caleb Durbin, 3B
- Nick Sogard, 2B
Sonny Gray will start on the mound.
Red Sox bring Duran back for crucial series finale
Duran's return is one of the most notable changes from Wednesday's lineup. The 30-year-old was not in the starting nine Wednesday, when Boston used Nate Eaton in center field and Isiah Kiner-Falefa at second base.
Red Sox lineup: Anthony LF, Jones DH, Abreu RF, Contreras 1B, Rutschman C, Story SS, Duran LF, Durbin 3B, Sogard 2B, Gray P
— Christopher Smith (@SmittyOnMLB) September 17, 2026
Neither is starting Thursday.
Instead, Duran returns to center, Sogard takes over at second and Trevor Story moves up one spot in the order to hit sixth.
Boston could certainly use a spark.
The Red Sox entered Texas with an opportunity to strengthen their postseason position but instead have lost consecutive games to a Rangers team fighting for its own playoff life. Texas improved to 76-76 with Wednesday's victory and has won four consecutive games. The Rangers are only one game behind the Chicago White Sox for the final American League wild-card spot.
Boston remains in much better shape, holding the second AL wild card with a five-game cushion over Chicago entering Thursday. That cushion is significant. It isn't comfortable enough to keep losing.
The Red Sox have gone 5-5 over their last 10 games, and Thursday represents their final opportunity to leave Texas with something positive before the schedule moves into its final nine games.
Sonny Gray gets the ball with Red Sox needing a win
If there is a pitcher Boston would want on the mound in this situation, Gray makes a compelling case. The veteran right-hander enters Thursday with a 17-5 record and 2.76 ERA.
Texas will counter with left-hander Tyler Alexander, who enters at 5-2 with a 3.38 ERA. The left-handed starter helps explain some of Boston's lineup decisions.
Jones, a right-handed hitter, remains in the No. 2 spot after starting there Wednesday. Contreras gives Boston another right-handed bat in the cleanup position, while Rutschman follows him from the fifth spot.
Anthony remains atop everything.
Boston has continued trusting the rookie in the leadoff role during the most important stretch of the season, and that won't change with a left-hander on the mound Thursday.
The larger question is whether the Red Sox can finally turn opportunities into enough runs.
Boston's postseason position remains favorable, but the Rangers have provided a reminder of how quickly September can become uncomfortable.
A sweep would send the Red Sox into the final nine games on a three-game losing streak. A win would allow them to leave Texas with their playoff cushion intact and Gray having stopped the bleeding. With Duran back in the lineup, Boston is hoping Thursday looks considerably different from the first two nights of the series. First pitch from Globe Life Field is scheduled for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
Yesterday was a winning day on the diamond as both MLB plays that I put out came through for us and cashed. We only have about 10 games remaining for the teams. The playoffs are within reach for some teams, and others are looking at some options for the future. Tonight we have a game between one team that has already locked up their spot, the Red Sox, and another team still battling to try and get in, the Rangers.
The Boston Red Sox are 12 games above .500, and they have been one of the best teams in baseball over the past couple of months. They've been very streaky, winning multiple games at a time and moving up the standings. The Red Sox are currently sitting in the second spot in the Wild Card, and they control their own destiny. Much of the early-season problem was how the team was playing in Boston. They are just one game over .500 at home, but they are 11 games above on the road.
One guy who did excel in Fenway is tonight's starter, Sonny Gray. He has been good on the road as well and has put together one of the best seasons of his career. Gray is 17-5 with a 2.76 ERA and a 1.17 WHIP. This has been the most games he has ever won, and if it stands will be his second-lowest ERA ever. His road ERA is actually better than his home ERA, and his night games have been fantastic this season. He has thrown 13 innings this month and allowed just three earned runs. Gray faced the Rangers once this season, and he allowed just one earned run over six innings.
The Texas Rangers have a much more difficult path to the postseason. The team is .500 for the year, and there are questions about whether anyone who wins the American League West will finish the season with a winning record. They have chosen a great time to get hot, though, as they've won their past four games and are now tied with the Astros for the division lead. They are also just one game behind the White Sox for the final Wild Card spot. This game would go a long way for the team in getting closer to one of those two options.
Coming into the season, I was expecting the Rangers to be one of the better teams in the division, mostly due to their rotation. Jacob deGrom, Nathan Eovaldi, and MacKenzie Gore were guys I expected to give them a good chance in the majority of games. Tonight, though, the Rangers won't rely on their starters. They are sending out Tyler Alexander to start the game. He brings a 3.38 ERA and a 1.28 WHIP to the table over 66.2 innings. The Rangers have a rough bullpen with a collective 4.27 ERA.
I'm not really sure why the line is moving toward the Rangers for this game. Sonny Gray is a significantly better pitcher and way more reliable than anyone from the Rangers bullpen. The smart move, to me, is not to worry about the full game and just isolate when we can assume Gray will be on the hill. Give me the Red Sox through five innings.
